questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which list names parts of the lymphatic system?
options: Interstitial fluid, blood capillaries, the liver, and the kidneys
Lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymphatic tissue and organs, and red bone marrow
Plasma, arteries, veins, and the spleen
Lymph, lymphatic vessels, the heart, and the venae cavae
questions.why: The lymphatic system is made of lymph (the fluid), the lymphatic vessels that carry it, the tissues and organs that contain lymphatic tissue such as lymph nodes, the spleen, the thymus, and the tonsils, and the red bone marrow where lymphocytes are made. It has no pump of its own, which is why the heart is not on the list.
notes: Interstitial fluid and blood capillaries are where lymph comes from, and the liver and kidneys are organs of other systems. This list fits a question about where fluid leaks out before lymphatics pick it up.
Correct. Lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymphatic tissue and organs, and red bone marrow make up the lymphatic system.
The spleen is a lymphatic organ, but plasma, arteries, and veins belong to the cardiovascular system. Students pick this when they confuse the two circulations.

Lymph and lymphatic vessels belong, but the heart and venae cavae are parts of the cardiovascular system. Students pick this because lymph does end up in the blood heading to the heart, but it rejoins the blood at the subclavian veins and is no longer part of the lymphatic system there.
questions.answerText: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymphatic tissue and organs, and red bone marrow

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: What is the main difference between interstitial fluid and lymph?
options: Where the fluid is located
Whether the heart pumps the fluid
Whether the fluid contains red blood cells
Which organ secretes the fluid
questions.why: Interstitial fluid is the fluid that leaks out of blood capillaries and bathes the cells. Once that same fluid enters a lymphatic capillary, it is called lymph. So the difference is location rather than makeup: the name changes when the fluid moves from the tissue spaces into the lymphatic vessels.
notes: Correct. Interstitial fluid and lymph are the same fluid in different places.
The heart pumps neither fluid; lymph moves without a pump of its own. Being pumped by the heart is what separates blood from both of these fluids.

Neither interstitial fluid nor ordinary lymph normally carries red blood cells, since those stay inside blood vessels. Pick red blood cells as the difference for a question comparing blood with lymph.
Neither fluid is secreted by an organ; both come from fluid that filtered out of blood capillaries. Students choose this when they picture lymph nodes making lymph, but nodes only filter it.
questions.answerText: Where the fluid is located

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: What is chyle?
options: The liquid part of blood left after the cells are removed
Clear, watery lymph draining from the limbs
Milky, fat-rich lymph from the lacteals of the small intestine
Fluid in the spaces between cells before it enters a vessel
questions.why: Chyle is lymph that carries absorbed dietary fat. It forms in the lacteals, the lymphatic capillaries in the center of each intestinal villus, and the fat gives it a milky color. Chyle drains toward the cisterna chyli and then up the thoracic duct.
notes: The liquid part of blood is plasma. Plasma leaks out to form interstitial fluid, but it is not lymph, so pick it for a question about the fluid portion of blood.
Clear, watery lymph is ordinary lymph, like the lymph draining the limbs. Pick it if the question asks what lymph looks like when it carries no dietary fat.
Correct. Chyle is milky, fat-rich lymph from the lacteals.
Fluid between cells before it enters a vessel is interstitial fluid. It becomes lymph only after it enters a lymphatic capillary, so choose this for a question about interstitial fluid.
questions.answerText: Milky, fat-rich lymph from the lacteals of the small intestine

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Where do lymphatic capillaries begin?
options: Inside the lymph nodes
Inside the lumen of blood capillaries
At the cisterna chyli
In the tissue spaces between cells
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries start as tiny dead-end tubes in the tissue spaces, woven among the blood capillaries in nearly every tissue. Their job is to take up the excess interstitial fluid that leaks out of the blood capillaries. From there, lymph moves into collecting vessels, through lymph nodes, and on to the trunks and ducts.
notes: Lymph nodes lie along the collecting vessels, later in the route. Pick them if the question asks where lymph is filtered.
Lymphatic capillaries are separate from blood capillaries; they collect fluid that has already left the blood. Students pick this because the two kinds of capillary lie side by side.
The cisterna chyli is a sac in the abdomen at the start of the thoracic duct, near the end of the route. Choose it for a question about where the thoracic duct begins.
Correct. Lymphatic capillaries begin in the tissue spaces between cells.
questions.answerText: In the tissue spaces between cells

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which group lists tissues that all lack lymphatic capillaries?
options: The dermis, skeletal muscle, and the cornea
The intestinal villi, the dermis, and the lungs
Cartilage, the dermis, and the intestinal wall
Cartilage, the cornea, and the central nervous system
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries are found in nearly every tissue, but a few lack them. These include the central nervous system, cartilage, bone and red bone marrow, the cornea, and avascular tissue such as the epidermis. Cartilage, the cornea, and the central nervous system are the only set here where every item is on that list.
notes: The cornea fits, but the dermis and skeletal muscle both have lymphatic capillaries. Pick the dermis and muscle for a question about tissues that do drain lymph.
All three of these contain lymphatics. The intestinal villi even hold the specialized lacteals, so this set fits a question about tissues rich in lymphatic drainage.
Cartilage fits, but the dermis and the intestinal wall both contain lymphatic capillaries. Students choose this when they remember only one tissue from the list.
Correct. Cartilage, the cornea, and the central nervous system all lack lymphatic capillaries.
questions.answerText: Cartilage, the cornea, and the central nervous system

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Anchoring filaments tie a lymphatic capillary to what?
options: The surrounding tissue
The nearest lymph node
A nearby blood capillary
The basement membrane of the epidermis
questions.why: Anchoring filaments are fine filaments that attach the endothelial cells of a lymphatic capillary to the surrounding tissue. Because a lymphatic capillary has no blood pressure inside to hold it open, these filaments keep it from collapsing. When fluid builds up and the tissue swells, they pull on the cells and widen the gaps between them so fluid can enter.
notes: Correct. Anchoring filaments attach the capillary to the surrounding tissue.
Lymph nodes lie along collecting vessels farther down the route, not at the capillary. Choose a node for a question about where lymph is filtered.

Lymphatic and blood capillaries lie side by side but are not tied together; fluid passes from one to the other only by first entering the tissue spaces. Pick a blood capillary for a question about where interstitial fluid comes from.
The epidermis is avascular and has no lymphatic capillaries at all. Pick the epidermis for a question about tissues that lack lymphatics.
questions.answerText: The surrounding tissue

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: What are lacteals?
options: Blood capillaries in the intestinal villi that absorb sugars
Lymphatic capillaries in the intestinal villi that absorb dietary fat
Ducts that carry milk through the mammary glands
Lymph nodes along the intestine that filter chyle
questions.why: Lacteals are specialized lymphatic capillaries in the center of each villus of the small intestine. Dietary fats are too large to enter the blood capillaries, so the lacteals absorb them instead. The fat turns the lymph milky, and this milky lymph is called chyle.
notes: Each villus also contains blood capillaries, which take up sugars and amino acids. Pick these for a question about where absorbed sugars enter the blood.
Correct. Lacteals are the lymphatic capillaries of the villi that absorb dietary fat.
Ducts carrying milk in the breast are lactiferous ducts. The names look alike because both come from the Latin word for milk, but those ducts belong to the mammary glands.
Lymph nodes do filter lymph from the intestine, but they lie along collecting vessels, not in the villi. Choose nodes for a question about where intestinal lymph is filtered.
questions.answerText: Lymphatic capillaries in the intestinal villi that absorb dietary fat

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: How does a lymphatic capillary end in the tissues?
options: Open at both ends as part of a loop
Closed at one end, a blind ending
Joined at one end to an arteriole
Ending in a valve that opens into a vein
questions.why: A lymphatic capillary is a dead-end tube, closed at the end that sits in the tissue. Fluid enters through gaps between its overlapping endothelial cells rather than from an upstream vessel. Lymph then flows one way only, away from the tissues and toward the heart.
notes: Open at both ends describes a blood capillary, which links an arteriole to a venule as part of a loop. Pick it for a question about blood capillaries.
Correct. A lymphatic capillary has a blind ending, closed at one end.
Arterioles feed blood capillaries, not lymphatic capillaries. Students choose this when they assume lymphatic capillaries are built like blood capillaries.
Lymph does not enter veins at the capillary level; it is returned to the blood only at the end of the route, where the ducts join the subclavian veins.
questions.answerText: Closed at one end, a blind ending

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Compared with blood capillaries, how permeable are lymphatic capillaries?
options: Impermeable until a lymph node opens them
More permeable, admitting proteins, cells, and pathogens
Less permeable, admitting only water
Equally permeable, admitting the same small molecules
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries are built with loosely overlapping endothelial cells, so they are more permeable than blood capillaries. They take up fluid along with large items such as proteins, cells, pathogens, and even cancer cells. Blood capillaries, with more tightly joined cells, mostly let small molecules through.
notes: Lymphatic capillaries take in fluid directly from the tissues; lymph nodes lie farther along the route and only filter what arrives. Pick nodes for a question about filtering lymph.
Correct. Lymphatic capillaries are more permeable than blood capillaries.
Lymphatic capillaries are more permeable, not less. A wall that admits mostly small molecules describes a blood capillary.
Blood capillaries mostly pass small molecules, but lymphatic capillaries also take in proteins and cells. Students choose this when they assume all capillaries are alike.
questions.answerText: More permeable, admitting proteins, cells, and pathogens

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: How does the diameter of a lymphatic capillary compare with that of a blood capillary?
options: The lymphatic capillary is narrower
The lymphatic capillary is as wide as a lymphatic duct
The lymphatic capillary is wider
The two are the same width
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries are slightly wider than blood capillaries. Their larger size, together with their loosely overlapping endothelial cells, suits their job of taking up fluid along with large particles such as proteins and cells. Blood capillaries are narrow enough that red blood cells pass through nearly single file.
notes: Narrower describes the blood capillary, which is just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file. Pick narrower if the question asked about the blood capillary.
Lymphatic ducts are the largest lymphatic vessels, at the end of the route, and far wider than any capillary. Choose a duct for a question about the largest lymphatic vessel.
Correct. A lymphatic capillary is wider than a blood capillary.
They are not the same width. Students pick this when they assume all capillaries share one size.
questions.answerText: The lymphatic capillary is wider

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which structural feature keeps lymph moving one way in lymphatic collecting vessels?
options: Lacteals
Anchoring filaments
Lymph nodes
Valves
questions.why: Lymphatic collecting vessels contain many one-way valves, even more than veins have. The valves let lymph move forward toward the heart and close if it starts to slip backward. Because the lymphatic system has no pump of its own, the valves are what turn every squeeze from muscles or breathing into forward movement.
notes: Lacteals are the lymphatic capillaries in the intestinal villi that absorb dietary fat. Choose them for a question about where chyle forms.
Anchoring filaments tie lymphatic capillaries to the surrounding tissue and hold them open. Pick them for a question about what keeps a lymphatic capillary from collapsing.
Lymph nodes filter lymph along the collecting vessels, but they do not set its direction. Pick them for a question about where lymph is cleaned before returning to the blood.
Correct. Valves keep lymph flowing one way in the collecting vessels.
questions.answerText: Valves

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: In what order does lymph travel from the tissues toward the lymphatic trunks?
options: Lymph nodes, then lymphatic capillaries, then collecting vessels, then lymphatic trunks
Collecting vessels, then lymphatic capillaries, then lymph nodes, then lymphatic trunks
Lymphatic capillaries, then collecting vessels, then lymph nodes, then lymphatic trunks
Lymphatic capillaries, then lymph nodes, then lymphatic trunks, then collecting vessels
questions.why: Lymph moves into larger and larger vessels as it goes. It starts in the lymphatic capillaries in the tissue spaces, flows into collecting vessels, and passes through lymph nodes, which filter it along the way. Collecting vessels then merge into the lymphatic trunks, which empty into the two ducts and finally the subclavian veins.
notes: Lymph nodes filter lymph that has already been collected, so they cannot be the starting point. Lymph has to be picked up by capillaries before it reaches a node.
Collecting vessels receive lymph from the capillaries, so they cannot come first. The route always begins where fluid is taken up in the tissues.
Correct. Capillaries, collecting vessels, nodes, then trunks.
This puts collecting vessels last, but nodes sit along the collecting vessels, and trunks are formed when collecting vessels merge. Collecting vessels must come before both.
questions.answerText: Lymphatic capillaries, then collecting vessels, then lymph nodes, then lymphatic trunks

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Where does the fluid that becomes lymph come from?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid draining from the brain
Plasma pumped directly into lymphatic vessels by the heart
Fluid secreted by the lymph nodes
Interstitial fluid that leaked out of blood capillaries
questions.why: Blood capillaries constantly leak some fluid and plasma proteins into the tissue spaces, where it is called interstitial fluid. Not all of it returns to the blood capillaries, so lymphatic capillaries take up the extra. Once inside a lymphatic vessel it is called lymph, and it is eventually returned to the blood.
notes: Cerebrospinal fluid fills the ventricles and surrounds the brain and spinal cord. The central nervous system has no lymphatic capillaries, so choose this for a question about the fluid made by the choroid plexus.
The heart pumps blood through blood vessels only; it does not push plasma into lymphatic vessels. The lymphatic system has no pump of its own.
Lymph nodes filter lymph but do not produce the fluid. Pick nodes for a question about where lymph is cleaned along its route.
Correct. Lymph begins as interstitial fluid that leaked from blood capillaries.
questions.answerText: Interstitial fluid that leaked out of blood capillaries

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which statement best describes lymph?
options: Fluid secreted into the small intestine by the liver
Interstitial fluid once it has entered a lymphatic vessel
Fluid that circulates through the ventricles of the brain
The liquid part of blood flowing in the arteries
questions.why: Lymph is interstitial fluid that has entered a lymphatic vessel. Ordinary lymph is clear and watery and carries proteins, cells such as lymphocytes, and anything else it picked up in the tissues. It travels one way through the lymphatic vessels and is returned to the blood at the subclavian veins.
notes: Fluid sent into the small intestine by the liver is bile, which helps break up fats. It fits a question about the liver's digestive secretion.
Correct. Lymph is interstitial fluid that has entered a lymphatic vessel.
Fluid in the brain's ventricles is cerebrospinal fluid, made by the choroid plexus. Choose it for a question about the fluid around the brain and spinal cord.
The liquid part of blood is plasma. Some plasma leaks out to become interstitial fluid, but in the arteries it is still plasma, so pick this for a question defining plasma.
questions.answerText: Interstitial fluid once it has entered a lymphatic vessel

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which vessels carry chyle?
options: The lacteals of the small intestine
The lymphatic capillaries of the lower limbs
The blood capillaries of the intestinal villi
The lymphatic capillaries of the lungs
questions.why: Chyle is milky, fat-rich lymph, and it forms in the lacteals, the lymphatic capillaries in the center of each villus of the small intestine. Dietary fats are too large to enter the blood capillaries, so the lacteals pick them up. Chyle then drains to the cisterna chyli and up the thoracic duct.
notes: Correct. The lacteals of the small intestine carry chyle.
Lymphatic capillaries of the lower limbs carry ordinary lymph, which is clear and watery. Choose them for a question about lymph that drains into the lumbar trunks.
The blood capillaries of the villi absorb sugars and amino acids into the blood. Fats are too large for them, so pick these for a question about where sugars are absorbed.
Lymphatic capillaries of the lungs carry ordinary lymph to the bronchomediastinal trunks. They fit a question about lymph from the thoracic organs, not fat-rich chyle.
questions.answerText: The lacteals of the small intestine

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: What lets interstitial fluid flow into a lymphatic capillary but not back out?
options: The valves of the collecting vessels downstream
A thick smooth muscle wall around the capillary
Overlapping endothelial cells that act as flap valves
Anchoring filaments that seal the capillary shut
questions.why: The endothelial cells of a lymphatic capillary overlap loosely at their edges like shingles. When fluid pressure in the tissue is higher, the edges swing inward and fluid enters. When pressure inside the capillary rises, the edges are pressed together and close, so fluid cannot leak back out into the tissue.
notes: Valves in the collecting vessels stop lymph from flowing backward along the vessels, but they are farther down the route. They do not control entry into the capillary from the tissue.

Lymphatic capillaries have a very thin wall of endothelium with no smooth muscle layer. Smooth muscle appears in the walls of larger lymphatic vessels, so pick it for a question about what helps move lymph along larger vessels.
Correct. Overlapping endothelial cells act as one-way flap valves at the capillary wall.

Anchoring filaments hold the capillary open and pull the gaps wider when fluid builds up. They do the opposite of sealing it, so choose them for a question about what keeps the capillary from collapsing.
questions.answerText: Overlapping endothelial cells that act as flap valves

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which statement about lymphatic capillaries is true?
options: They are held open by anchoring filaments tied to the tissue
They have a smaller diameter than blood capillaries
They are less permeable than blood capillaries
They are open at both ends like a continuous tube
questions.why: A lymphatic capillary has no blood pressure inside to hold it open, so anchoring filaments attach its endothelial cells to the surrounding tissue. When fluid collects and the tissue swells, the filaments pull the cells apart and let more fluid in. The capillary is also blind-ended, wider than a blood capillary, and more permeable.
notes: Correct. Anchoring filaments tie lymphatic capillaries to the surrounding tissue and hold them open.
Lymphatic capillaries are slightly wider than blood capillaries, not narrower. A smaller diameter describes the blood capillary, which red blood cells pass through nearly single file.
Lymphatic capillaries are more permeable than blood capillaries, letting in proteins, cells, and pathogens. This reverses the comparison.
Being open at both ends describes a blood capillary, which links an arteriole to a venule. Lymphatic capillaries are closed at one end, so pick this for a question about blood capillaries.
questions.answerText: They are held open by anchoring filaments tied to the tissue

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: What do anchoring filaments do when interstitial fluid builds up in a tissue?
options: They seal the capillary so no fluid can enter
They pull the endothelial cells apart so more fluid enters
They pump lymph toward the heart
They form the valves inside the collecting vessels
questions.why: When fluid collects in a tissue, the tissue swells and stretches the anchoring filaments. Because the filaments are tied to the endothelial cells of the lymphatic capillary, they pull those cells apart and widen the gaps between them. More fluid can then flow in, which helps drain the swelling.
notes: Sealing the capillary would stop drainage just when it is needed most. Anchoring filaments do the opposite, opening the capillary wider.
Correct. Anchoring filaments pull the endothelial cells apart so more fluid can enter.
Anchoring filaments do not pump. Lymph is moved by outside forces such as the skeletal muscle pump and the respiratory pump, so pick those for a question about what pushes lymph along.
The valves in collecting vessels are folds of the vessel lining, not anchoring filaments. Choose valves for a question about what keeps lymph from flowing backward.
questions.answerText: They pull the endothelial cells apart so more fluid enters

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which vessels carry lymph directly out of the lymphatic capillaries?
options: The subclavian veins
The thoracic duct
Lymphatic collecting vessels
Lymphatic trunks
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries drain into collecting vessels, the next step on the route. Collecting vessels are built like small veins, with thin walls and many valves, and they pass through lymph nodes as they go. Only later do they merge to form the larger lymphatic trunks.
notes: The subclavian veins are where the lymphatic ducts finally return lymph to the blood. They fit a question about the last step of the route.
The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel, near the end of the route. Choose it for a question about where most trunks empty.
Correct. Collecting vessels carry lymph directly from the lymphatic capillaries.
Lymphatic trunks form when many collecting vessels merge, after the lymph has passed through nodes. Pick trunks for a question about the large vessels that each drain a major region.
questions.answerText: Lymphatic collecting vessels

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three main jobs of the lymphatic system?
options: Transporting dietary fats
Carrying out immune defense
Draining excess interstitial fluid
Pumping oxygenated blood to the tissues
questions.why: The lymphatic system has three jobs: returning leaked fluid and proteins to the blood (fluid balance), absorbing dietary fats through the lacteals, and defending the body through lymph nodes, the spleen, tonsils, and MALT. Pumping oxygenated blood is the work of the heart and arteries. The lymphatic system has no pump at all.
notes: Transporting dietary fats is a real lymphatic job, done by the lacteals of the small intestine. It would be the answer to a question about what lacteals do.
Immune defense is a real lymphatic job, carried out in lymph nodes, the spleen, tonsils, and MALT. It would answer a question about what lymphocytes and macrophages do there.

Draining excess interstitial fluid is a real lymphatic job, called fluid balance, done by lymphatic capillaries in nearly every tissue. It would be the answer if the question asked which job keeps blood volume steady.
Correct. Pumping oxygenated blood is the job of the heart and arteries, not the lymphatic system.
questions.answerText: Pumping oxygenated blood to the tissues

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: A vessel is described as a blind-ended tube in the tissue spaces that is more permeable than a blood capillary. Which vessel is it?
options: A lymphatic collecting vessel
A lymphatic trunk
A blood capillary
A lymphatic capillary
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries are the only vessels in this list that begin as dead-end tubes in the tissue spaces. Their loosely overlapping endothelial cells make them more permeable than blood capillaries, so they can take up fluid along with proteins and cells. Every other lymphatic vessel receives lymph from somewhere upstream.
notes: A collecting vessel carries lymph onward from the capillaries and has valves. It is not blind-ended, so pick it for a question about the vessels that pass through lymph nodes.
A lymphatic trunk is a large vessel formed by merging collecting vessels, draining a whole region. Choose it for a question about the vessels that empty into the ducts.
A blood capillary is open at both ends, linking an arteriole to a venule, and is less permeable. It fits a question about exchange vessels of the blood.
Correct. A blind-ended, highly permeable tube in the tissue spaces is a lymphatic capillary.
questions.answerText: A lymphatic capillary

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: After a fatty meal, a vessel in the center of an intestinal villus fills with milky fluid. What is the vessel, and what is the fluid?
options: A lymph node holding lymph
A collecting vessel carrying bile
A lacteal carrying chyle
A blood capillary carrying plasma
questions.why: The lymphatic capillary in the center of each villus is a lacteal. Dietary fats are too large to enter the blood capillaries of the villus, so the lacteal absorbs them, and the fat turns the lymph milky. That milky, fat-rich lymph is called chyle.
notes: Lymph nodes sit along collecting vessels and filter lymph, not in the center of a villus. Choose a node for a question about where intestinal lymph is filtered.
Bile is made by the liver and carried in bile ducts to the duodenum, never in lymphatic vessels. It fits a question about the liver's digestive secretion.
Correct. The milky fluid in the center of a villus is chyle in a lacteal.
Blood capillaries in the villus carry plasma and absorb sugars and amino acids, but the fat is too large for them. Pick this pair for a question about where absorbed sugars enter the blood.
questions.answerText: A lacteal carrying chyle

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which of these tissues has no lymphatic capillaries?
options: Skeletal muscle
The dermis of the skin
The wall of the intestine
The cornea
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries are found in nearly every tissue, but the cornea is one of the few without them. The others include the central nervous system, cartilage, bone and red bone marrow, and avascular tissue such as the epidermis. The cornea has no blood vessels either, which helps keep it transparent.
notes: Skeletal muscle has lymphatic capillaries in the connective tissue around its fibers. Choose it for a question about tissues where the skeletal muscle pump pushes lymph along.
The dermis is a vascular connective tissue layer with many lymphatic capillaries. Pick it for a question about which skin layer drains lymph.
The intestinal wall is rich in lymphatics, including the lacteals in the villi. It fits a question about where dietary fat enters the lymph.
Correct. The cornea has no lymphatic capillaries.
questions.answerText: The cornea

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which lymphatic job is carried out by the lymphatic capillaries in nearly every tissue?
options: Returning excess interstitial fluid to the blood
Absorbing dietary fats
Producing red blood cells
Filtering lymph and housing lymphocytes
questions.why: Blood capillaries leak more fluid and protein into the tissues than they take back. Lymphatic capillaries in nearly every tissue pick up that excess and return it to the blood, about 3 liters a day, which keeps fluid from building up in the tissues and keeps blood volume steady. This job is called fluid balance.
notes: Correct. Lymphatic capillaries in nearly every tissue drain excess interstitial fluid back to the blood.
Absorbing dietary fats is done only by the lacteals in the small intestine, not by lymphatic capillaries everywhere. Pick it for a question about what lacteals do.
Red blood cells are made in the red bone marrow, not by lymphatic capillaries. Pick this for a question about where blood cells form.
Filtering lymph and housing lymphocytes happens in lymph nodes, the spleen, tonsils, and MALT. Choose it for a question about the defense job of the system.
questions.answerText: Returning excess interstitial fluid to the blood

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: How does the wall of a lymphatic collecting vessel compare with the wall of a vein?
options: Thicker walls with fewer valves
The same walls but with no valves
A muscular pumping chamber in place of valves
Thinner walls with more valves
questions.why: Collecting vessels are built like veins, with three thin layers, but their walls are thinner and they have more valves. The extra valves matter because lymph moves under very low pressure with no pump of its own. Each valve stops lymph from slipping backward between squeezes from muscles and breathing.
notes: This reverses both features. Thicker walls with fewer valves would describe a vein compared with a collecting vessel.

Collecting vessels have many valves, more than veins, so they cannot be valveless. Students choose this when they confuse collecting vessels with lymphatic capillaries, which rely on overlapping endothelial cells instead.
The lymphatic system has no pumping chamber; lymph is moved by outside forces like the skeletal muscle and respiratory pumps. A muscular pumping chamber describes the heart.
Correct. Collecting vessels have thinner walls and more valves than veins.
questions.answerText: Thinner walls with more valves

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Where are lacteals located?
options: In the villi of the small intestine
In the lobules of the liver
In the gastric pits of the stomach lining
In the mucosa of the large intestine
questions.why: Lacteals are lymphatic capillaries that run up the center of each villus, the finger-like folds of the small intestine's lining. That is where dietary fats are absorbed, and fats are too large to enter the blood capillaries of the villus. The lacteals take them up instead, forming chyle.
notes: Correct. Lacteals run up the center of each intestinal villus.
Liver lobules are the functional units of the liver, built around a central vein. They fit a question about liver structure, not fat absorption.
Gastric pits are openings in the stomach lining that lead to the gastric glands. Pick them for a question about where stomach secretions are released.
The large intestine lacks villi, so it has no lacteals. Choose the large intestine for a question about where water is absorbed from the remaining waste.
questions.answerText: In the villi of the small intestine

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which of these tissues would you expect to contain lymphatic capillaries?
options: The central nervous system
The epidermis
The dermis of the skin
Hyaline cartilage
questions.why: The dermis is a vascular connective tissue layer with blood capillaries, and lymphatic capillaries lie among them to drain the fluid that leaks out. The other tissues listed are among the few that lack lymphatic capillaries: avascular tissue such as the epidermis, cartilage, and the central nervous system.
notes: The central nervous system has no lymphatic capillaries. It fits a question about tissues where lymphatic capillaries are absent.
The epidermis is avascular epithelium, with no blood vessels or lymphatic capillaries. Pick it for a question about a skin layer that gets nutrients by diffusion from the dermis.
Correct. The dermis contains lymphatic capillaries.
Hyaline cartilage is avascular and has no lymphatic capillaries. Choose it for a question about a tissue that heals slowly because it lacks blood vessels.
questions.answerText: The dermis of the skin

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Chyle looks milky white rather than clear. What in it explains this?
options: Its high dietary fat content
Dissolved oxygen
A high red blood cell count
A large number of platelets
questions.why: Chyle is lymph from the lacteals of the small intestine, and it carries absorbed dietary fats. The fat droplets scatter light and give the fluid its milky color. Ordinary lymph, which carries little fat, is clear and watery.
notes: Correct. The dietary fat in chyle makes it milky.
Dissolved oxygen does not change the color of a fluid this way. Oxygen bound to hemoglobin is what makes arterial blood bright red.
Red blood cells would color the fluid red, and they stay inside blood vessels rather than entering lymph. Pick red cells for a question about why blood is red.
Platelets are tiny cell fragments in blood that help it clot. They do not make lymph milky, so choose them for a question about clotting.
questions.answerText: Its high dietary fat content

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which statement best explains why the lymphatic system is closely linked with the circulatory system?
options: It replaces the veins as the return route from the legs
It pumps arterial blood out to the tissues alongside the heart
It drains fluid leaked from the blood and returns it to the veins
It makes red blood cells inside its own vessels
questions.why: The fluid in lymphatic vessels starts as plasma that leaked out of blood capillaries. The lymphatic system collects that excess fluid and its proteins and returns them to the blood where the lymphatic ducts empty into the subclavian veins. Without this return, fluid would build up in the tissues and blood volume would fall.
notes: Lymphatic vessels run alongside veins, but they do not replace them. Superficial collecting vessels travel with the superficial veins, which fits a question about where those vessels run.
The lymphatic system has no pump and carries no arterial blood. Lymph moves through outside forces such as the skeletal muscle and respiratory pumps.
Correct. The lymphatic system returns fluid that leaked from the blood back into the venous blood.
Red blood cells are made in red bone marrow, not inside lymphatic vessels. Red bone marrow fits a question about where blood cells and lymphocytes form.

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: How does ordinary lymph (not chyle) look?
options: Bright red
Clear and watery
Milky white
Greenish yellow
questions.why: Ordinary lymph is interstitial fluid that has entered a lymphatic vessel, so it looks much like the clear, watery fluid that bathes the cells. It carries proteins and white blood cells but no red blood cells. Only lymph from the small intestine, chyle, turns milky because of absorbed fat.
notes: Bright red is the color of oxygen-rich blood, colored by hemoglobin in red blood cells. Lymph normally has no red blood cells.
Correct. Ordinary lymph is clear and watery.
Milky white describes chyle, the fat-rich lymph from the lacteals of the small intestine. Pick it for a question about lymph after a fatty meal.
Greenish yellow is the color of bile, made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder. It fits a question about the fluid released into the duodenum.

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which list names the five kinds of lymphatic trunks?

Femoral, mesenteric, pulmonary, brachial, and jugular
Lumbar, intestinal, thoracic, axillary, and cervical
Lumbar, intestinal, bronchomediastinal, subclavian, and jugular

The digestive organs of the abdomen
The upper limbs
The head and neck

The lower limbs and pelvis
The head and neck

The left jugular and left subclavian trunks
The two lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk
The right jugular, right subclavian, and right bronchomediastinal trunks

The upper left side of the body and everything below the diaphragm
Only the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdomen
The right side of the head, neck, and thorax and the right upper limb

Directly into the right atrium
At the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins
At the junction of the right subclavian and right internal jugular veins

The intestinal, right jugular, and right subclavian trunks
The left jugular, left subclavian, and left bronchomediastinal trunks

questions.q: Which is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body?
options: The intestinal trunk
The right lymphatic duct
The lumbar trunk
The thoracic duct
questions.why: The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel. It begins at the cisterna chyli in the abdomen, runs up through the thorax, and empties at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins. questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Lymph has no heart of its own. Which two named pumps help keep it moving?
options: The left ventricle and the right ventricle
The skeletal muscle pump and the lymph node pump
The respiratory pump and the splenic pump
The skeletal muscle pump and the respiratory pump
questions.why: The skeletal muscle pump works when contracting muscles squeeze nearby lymphatic vessels. The respiratory pump works through pressure changes in the thorax with each breath. Smooth muscle in larger lymphatic walls and the pulsing of nearby arteries help too, and valves make sure all of this pushes lymph one way, toward the heart.
notes: The ventricles pump blood, not lymph; the lymphatic system has no pump of its own. Pick the ventricles for a question about which chambers pump blood out of the heart.
The skeletal muscle pump is real, but lymph nodes filter lymph rather than pump it. Pick nodes for a question about where lymph is cleaned.
The respiratory pump is real, but the spleen filters blood and does not pump lymph. Choose the spleen for a question about removing old red blood cells.
Correct. The skeletal muscle pump and the respiratory pump help move lymph.
questions.answerText: The skeletal muscle pump and the respiratory pump

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: How does the skeletal muscle pump move lymph?
options: Contracting skeletal muscles squeeze nearby lymphatic vessels
Nearby arteries pulse against the lymphatic vessels
Pressure in the thorax changes with each breath
Smooth muscle in the walls of larger lymphatic vessels contracts in rhythm
questions.why: When skeletal muscles contract, they bulge and squeeze the lymphatic vessels running between them. That squeeze pushes lymph along, and the valves make sure it can only move forward toward the heart. This is why movement and exercise speed lymph flow, and why long periods of sitting still let fluid collect in the legs.
notes: Correct. The skeletal muscle pump works by contracting muscles squeezing lymphatic vessels.
Pulsing of nearby arteries also nudges lymph along, but that push comes from the heartbeat, not from skeletal muscles. Pick it for a question about how arteries next to lymphatic vessels help.
Pressure changes in the thorax with each breath describe the respiratory pump. Pick this for a question about how breathing moves lymph.

Rhythmic contraction of smooth muscle in the walls of larger lymphatic vessels is a real mechanism, but it comes from the vessel itself, not from skeletal muscle. Choose it for a question about how lymphatic vessels help move lymph on their own.
questions.answerText: Contracting skeletal muscles squeeze nearby lymphatic vessels

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: How does the respiratory pump move lymph?
options: The lungs pump lymph out through the bronchomediastinal trunks
Contracting leg muscles squeeze the lymphatic vessels
Each breath pushes air into the lymphatic vessels
Pressure changes in the thorax with each breath move lymph upward
questions.why: With each breath, pressure in the thorax rises and falls. During inhalation the pressure in the thorax drops, and lymph is drawn from the abdominal vessels up into the thoracic duct. Valves keep it from sliding back down, so every breath helps move lymph toward the heart.
notes: The lungs do not pump lymph; the bronchomediastinal trunks simply drain the thoracic organs and wall. Pick those trunks for a question about lymph from the lungs and heart.
Contracting leg muscles squeezing the vessels is the skeletal muscle pump. Choose this for a question about how exercise speeds lymph flow.
Air stays in the airways and never enters lymphatic vessels. The respiratory pump works through pressure changes, not by moving air into the vessels.
Correct. Pressure changes in the thorax with breathing move lymph toward the heart.
questions.answerText: Pressure changes in the thorax with each breath move lymph upward

The right bronchomediastinal trunk drains the right side of the thoracic organs and wall. Choose it for lymph from the right lung.
questions.answerText: The right jugular trunk

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which of these is a lymphatic duct rather than a trunk?
options: The jugular trunk
The lumbar trunk
The subclavian trunk
The right lymphatic duct
questions.why: There are only two lymphatic ducts, the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct. They are the last vessels on the lymph route, receiving lymph from the trunks and emptying it into the veins of the neck. The trunks come one step earlier, each draining one major region.
notes: The jugular trunk is a trunk that drains the head and neck. Choose it for a question about lymph from the face or scalp.
The lumbar trunk is a trunk that drains the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdominal wall. It fits a question about lymph from the legs.
The subclavian trunk is a trunk that drains the upper limb. It would be the answer for a question about which trunk drains the arm.
Correct. The right lymphatic duct is one of the two lymphatic ducts.
questions.answerText: The right lymphatic duct

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which region does the thoracic duct NOT drain?
options: Everything below the diaphragm
The right upper limb
The left upper limb
The left side of the head and neck
questions.why: The thoracic duct drains about three quarters of the body: everything below the diaphragm plus the upper left side. The upper right quarter, which includes the right upper limb and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax, drains into the right lymphatic duct instead. So the right arm is the region outside the thoracic duct's territory.
notes: Everything below the diaphragm drains into the thoracic duct through the lumbar and intestinal trunks. It fits a question about the cisterna chyli.
Correct. The right upper limb drains into the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.
The left upper limb drains through the left subclavian trunk into the thoracic duct. It would be the answer for a question about a region the thoracic duct does drain.
The left side of the head and neck drains through the left jugular trunk into the thoracic duct. Choose it for a question about lymph that enters the thoracic duct in the neck.
questions.answerText: The right upper limb

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Where do the lymphatic ducts return lymph to the bloodstream?
options: Into the inferior vena cava in the abdomen
Directly into the right atrium of the heart
Where the subclavian and internal jugular veins meet
Into the hepatic portal vein near the liver
questions.why: The last step on the lymph route is the return to the blood. Each lymphatic duct empties where a subclavian vein meets an internal jugular vein, low in the neck: the thoracic duct on the left and the right lymphatic duct on the right. From there the lymph travels with venous blood to the heart.
notes: The inferior vena cava returns blood from the lower body, but the lymphatic ducts do not empty into it. Pick it for a question about where blood from the legs returns.
The right atrium receives blood from the venae cavae and coronary sinus, not directly from lymphatic vessels. Choose it for a question about where systemic venous blood enters the heart.
Correct. The ducts empty at the junctions of the subclavian and internal jugular veins.
The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the digestive organs to the liver. It fits a question about the portal system, not the lymph route.
questions.answerText: Where the subclavian and internal jugular veins meet

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: During a workout, a weightlifter's repeated muscle contractions speed lymph return from the limbs. Which mechanism is at work?
options: The respiratory pump
The skeletal muscle pump
Smooth muscle in the lymphatic vessel walls
Pulsing of nearby arteries
questions.why: Each time a skeletal muscle contracts, it bulges and squeezes the lymphatic vessels around it, pushing lymph forward. The valves in the vessels keep it from flowing back when the muscle relaxes. Repeated contractions, as in lifting or walking, act like a series of squeezes that speed lymph toward the heart.
notes: The respiratory pump works through pressure changes in the thorax with each breath, not through the squeeze of working limb muscles. Pick it for a question about how breathing moves lymph.
Correct. Contracting skeletal muscles squeezing the vessels is the skeletal muscle pump.

Smooth muscle in the walls of larger lymphatic vessels contracts in its own rhythm, so it does not depend on the weightlifter's muscle contractions. Pick it for a question about how the vessels themselves help move lymph.

Pulsing of nearby arteries does help move lymph, but that push comes from the heartbeat, not from the weightlifter's skeletal muscles. Choose it for a question about how arteries next to lymphatic vessels help.
questions.answerText: The skeletal muscle pump

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: About how much of the body does the thoracic duct drain?
options: About half
About three quarters
All of it
About one quarter
questions.why: The thoracic duct drains everything below the diaphragm plus the upper left side of the body, which adds up to about three quarters. The remaining quarter, the right upper limb and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax, drains into the right lymphatic duct. That uneven split is why the thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel.
notes: Students choose half when they picture the body split evenly into right and left sides. The split is uneven, because the thoracic duct takes the whole lower body from both sides.
Correct. The thoracic duct drains about three quarters of the body.
The right upper limb and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax drain into the right lymphatic duct, so the thoracic duct does not drain all of the body.
About one quarter is the share drained by the right lymphatic duct, the upper right quarter of the body. Pick it for a question about the right lymphatic duct.
questions.answerText: About three quarters

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Lymph from the left lung passes through which trunk on its way to a duct?
options: The intestinal trunk
The left jugular trunk
The left subclavian trunk
The left bronchomediastinal trunk
questions.why: The lungs are thoracic organs, and the bronchomediastinal trunks drain the thoracic organs and wall. Lymph from the left lung therefore enters the left bronchomediastinal trunk. That trunk empties into the thoracic duct.
notes: The intestinal trunk drains the digestive organs of the abdomen. It fits a question about lymph from the stomach and intestines.
The left jugular trunk drains the left side of the head and neck. Choose it for lymph from the left side of the face or scalp.
The left subclavian trunk drains the left upper limb. Pick it for lymph from the left arm.
Correct. Lymph from the left lung passes through the left bronchomediastinal trunk.
questions.answerText: The left bronchomediastinal trunk

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which structure is a dilated sac rather than a duct or a trunk?
options: The right lymphatic duct
The thoracic duct
The jugular trunk
The cisterna chyli
questions.why: The cisterna chyli is an enlarged, sac-like start to the thoracic duct, lying in the abdomen in front of the upper lumbar vertebrae. Cisterna means a reservoir, and chyli refers to chyle, the fat-rich lymph from the intestine that drains into it. The lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk empty into this sac.
notes: The right lymphatic duct is the short duct that drains the upper right quarter of the body. Choose it for a question about lymph from the right arm.
The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic duct; the cisterna chyli is the sac at its lower end. Pick the thoracic duct for a question about the vessel that drains three quarters of the body.
The jugular trunk is a trunk that drains the head and neck. It fits a question about lymph from the face or scalp.
Correct. The cisterna chyli is a dilated sac.
questions.answerText: The cisterna chyli

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Lymph from the left foot passes through a lumbar trunk, the cisterna chyli, the thoracic duct, and a subclavian vein. Which sequence is correct?
options: Thoracic duct, cisterna chyli, lumbar trunk, subclavian vein
Lumbar trunk, thoracic duct, cisterna chyli, subclavian vein
Cisterna chyli, lumbar trunk, thoracic duct, subclavian vein
Lumbar trunk, cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, subclavian vein
questions.why: Lymph from the foot first reaches the left lumbar trunk, which drains the lower limb. The lumbar trunk empties into the cisterna chyli, the sac at the start of the thoracic duct. The thoracic duct then carries the lymph up through the thorax to the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.
notes: This starts at the thoracic duct, the largest and last lymphatic vessel. Lymph moves from smaller to larger vessels, so the trunk comes before the duct.
This puts the cisterna chyli after the thoracic duct, but the cisterna chyli is the start of the duct, not something beyond it.
The cisterna chyli receives the lumbar trunk, so the trunk has to come first. Lymph from the limb reaches its trunk before it reaches the sac.
Correct. Lumbar trunk, cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, then subclavian vein.
questions.answerText: Lumbar trunk, cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, subclavian vein

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Lymph has no pump of its own. Which of these is NOT one of the ways lymph keeps moving?
options: Direct pumping by the left ventricle
Rhythmic contraction of smooth muscle in larger lymphatic walls
Contracting skeletal muscles squeezing the vessels
Pressure changes in the thorax with each breath
questions.why: Several forces work together to move lymph: skeletal muscles squeeze the vessels, pressure in the thorax changes with each breath, smooth muscle in the walls of larger lymphatic vessels contracts in rhythm, and nearby arteries pulse against the vessels. Valves keep all of it moving one way, toward the heart. The left ventricle pumps blood into the aorta and has no connection to lymphatic vessels.
notes: Correct. The left ventricle pumps blood, not lymph; the lymphatic system has no pump of its own.
Rhythmic contraction of smooth muscle in larger lymphatic walls is a real way lymph moves. It would be the answer for a question about how the vessels themselves help.
Contracting skeletal muscles squeezing the vessels is the skeletal muscle pump, a real way lymph moves. It would be the answer for a question about how exercise speeds lymph flow.
Pressure changes in the thorax with breathing are the respiratory pump, a real way lymph moves. It would be the answer for a question about how breathing helps.
questions.answerText: Direct pumping by the left ventricle

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Months after surgery that removed many lymph nodes from her armpit, a patient has long-lasting swelling of that arm. Which disorder is most likely?
options: Varicose veins
Lymphedema
Lymphoma
Lymphadenitis
questions.why: Lymphedema is long-term swelling caused by blocked or missing lymphatic vessels, so fluid builds up in the tissues instead of draining away. Removing many axillary lymph nodes also removes the lymphatic vessels that pass through them. The arm then cannot drain its interstitial fluid well, and it stays swollen.
notes: Varicose veins are twisted superficial veins from failed valves, most often in the legs. They fit a question about visibly bulging leg veins, not arm swelling after node removal.
Correct. Long-lasting swelling after lymph node removal is lymphedema.
Lymphoma is cancer of the lymphocytes in lymphatic tissue. Choose it for a question about a cancer arising in lymph nodes or other lymphatic tissue.
Lymphadenitis is swollen, tender lymph nodes that are fighting an infection. Pick it for tender nodes during an infection, not for swelling after the nodes were removed.
questions.answerText: Lymphedema

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which statement describes the direction lymph flows?
options: Outward from the heart to the tissues
Back and forth in the vessels with each breath
In a closed loop from the heart to the tissues and back
One way only, from the tissues toward the heart
questions.why: The lymphatic system is a one-way drainage network. Lymph starts in blind-ended capillaries in the tissues, moves through larger and larger vessels, and ends where the ducts empty into the subclavian veins near the heart. Valves along the way keep it from flowing backward.
notes: Flow outward from the heart describes arteries. Lymph moves the opposite way, returning fluid to the blood.
Breathing helps push lymph forward through the respiratory pump, but valves stop it from moving backward. Students pick this when they confuse the pump with the direction of flow.
A closed loop from the heart and back describes blood in the cardiovascular system. The lymphatic system has no loop because its capillaries begin as dead ends.
Correct. Lymph flows one way, from the tissues toward the heart.
questions.answerText: One way only, from the tissues toward the heart

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Where do the superficial lymphatic collecting vessels run?
options: Inside the epidermis
Alongside the deep arteries, between the muscles
In the subcutaneous layer, alongside the superficial veins
Inside the lumen of the veins
questions.why: Collecting vessels travel in two sets. The superficial ones run in the subcutaneous layer next to the superficial veins, while the deep ones run with the deep arteries. Both sets have valves and pass through lymph nodes along the way.
notes: The epidermis is avascular and has no lymphatic vessels at all. Choose it for a question about a tissue without lymphatic capillaries.
Running with the deep arteries describes the deep collecting vessels. Pick this for a question about lymphatic vessels that drain muscles and deeper organs.
Correct. Superficial collecting vessels run in the subcutaneous layer with the superficial veins.
Lymphatic vessels are separate tubes that run beside veins, not inside them. Lymph enters a vein only at the end of the route, where the ducts empty in the neck.
questions.answerText: In the subcutaneous layer, alongside the superficial veins

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: What is interstitial fluid?
options: The milky, fat-rich fluid that drains from the lacteals of the small intestine
The fluid in the spaces between cells, filtered out of the blood capillaries
The fluid inside a lymphatic vessel after it has been collected from the tissues
The liquid part of blood that stays inside the blood vessels
questions.why: Interstitial fluid is the fluid that bathes the cells, sitting in the tissue spaces between them. It forms when fluid filters out of the blood capillaries. The blood capillaries take most of it back, and the lymphatic system collects the rest. Once that fluid enters a lymphatic vessel, its name changes to lymph.
notes: This describes chyle, the lymph that turns milky after the lacteals absorb dietary fat. Pick chyle if the question asked about the lymph draining from the small intestine after a meal.
Correct. Interstitial fluid fills the spaces between cells and comes from fluid that leaves the blood capillaries.
This describes lymph, which is the same fluid after it has entered a lymphatic capillary. Pick lymph if the question asked what interstitial fluid is called once it is inside the lymphatic vessels.
This describes plasma, the liquid matrix of blood that stays inside the vessels. Pick plasma if the question asked about the fluid portion of whole blood.
questions.answerText: The fluid in the spaces between cells, filtered out of the blood capillaries

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: In which direction does the lymphatic system move lymph?
options: Outward from the heart to the tissues
Back and forth with each heartbeat
In a continuous loop, like the blood
In one direction only, toward the heart
questions.why: The lymphatic system is a one-way drainage network rather than a circuit. It begins with dead-end lymphatic capillaries in the tissues and carries lymph through larger and larger vessels until the ducts empty it into the veins near the heart. Valves along the vessels keep lymph from flowing backward.
notes: This is the direction arteries carry blood, away from the heart and out to the tissues. Lymph moves the opposite way, from the tissues back toward the heart.
This mixes up lymph with the pulsing of arterial blood. The heart does not pump lymph, and valves in the lymphatic vessels stop any backward flow.

The blood travels in a closed loop, leaving the heart in arteries and returning in veins. The lymphatic system is not a loop, because its capillaries start blind in the tissues and it only drains toward the heart.
Correct. Lymph flows one way, from the tissues toward the heart, and valves keep it from backing up.
questions.answerText: In one direction only, toward the heart

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which lymphatic duct drains most of the body?
options: The cisterna chyli
The right lymphatic duct
The thoracic duct
The cystic duct
questions.why: The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel and drains about three quarters of the body: both lower limbs, the abdomen, the left arm, and the left side of the head, neck, and thorax. It begins at the cisterna chyli in the abdomen, runs up through the thorax, and empties where the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins meet.
notes: The cisterna chyli is the sac in the abdomen where the thoracic duct begins. It collects lymph from the lumbar and intestinal trunks, but it is the starting point of the duct, not the duct itself.

The right lymphatic duct is short and small and drains only the right arm and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax. Pick it if the question asked which duct drains the upper right part of the body.
Correct. The thoracic duct drains everything except the upper right part of the body.
The cystic duct belongs to the digestive system and connects the gallbladder to the common bile duct. It is a look-alike name and would be the answer for a question about the bile pathway.
questions.answerText: The thoracic duct

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which region of the body does the right lymphatic duct drain?
options: The left arm and the left side of the head and neck
The right arm and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax
Everything below the diaphragm on both sides
The lower limbs and the abdomen
questions.why: The right lymphatic duct is a short vessel that receives the right jugular, right subclavian, and right bronchomediastinal trunks. Those trunks drain the right side of the head and neck, the right arm, and the right side of the thorax, so the duct covers only the upper right part of the body. It empties where the right subclavian and right internal jugular veins meet.
notes: The left arm and the left side of the head and neck drain through the left subclavian and left jugular trunks into the thoracic duct. This is the mirror-image region of the correct answer.
Correct. The right lymphatic duct drains only the upper right part of the body.
Everything below the diaphragm drains into the thoracic duct by way of the cisterna chyli. This region belongs to the thoracic duct, not the right lymphatic duct.

The lower limbs and abdomen drain through the lumbar and intestinal trunks into the cisterna chyli and then the thoracic duct. Pick this region if the question asked what the thoracic duct receives from below the diaphragm.
questions.answerText: The right arm and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: What is the smallest type of lymphatic vessel?
options: The lymphatic trunk
The thoracic duct
The lymphatic capillary
The collecting vessel
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries are the smallest lymphatic vessels and the starting point of the whole system. They are dead-end tubes woven between the blood capillaries, and their overlapping endothelial cells let excess interstitial fluid in. From there lymph moves into progressively larger vessels on its way back to the blood.
notes: Lymphatic trunks are large vessels formed when collecting vessels merge, each draining a major body region. They are near the end of the pathway, just before the ducts.
The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body. Pick it if the question asked for the biggest lymphatic vessel rather than the smallest.
Correct. Lymphatic capillaries are the smallest vessels and where lymph first forms.
Collecting vessels are the next step after the capillaries. They have valves and pass through lymph nodes, so pick them if the question asked where lymph goes after the capillaries.
questions.answerText: The lymphatic capillary

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Lymph leaves the tissue spaces in the lymphatic capillaries. Which vessels does it enter next?
options: The lymphatic ducts
The lymphatic collecting vessels
The lymphatic trunks
The subclavian veins
questions.why: The pathway of lymph runs from lymphatic capillaries to collecting vessels, through lymph nodes, into lymphatic trunks, then into a lymphatic duct, and finally into a subclavian vein. Collecting vessels come right after the capillaries. They are built like thin veins with even more valves, and they carry lymph to the nodes for filtering.
notes: The lymphatic ducts are the last lymphatic vessels in the pathway, receiving lymph from the trunks. Pick them if the question asked where the trunks empty.
Correct. Collecting vessels receive lymph directly from the lymphatic capillaries.

The lymphatic trunks form when collecting vessels merge after passing through nodes. They come two steps later than the capillaries, so pick them for a question about what the collecting vessels drain into.
The subclavian veins are where lymph finally rejoins the blood, at their junctions with the internal jugular veins. They are the end of the pathway, not the step after the capillaries.
questions.answerText: The lymphatic collecting vessels

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: The lymphatic system has no pump of its own. What mainly moves lymph along the vessels?
options: Gravity pulling lymph down toward the feet
Cilia on the vessel walls sweeping it along
Contractions of the heart pushing it forward
Skeletal muscle squeeze and breathing movements
questions.why: Lymph is moved by forces outside the vessels. Contracting skeletal muscles squeeze nearby lymphatic vessels (the skeletal muscle pump), and pressure changes in the thorax with each breath pull lymph upward (the respiratory pump). Smooth muscle in larger vessel walls and the pulsing of nearby arteries help, and valves keep all of this flow moving one way toward the heart.
notes: Gravity would pull lymph away from the heart in the legs, which is the opposite of the direction it needs to travel. Lymph moves upward against gravity because muscle squeeze and valves push it.
Cilia are found on the lining of the airways, where they sweep mucus. Lymphatic vessels are lined by endothelium without cilia, so this mixes up the respiratory lining with the lymphatic wall.
The heart pumps blood, not lymph. Lymph only reaches the heart after the ducts empty into the veins, so heart contractions are not what push lymph through the lymphatic vessels.
Correct. The skeletal muscle pump and the respiratory pump are the main forces that move lymph.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle squeeze and breathing movements

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: How do the walls of a lymphatic capillary let fluid in but not back out?
options: Overlapping endothelial cells act as one-way flap valves
Tight junctions seal the cells completely together
Anchoring filaments squeeze the capillary shut after each beat
Smooth muscle in the wall pumps fluid inward
questions.why: The endothelial cells of a lymphatic capillary overlap loosely at their edges like shingles. When fluid pressure outside is higher, the edges push inward and fluid enters, and when pressure inside rises, the edges press shut. This flap-valve arrangement lets in fluid, proteins, cells, and even pathogens, but keeps them from leaking back out.
notes: Correct. The overlapping endothelial cells work as one-way flap valves.
Tight junctions would seal the wall and keep most material out. Blood capillary cells are joined more tightly than lymphatic ones, so this describes the opposite of how a lymphatic capillary works.

Anchoring filaments tie the lymphatic capillary to the surrounding tissue and hold it open, so they help fluid enter rather than closing the vessel. Pick them if the question asked what keeps a lymphatic capillary from collapsing.
Lymphatic capillaries are a single layer of endothelium with no smooth muscle. Smooth muscle appears only in the walls of larger lymphatic vessels, where it helps move lymph along.
questions.answerText: Overlapping endothelial cells act as one-way flap valves

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which sac in the abdomen marks the beginning of the thoracic duct?
options: The subcapsular sinus
The cisterna chyli
A lacteal
The right lymphatic duct
questions.why: The cisterna chyli is an enlarged sac in the abdomen that collects lymph from the lumbar and intestinal trunks. The thoracic duct begins at this sac and runs upward through the thorax. Its name refers to chyle, the milky, fat-rich lymph that drains into it from the intestine.
notes: The subcapsular sinus is the space just under the capsule of a lymph node where lymph first enters. Pick it if the question asked where lymph goes after the afferent vessels.
Correct. The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli.
A lacteal is a lymphatic capillary in an intestinal villus that absorbs dietary fat. Lacteals feed chyle toward the cisterna chyli, but they are tiny vessels, not a large sac.
The right lymphatic duct is the smaller of the two ducts, starting in the right side of the neck and thorax. It has no abdominal sac and drains only the upper right part of the body.
questions.answerText: The cisterna chyli

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: After surgery that removes many lymph nodes from the armpit, a patient develops long-term swelling of that arm. Which disorder is this?
options: Lymphedema
Tonsillitis
Splenomegaly
Lymphadenopathy
questions.why: Lymphedema is long-term swelling caused by blocked or missing lymphatic vessels. When many nodes and the vessels running through them are removed, fluid from that limb can no longer drain well, so interstitial fluid builds up. The swelling lasts because the drainage pathway itself has been lost.
notes: Correct. Lymphedema is long-term limb swelling after lymphatic drainage is blocked or removed.
Tonsillitis is infection and inflammation of the tonsils, common in childhood. Pick it for a question about a sore, swollen throat with enlarged tonsils.
Splenomegaly is an enlarged spleen, seen in mononucleosis and leukemia. Pick it for a question about swelling of the organ in the upper left abdomen.
Lymphadenopathy means enlargement of the lymph nodes themselves. Here the nodes were removed, and the swelling is in the whole limb, so the problem is drainage, not node enlargement.
questions.answerText: Lymphedema

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Tissue swells because fluid leaks out of the blood capillaries faster than the lymphatic vessels can drain it. Which condition is this?
options: Lymphoma
Lymphadenopathy
Tonsillitis
Edema
questions.why: Edema is swelling of the interstitial space, the tissue spaces between cells. It happens when fluid leaves the blood capillaries faster than the lymphatics can return it. The lymphatics normally carry about 3 liters of leaked fluid back to the blood each day, so any imbalance shows up as swelling.
notes: Lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes in lymphatic tissue. Pick it for a question about Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin disease.
Lymphadenopathy is enlargement of the lymph nodes. Pick it if the question described swollen nodes rather than swollen tissue.
Tonsillitis is inflammation of infected tonsils. It causes a swollen throat, but it is an infection of lymphatic tissue rather than general fluid buildup.
Correct. Edema is swelling of the interstitial spaces when drainage cannot keep up.
questions.answerText: Edema

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Lymphatic capillaries have overlapping cells that act as one-way flaps. What does this one-way design accomplish?
options: Only water and small ions are allowed in
Lymph can flow back and forth between nodes
Fluid is actively pumped into the capillary
Tissue fluid can enter but cannot leak back out
questions.why: The overlapping cell edges open inward when fluid builds up in the tissue spaces and press closed when pressure inside the capillary rises. That arrangement lets interstitial fluid, proteins, and even cells enter, while stopping them from flowing back out. Once inside, the fluid is lymph and can only move onward toward the heart.
notes: Lymphatic capillaries are more permeable than blood capillaries, so they take in proteins, cells, pathogens, and even cancer cells, not only small molecules. Students sometimes mix this up with blood capillaries, which mostly pass small molecules.
Lymph never flows back and forth. The flap valves and the valves of the collecting vessels keep it moving only one way, toward the heart.
The capillary wall does not pump. Fluid enters passively when pressure outside is higher, and the flaps only control direction.
Correct. The flaps let excess fluid in and keep it from leaking back out.
questions.answerText: Tissue fluid can enter but cannot leak back out

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: A patient on long bed rest develops puffy, swollen ankles. Why does inactivity slow the flow of lymph out of the legs?
options: The lymphatic valves open in both directions when muscles relax
The heart stops pumping lymph while the body is lying at rest
The inguinal lymph nodes close off when the legs are not moving
Idle leg muscles stop squeezing the vessels, so less lymph is pushed upward
questions.why: The lymphatic system has no central pump, so lymph in the legs depends on the skeletal muscle pump. Each time leg muscles contract, they squeeze nearby lymphatic vessels, and the valves make sure the lymph can only move upward. With little muscle activity, this push weakens and fluid collects in the lowest tissues.
notes: Lymphatic valves stay one-way at all times, which is what keeps lymph from sliding back down. The problem during bed rest is too little push, not leaky valves.
The heart never pumps lymph, at rest or during activity. Lymph only meets the heart after the ducts empty it into the veins in the neck.
Lymph nodes do not open and close with movement. Lymph passes through them continuously, whether the legs are active or still.
Correct. Inactive muscles stop squeezing the vessels, so lymph moves upward more slowly.
questions.answerText: Idle leg muscles stop squeezing the vessels, so less lymph is pushed upward

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: When lymphatic drainage from a limb is blocked, the limb swells. Based on the normal job of the lymphatic vessels, why does this happen?
options: Leaked fluid is no longer carried away, so it builds up in the tissues
The lymph nodes swell and take up the extra room inside the limb
Blood can no longer leave the arteries to reach the limb tissues
Lymph backs up into the veins of the limb and stretches their walls
questions.why: Blood capillaries constantly leak fluid into the tissue spaces, and the lymphatic vessels normally return the excess to the blood. When those vessels are blocked, the leaking continues but the return does not, so interstitial fluid accumulates. That swelling is called lymphedema when it lasts.
notes: Correct. Without drainage, leaked fluid collects in the tissue spaces and causes swelling.
Swollen nodes are lymphadenopathy, which makes lumps at node clusters. The swelling here spreads through the tissue of the whole limb because fluid is not being drained.
Arterial blood flow into the limb is unaffected by a lymphatic blockage. Swelling comes from fluid that has already left the blood and cannot be returned.
Lymph does not drain into the limb veins. It only reaches the venous system at the subclavian and internal jugular veins in the neck.
questions.answerText: Leaked fluid is no longer carried away, so it builds up in the tissues

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Most absorbed nutrients enter the blood capillaries of the intestinal villi, but absorbed dietary fats enter the lacteals instead. Why do fats take the lymphatic route?
options: Fat particles are too large for blood capillaries but fit into lacteals
Fat must first be filtered by the spleen before it can enter the blood
The lacteals digest the fat before it can be allowed to reach the blood
Blood capillaries in the villi are blind-ended and cannot take up nutrients
questions.why: Lacteals are lymphatic capillaries in the center of each intestinal villus. Absorbed fats are packed into particles too big to cross into blood capillaries, but lymphatic capillaries are wider and more permeable, so the fat enters the lacteals. The fat turns the lymph milky (chyle), which drains to the cisterna chyli and up the thoracic duct.
notes: Correct. Fat particles are too large for blood capillaries but can enter the lacteals.
The spleen filters blood, not fat. Fat travels with lymph through the thoracic duct and reaches the blood at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.
Digestion of fat happens in the lumen of the small intestine before absorption. Lacteals only carry absorbed fat away.
This swaps the two kinds of capillaries. Lymphatic capillaries are the blind-ended ones, while blood capillaries are open at both ends and absorb most other nutrients.
questions.answerText: Fat particles are too large for blood capillaries but fit into lacteals

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which lymphatic trunks drain the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdominal wall?
options: The bronchomediastinal trunks
The lumbar trunks
The intestinal trunk
The subclavian trunks
questions.why: Collecting vessels merge into nine large lymphatic trunks, each named for the region it drains. The paired lumbar trunks collect lymph from the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdominal wall. Both lumbar trunks empty into the cisterna chyli at the start of the thoracic duct.
notes: The bronchomediastinal trunks drain the thoracic organs and the thoracic wall. Pick them for a question about lymph from the lungs and mediastinum.
Correct. The lumbar trunks drain the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdominal wall.
The intestinal trunk is a single trunk that drains the digestive organs of the abdomen. Pick it if the question asked which trunk carries chyle from the intestine.
The subclavian trunks drain the upper limbs. Pick them for a question about lymph from the arms.
questions.answerText: The lumbar trunks

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Lymph from the left arm travels through the left subclavian trunk. Which vessel does that trunk empty into?
options: The left lumbar trunk
The right lymphatic duct
The cisterna chyli
The thoracic duct
questions.why: The right lymphatic duct only receives the trunks from the upper right part of the body.
