Every other trunk, including the left subclavian trunk from the left arm, empties into the thoracic duct. The thoracic duct then returns that lymph to the blood where the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins meet.
notes: The lumbar trunks drain the lower limbs and pelvis and empty into the cisterna chyli. Trunks do not drain into other trunks.
The right lymphatic duct receives only the right jugular, right subclavian, and right bronchomediastinal trunks. Pick it if the question asked about lymph from the right arm.
The cisterna chyli is the abdominal sac that receives the lumbar and intestinal trunks. Lymph from the arm enters the thoracic duct much higher, in the neck region.
Correct. The left subclavian trunk empties into the thoracic duct.
questions.answerText: The thoracic duct

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which list traces the path of lymph from the tissues back to the blood in the correct order?
options: Collecting vessels, lymphatic capillaries, lymph nodes, lymphatic ducts, lymphatic trunks, subclavian veins
Lymphatic capillaries, collecting vessels, lymph nodes, lymphatic trunks, lymphatic ducts, subclavian arteries
Lymphatic capillaries, collecting vessels, lymph nodes, lymphatic trunks, lymphatic ducts, subclavian veins
Lymphatic capillaries, lymphatic trunks, lymph nodes, collecting vessels, lymphatic ducts, subclavian veins
questions.why: Lymph starts when excess interstitial fluid enters blind-ended lymphatic capillaries. These drain into collecting vessels, which pass through lymph nodes for filtering, then merge into the large lymphatic trunks. The trunks empty into the right lymphatic duct or the thoracic duct, which return lymph to the blood where the subclavian and internal jugular veins meet.
notes: This starts with collecting vessels and swaps the ducts and trunks. Lymph always enters capillaries first, and trunks drain into ducts, not the other way around.

The steps are right until the end, but lymph returns to veins, not arteries. Students pick this when they forget that the lymphatic system is a drainage system that feeds into the low pressure venous side.
Correct. Lymph moves into larger and larger vessels, with nodes filtering it along the way.

This puts the trunks before the nodes and the collecting vessels. Trunks are the large vessels formed after collecting vessels have passed through nodes, so this order runs from large to small in the middle of the route.
questions.answerText: Lymphatic capillaries, collecting vessels, lymph nodes, lymphatic trunks, lymphatic ducts, subclavian veins

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which two vessels return lymph to the blood, and where do they empty?
options: The right lymphatic duct and the thoracic duct, directly into the right atrium
The right lymphatic duct and the thoracic duct, where the subclavian and internal jugular veins meet
The right and left lumbar trunks, into the common iliac veins
The cisterna chyli and the thoracic duct, into the inferior vena cava
questions.why: All lymph ends up in one of two lymphatic ducts. The right lymphatic duct empties at the junction of the right subclavian and right internal jugular veins, and the thoracic duct empties at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins. From there the returned fluid joins venous blood heading to the heart through the brachiocephalic veins and superior vena cava.
notes: The two ducts are named correctly, but they join large veins in the root of the neck, not the heart itself. Students pick this when they assume all returning fluid must enter the heart directly.
Correct. Both ducts empty at the junction of a subclavian vein and an internal jugular vein.

The lumbar trunks drain the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdominal wall, and they empty into the thoracic duct, not into veins. They would be the answer if the question asked which trunks carry lymph from the legs.
The cisterna chyli is the sac in the abdomen where the thoracic duct begins, not a separate duct. Pick the cisterna chyli if the question asked where the thoracic duct starts.
questions.answerText: The right lymphatic duct and the thoracic duct, where the subclavian and internal jugular veins meet

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the drainage areas of the right lymphatic duct and the thoracic duct?
options: The thoracic duct drains the right arm and right side of the head, neck, and thorax, and the right lymphatic duct drains the rest
The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and right side of the head, neck, and thorax, and the thoracic duct drains the rest
The right lymphatic duct drains everything above the diaphragm, and the thoracic duct drains everything below it
The right lymphatic duct drains the entire right half of the body, and the thoracic duct drains the entire left half
questions.why: The right lymphatic duct is short and small, and it receives only the right jugular, right subclavian, and right bronchomediastinal trunks. That limits its territory to the right arm and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax. The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel and drains everything else, about three quarters of the body, including both legs and the abdomen.
notes: This swaps the two ducts. The thoracic duct is the large one, so it drains the larger territory, not the small upper right region.
Correct. The right lymphatic duct drains the upper right region only, and the thoracic duct drains about three quarters of the body.
The diaphragm is not the dividing line. The thoracic duct also drains the left arm and the left side of the head, neck, and thorax, which are above the diaphragm.
The drainage is not split evenly down the midline. The right leg and the right side of the abdomen drain through the lumbar and intestinal trunks into the thoracic duct, not the right lymphatic duct.
questions.answerText: The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and right side of the head, neck, and thorax, and the thoracic duct drains the rest

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: The lymphatic system has no pump of its own, yet lymph still moves toward the heart. Which explanation is correct?
options: The heart pumps lymph through the vessels, and valves keep it flowing one way
Skeletal muscle contractions and breathing squeeze the vessels, and valves keep lymph flowing one way
Gravity carries lymph toward the heart, so the vessels need no valves
Lymph nodes contract in rhythm to push lymph, and sphincters keep it flowing one way
questions.why: Lymph is moved by forces outside the vessels. Contracting skeletal muscles squeeze nearby lymphatic vessels (the skeletal muscle pump), pressure changes in the thorax with each breath pull lymph upward (the respiratory pump), and smooth muscle in larger vessel walls and pulsing nearby arteries also help. Collecting vessels have even more valves than veins, so every squeeze can push lymph only toward the heart.
notes: The heart pumps blood, but it is not connected to the start of the lymphatic vessels, which begin as blind-ended capillaries in the tissues. Students pick this because blood and lymph both return to the heart.
Correct. Outside squeezing moves lymph, and valves make the flow one way.
Most lymph from the legs and abdomen has to move upward against gravity, so gravity cannot be the driving force. The vessels also have many valves, so this choice is wrong on both counts.
Lymph nodes are filters with a fibrous capsule, not pumps, and lymphatic vessels use valves rather than sphincters. This choice mixes up nodes with the muscular parts of the system.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle contractions and breathing squeeze the vessels, and valves keep lymph flowing one way

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: What is a lacteal?
options: A blood capillary in an intestinal villus that absorbs sugars
A cluster of lymphatic follicles in the wall of the ileum
A lymphatic capillary in an intestinal villus that absorbs dietary fat
A sac in the abdomen where the thoracic duct begins
questions.why: Lacteals are specialized lymphatic capillaries in the center of each villus of the small intestine. Dietary fats are packaged into particles too large to enter blood capillaries, so they enter the lacteals instead. The fat turns the lymph milky white, and this fat-rich lymph, called chyle, drains to the cisterna chyli and up the thoracic duct.
notes: Blood capillaries in the villus do take up absorbed nutrients such as sugars, but they are not lacteals. Students pick this because both vessels sit side by side in the villus.
This describes Peyer patches, a form of MALT that watches the intestinal contents. It would be the answer if the question asked about lymphatic tissue in the wall of the ileum.
Correct. A lacteal is the lymphatic capillary of a villus, and it absorbs fat.
This describes the cisterna chyli, which receives chyle from the intestinal trunk. Pick it if the question asked where the thoracic duct starts.
questions.answerText: A lymphatic capillary in an intestinal villus that absorbs dietary fat

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: How does a lymphatic capillary let fluid in but keep it from leaking back out?
options: Its endothelial cells overlap loosely and act as one-way flap valves
Its endothelial cells are joined by tight seals that admit only small molecules
Cup-shaped valves made of muscle close the open end of the capillary
Smooth muscle in its wall squeezes fluid forward in one direction
questions.why: A lymphatic capillary is blind at one end, and its endothelial cells overlap at their edges without being tightly joined. When fluid pressure in the tissue is higher, it pushes the flaps inward and fluid enters; when pressure inside the capillary rises, the flaps are pressed shut. Anchoring filaments tie the cells to the surrounding tissue so the capillary stays open.
notes: Correct. The overlapping endothelial cells work as minivalves that open inward only.

Tightly joined endothelial cells are a feature of blood capillaries, which mostly let small molecules through. Lymphatic capillaries are looser, which is why proteins, cells, and even cancer cells can enter them.

Lymphatic capillaries are closed at one end, so there is no open end to cover, and their valves are not made of muscle. Collecting vessels do have valves, but those are folds of the lining, not muscle.

Smooth muscle is found in the walls of larger lymphatic vessels, not the capillaries, which are just a single layer of endothelium. Pick smooth muscle if the question asked how larger vessels help move lymph.
questions.answerText: Its endothelial cells overlap loosely and act as one-way flap valves

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: What is lymphedema?
options: Enlargement of the spleen, as seen in mononucleosis
Long-term tissue swelling from blocked or missing lymphatic vessels
Swollen, tender lymph nodes that are fighting an infection
Cancer of the lymphocytes within lymphatic tissue
questions.why: Lymphedema is long-lasting swelling that develops when lymphatic vessels are blocked, damaged, or missing, so interstitial fluid cannot drain back to the blood. It can follow surgery that removes many lymph nodes, such as in breast cancer treatment, and it often affects a limb. In its most extreme form, when parasitic roundworms block the vessels, it is called elephantiasis.
notes: An enlarged spleen is splenomegaly, seen in mononucleosis and leukemia. Choose it if the question asked why a patient with mono should avoid contact sports.
Correct. Lymphedema is chronic swelling from failed lymphatic drainage.
Swollen, tender nodes fighting an infection is lymphadenitis. Pick it if the question asked what swollen glands in the neck during a sore throat are called.
Cancer of the lymphocytes in lymphatic tissue is lymphoma, which can be Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin. It would be the answer if the question asked about a cancer arising in lymph nodes.
questions.answerText: Long-term tissue swelling from blocked or missing lymphatic vessels

questions.topic: Lymph, lymphatic vessels, trunks and ducts
questions.q: Where does the thoracic duct begin?
options: At a lacteal, in the center of an intestinal villus
At the right lymphatic duct, in the right side of the neck
At the cisterna chyli, a sac in the abdomen
At the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins
questions.why: The thoracic duct starts at the cisterna chyli, a sac in the abdomen that receives lymph from the lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk. From there the duct runs up through the thorax, collecting more trunks along the way. It is the largest lymphatic vessel and drains about three quarters of the body.
notes: A lacteal is a lymphatic capillary in an intestinal villus, the very start of fat-rich lymph, far upstream of any duct. Choose it if the question asked where chyle is first formed.

The right lymphatic duct is a separate, small duct that drains the upper right region of the body. It would be the answer if the question asked which duct receives the right jugular and right subclavian trunks.
Correct. The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli.

The junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins is where the thoracic duct ends, not where it begins. Pick it if the question asked where the thoracic duct returns lymph to the blood.
questions.answerText: At the cisterna chyli, a sac in the abdomen

questions.q: Which tissue forms lymphatic tissue?
options: Hyaline cartilage packed with chondrocytes
Adipose tissue packed with fat cells
Reticular connective tissue packed with lymphocytes
Dense regular connective tissue packed with fibroblasts
questions.why: Lymphatic tissue is built on reticular connective tissue, a fine meshwork of reticular fibers that acts like a soft internal scaffold. Large numbers of lymphocytes sit within that mesh. This same framework supports lymph nodes, the spleen, and red bone marrow.
notes: Hyaline cartilage, with chondrocytes in lacunae, covers the ends of long bones and forms the costal cartilages. It fits a question about cartilage, and cartilage has no lymphatic capillaries at all.
Adipose tissue stores fat and is found in the hypodermis and around organs. Choose it for a question about fat storage or insulation.
Correct. Lymphatic tissue is reticular connective tissue packed with lymphocytes.
Dense regular connective tissue, with parallel collagen fibers and fibroblasts, forms tendons and ligaments. Pick it for a question about what connects muscle to bone.
questions.answerText: Reticular connective tissue packed with lymphocytes

questions.q: All lymphocytes form in red bone marrow. Which lymphocytes travel to the thymus to finish maturing?
options: T cells
Plasma cells
B cells
NK cells
questions.why: T cells start in red bone marrow, but their precursors travel to the thymus to mature, which is where the T in their name comes from. The thymus sits in the mediastinum behind the sternum and is a primary lymphatic organ. T cells make up about 80% of circulating lymphocytes and attack infected cells directly.
notes: Correct. T cells finish maturing in the thymus.
Plasma cells develop from activated B cells and make antibodies. They are not a group that matures in the thymus, so pick them for a question about what B cells become.
B cells stay in the red bone marrow to mature. Pick them if the question asks which lymphocytes mature in the marrow or become antibody-making plasma cells.
NK (natural killer) cells also mature in the red bone marrow. Choose them for a question about lymphocytes that attack virus-infected and cancer cells as part of innate defense.
questions.answerText: T cells

questions.q: Reticular connective tissue is the framework of lymphatic tissue. What kind of fibers form its meshwork?
options: Thick parallel collagen bundles
Reticular fibers
Fibrin threads
Elastic fibers
questions.why: Reticular connective tissue is named for its reticular fibers, very thin fibers that branch and interweave into a fine net. That net forms a soft internal skeleton, called a stroma, for lymph nodes, the spleen, and red bone marrow. Lymphocytes and other cells sit in the spaces of the mesh.
notes: Thick parallel collagen bundles make up dense regular connective tissue in tendons and ligaments. Pick them for a question about tissue that resists pulling in one direction.
Correct. Reticular fibers form the meshwork of reticular connective tissue.
Fibrin threads form a blood clot, not a connective tissue framework. They fit a question about how a clot traps blood cells.
Elastic fibers dominate elastic connective tissue, such as in the walls of large arteries. Choose them for a question about tissue that stretches and recoils.
questions.answerText: Reticular fibers

questions.q: A breast tumor sheds cancer cells into nearby lymphatic capillaries. Where are those cells most likely to lodge first?
options: In the first lymph node the region drains into
In the thoracic duct
In the right atrium of the heart
In the spleen
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries are permeable enough to take in cells, including cancer cells. Lymph then flows through collecting vessels to the lymph nodes, which filter it before it moves on. The first node a region drains into, called the sentinel node, is where cancer cells usually lodge first, which is why surgeons check it to see whether a cancer has begun to spread.
notes: Correct. Cancer cells in lymph usually lodge first in the sentinel lymph node.
The thoracic duct is near the end of the lymph route. Lymph must pass through nodes before reaching it, so pick it for a question about where most trunks empty.
Lymph returns to the blood at the subclavian veins, and nodes filter it long before that point. The heart fits a question about where a clot from a leg vein travels.
The spleen filters blood, not lymph, so cancer cells carried in lymph do not pass through it on the way. Choose the spleen for a question about where old red blood cells are removed.
questions.answerText: In the first lymph node the region drains into

questions.q: A histology slide shows a fine mesh of reticular fibers packed with small round cells that have large nuclei and no visible granules. What tissue is this?
options: Lymphatic tissue
Dense regular connective tissue
Hyaline cartilage
Adipose tissue
questions.why: The cells described are lymphocytes, agranular white blood cells with a large round nucleus. A reticular fiber mesh packed with lymphocytes is lymphatic tissue, the tissue found in lymph nodes, the spleen, tonsils, and MALT. The reticular fibers provide the framework and the lymphocytes fill the spaces.
notes: Correct. A reticular mesh packed with lymphocytes is lymphatic tissue.
Dense regular connective tissue shows tightly packed parallel collagen fibers with flattened fibroblasts between them. Pick it for a slide of a tendon or ligament.
Hyaline cartilage shows chondrocytes in lacunae within a smooth, glassy matrix. It fits a slide of articular cartilage or the trachea.
Adipose tissue shows large empty-looking fat cells with the nucleus pushed to the edge. Choose it for a slide of fat from the hypodermis.
questions.answerText: Lymphatic tissue

questions.q: Which lymphocytes become plasma cells that make antibodies?
options: NK cells
B cells
Neutrophils
T cells
questions.why: B cells form and mature in the red bone marrow. When a B cell is activated by an invader, it can become a plasma cell, which makes antibodies. This antibody-based defense is called humoral immunity, and it complements the direct attack carried out by T cells.
notes: NK (natural killer) cells attack virus-infected and cancer cells as part of innate defense, without making antibodies. Choose them for a question about the third type of lymphocyte.
Correct. B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies.
Neutrophils are granular white blood cells that engulf bacteria. They are not lymphocytes, so pick them for a question about the most common white blood cell.
T cells mature in the thymus and attack infected cells directly or direct other immune cells. Pick them for a question about cell-mediated immunity.
questions.answerText: B cells

questions.q: Which pair names the two primary lymphatic organs?
options: The thymus and the spleen
Red bone marrow and the lymph nodes
The spleen and the tonsils
Red bone marrow and the thymus
questions.why: Primary lymphatic organs are where lymphocytes are made and where they mature. All lymphocytes form in red bone marrow, and B cells also mature there, while T cell precursors travel to the thymus to finish maturing. Every other lymphatic organ is secondary, meaning it is a place where mature lymphocytes meet invaders.
notes: The thymus is primary, but the spleen is a secondary organ that filters blood and houses mature lymphocytes. Pick the spleen if the question asked which organ filters the blood.

Red bone marrow is primary, but lymph nodes are secondary organs that filter lymph along the collecting vessels. Lymph nodes would be the answer for an organ that cleans lymph before it returns to the blood.

Both of these are secondary lymphatic tissue where mature lymphocytes meet pathogens. The tonsils would fit a question about lymphatic tissue guarding the entrance to the throat, and the spleen a question about filtering blood.
Correct. Lymphocytes form in red bone marrow and finish maturing either there (B cells) or in the thymus (T cells).
questions.answerText: Red bone marrow and the thymus

questions.q: Where is red bone marrow found in an adult?
options: In the articular cartilage at the ends of long bones
In the compact bone of the outer skull surface
In the medullary cavity of every long bone shaft
In the spongy bone of the axial skeleton and limb girdles
questions.why: In adults, red bone marrow fills the spaces of spongy bone in the axial skeleton (skull, vertebrae, ribs, sternum) and the limb girdles, plus the proximal ends of the humerus and femur. This is why marrow samples are drawn from the sternum or the iliac crest of the hip bone. Over childhood, the marrow in the shafts of long bones is replaced by fatty yellow marrow.
notes: Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage that covers joint surfaces, and cartilage has no marrow or blood vessels inside it. It would be the answer for the smooth tissue that reduces friction in a synovial joint.

Compact bone is the dense outer layer of bone built from osteons, with no marrow-filled spaces. Choose compact bone if the question asked which bone tissue resists bending and forms the hard outer shell.

The medullary cavity of a long bone shaft holds red marrow in children, but in adults it is filled mostly with yellow marrow, which is fat. Pick the medullary cavity if the question asked where yellow marrow is stored in an adult.
Correct. Adult red marrow sits in spongy bone of the axial skeleton and the girdles.
questions.answerText: In the spongy bone of the axial skeleton and limb girdles

questions.q: Which cells in red bone marrow give rise to lymphocytes?
options: Megakaryocytes
Reticulocytes
Pluripotent stem cells
Plasma cells
questions.why: Red bone marrow holds pluripotent stem cells, also called hemocytoblasts. Pluripotent means one stem cell can become many different cell types, so these cells give rise to every formed element of blood, including the lymphocytes. The lymphoid line of these stem cells produces the B cells, T cell precursors, and NK cells.
notes: Megakaryocytes are giant marrow cells whose cytoplasm breaks apart into platelets. Pick megakaryocytes if the question asked which cell produces platelets.
Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells that still hold ribosome remnants. They would be the answer for the cell stage just before a mature erythrocyte.
Correct. Pluripotent stem cells in red marrow give rise to all blood cells, lymphocytes included.
Plasma cells are what activated B cells become, and they make antibodies. They are the end of the B cell story, not the start, so choose them for a question about which cells secrete antibodies.
questions.answerText: Pluripotent stem cells

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the B cells and T cells that leave the red bone marrow?
options: Both leave immature and finish maturing in the spleen
T cells leave mature, while B cells leave as immature pre-B cells
Both B cells and T cells leave the marrow fully mature
B cells leave mature, while T cells leave as immature pre-T cells
questions.why: Both B cells and T cells start from stem cells in the red bone marrow. B cells stay in the marrow until they are mature, so the marrow is where B cells both form and mature. T cells leave the marrow as pre-T cells and travel to the thymus to finish maturing, which is why the thymus is also a primary lymphatic organ.
notes: The spleen is a secondary organ where mature lymphocytes meet blood-borne invaders, not a place where lymphocytes mature. Pick the spleen for a question about filtering blood or removing old red cells.
This reverses the two cell types. Students often mix them up, so link the letters to places: B cells mature in the bone marrow, and T cells mature in the thymus.
T cells cannot be fully mature when they leave the marrow, because they still need the thymus. This choice would be true only of B cells, which do complete their maturation in the marrow.
Correct. B cells mature in the marrow, and pre-T cells finish maturing in the thymus.
questions.answerText: B cells leave mature, while T cells leave as immature pre-T cells

questions.q: Where do pre-T cells travel after they leave the red bone marrow?
options: The thymus
The spleen
The tonsils
The lymph nodes
questions.why: Pre-T cells are immature T cells made in the red bone marrow. They travel in the blood to the thymus, the primary lymphatic organ in the mediastinum behind the sternum, where they multiply and learn to recognize foreign antigens. Only after maturing in the thymus do T cells move on to secondary organs.
notes: Correct. The thymus is where pre-T cells go to mature into T cells.

The spleen is a secondary organ in the upper left abdomen that filters blood. Mature T cells do live in its white pulp, so pick the spleen if the question asked where mature lymphocytes respond to blood-borne pathogens.
The tonsils are secondary lymphatic tissue in a ring around the throat that meet inhaled and swallowed pathogens. They would be the answer for lymphatic tissue guarding the entrance to the pharynx.

Lymph nodes are secondary organs along the collecting vessels, and their deep cortex holds mostly T cells, but only after the T cells have matured. Choose lymph nodes for a question about filtering lymph.
questions.answerText: The thymus

questions.q: Which description matches the internal organization of the thymus?
options: Clusters of follicles scattered through a mucous membrane with no capsule
Two lobes divided into lobules, each with a cortex and a medulla
An outer cortex, a deep cortex, and a medulla fed by afferent vessels
Small islands of lymphocytes around central arteries within red pulp
questions.why: The thymus is bilobed, meaning it has two lobes, and a connective tissue capsule sends extensions inward that split each lobe into smaller lobules. Each lobule has a darker outer cortex packed with immature T cells and a paler inner medulla with fewer, more mature T cells. Recognizing this pattern lets you tell the thymus apart from the spleen, lymph nodes, and MALT on a slide.
notes: This describes MALT, such as Peyer patches in the ileum, which is lymphatic tissue in the mucosa without a surrounding capsule. Choose it for a question about unencapsulated lymphatic tissue in the gut wall.
Correct. Two lobes, lobules, and a cortex and medulla in each lobule is the pattern of the thymus.

This describes a lymph node, with B cell follicles in the outer cortex, T cells in the deep cortex, and lymph arriving through afferent vessels. The thymus has no afferent vessels because it does not filter lymph.

This describes the spleen, where white pulp forms small islands of lymphocytes around central arteries and red pulp makes up most of the organ. Pick it for a question about the spleen's internal structure.
questions.answerText: Two lobes divided into lobules, each with a cortex and a medulla

questions.q: What are the two regions of each thymic lobule?
options: An outer cortex and an inner medulla
A capsule and a hilum
An outer cortex and a deep cortex
White pulp and red pulp
questions.why: Each lobule of the thymus has an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The cortex is densely packed with immature T cells, so it stains darker, while the medulla holds fewer, more mature T cells and the thymic corpuscles. T cells develop as they move from the cortex toward the medulla.
notes: Correct. Every thymic lobule has an outer cortex and an inner medulla.

A capsule is the covering of an organ, and a hilum is the indented spot where vessels enter or leave, as on a lymph node or the spleen. These are surface features, not the two internal regions of a thymic lobule.
The outer cortex and deep cortex are regions of a lymph node, holding mostly B cells and mostly T cells. Choose this pair for a question about the zones of a lymph node.
White pulp and red pulp are the two tissues of the spleen, not the thymus. Pick them if the question asked about the regions of the spleen.
questions.answerText: An outer cortex and an inner medulla

questions.q: Which cells are most densely packed in the cortex of the thymus?
options: Red blood cells
Immature T cells
Mature B cells
Plasma cells
questions.why: The thymic cortex is crowded with immature T cells that arrived from the red bone marrow as pre-T cells. Dendritic cells, epithelial cells, and macrophages are scattered among them and support their development. Because the cortex is so densely packed with these lymphocytes, it stains darker than the medulla.
notes: Red blood cells are not a feature of thymic tissue. Choose red blood cells for a question about what fills the splenic cords and sinuses of the red pulp.
Correct. The thymic cortex is packed with immature T cells that are multiplying and maturing.
B cells mature in the red bone marrow, not in the thymus. Mature B cells fill the follicles of the outer cortex of a lymph node, so pick them for a question about that region.
Plasma cells are activated B cells that make antibodies, and they are not residents of the thymic cortex. They would be the answer for cells found in the medulla of a lymph node.
questions.answerText: Immature T cells

questions.q: What happens to pre-T cells in the thymic cortex?
options: They are filtered out of lymph and destroyed
They multiply and begin maturing into T cells
They are first formed from pluripotent stem cells
They become plasma cells that make antibodies
questions.why: Pre-T cells arrive in the thymic cortex from the red bone marrow and multiply there. Thymic epithelial cells and dendritic cells support them as they mature and learn to recognize foreign antigens. The cells that pass this process move on to the medulla and then leave the thymus as mature T cells.
notes: Filtering lymph is the job of lymph nodes, and the thymus has no afferent lymphatic vessels at all. This would be the answer for what macrophages in a lymph node do to bacteria and debris.
Correct. The cortex is where pre-T cells proliferate and mature.
Pre-T cells are formed from pluripotent stem cells in the red bone marrow, before they ever reach the thymus. Pick this for a question about what happens to lymphocytes in the red bone marrow.
Becoming a plasma cell is what an activated B cell does, for example in the follicles of a lymph node. T cells never become plasma cells, so choose this for a question about B cell activation.
questions.answerText: They multiply and begin maturing into T cells

questions.q: Compared with the thymic cortex, what kind of T cells does the thymic medulla hold?
options: Only B cells and plasma cells, with no T cells
More T cells that are less mature
No lymphocytes at all, only epithelial cells
Fewer T cells that are more mature
questions.why: T cells develop in the cortex and then move inward to the medulla as they mature. The medulla therefore holds fewer T cells than the cortex, but the ones there are more mature and nearly ready to leave the thymus. The medulla also contains epithelial cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, and the thymic corpuscles.
notes: B cells and plasma cells are typical of the medulla of a lymph node, not the thymus. Choose this for a question about the inner region of a lymph node.
This describes the cortex, which is densely packed with immature T cells. Pick it for a question about the outer region of a thymic lobule.

The medulla does contain epithelial cells, but it also holds mature T cells and other support cells. Thinking it has no lymphocytes comes from confusing it with a thymic corpuscle, which is made only of epithelial cells.
Correct. The medulla has fewer T cells, and they are more mature.
questions.answerText: Fewer T cells that are more mature

questions.q: What is another name for the thymic corpuscles?
options: Hassall's corpuscles
Peyer patches
Billroth's cords
Germinal centers
questions.why: Thymic corpuscles are also called Hassall's corpuscles, named for the scientist who first described them. They are rounded clusters of epithelial cells arranged in concentric layers, like the layers of an onion, and they are found only in the medulla of the thymus. They are one of the easiest features for identifying thymus tissue on a slide.
notes: Correct. Thymic corpuscles and Hassall's corpuscles are the same structure.
Peyer patches are clusters of lymphatic follicles in the wall of the ileum, a form of MALT. Pick them if the question asked about lymphatic tissue in the small intestine.
Billroth's cords are the splenic cords of the red pulp, found between the venous sinuses of the spleen. They would be the answer for a question about red pulp structure.

Germinal centers are the pale centers of lymphatic follicles where B cells multiply, as in a lymph node's outer cortex. Choose germinal centers for a question about where B cells proliferate in a follicle.
questions.answerText: Hassall's corpuscles

questions.q: Which description fits a Hassall's (thymic) corpuscle?
options: A cord of red cells and macrophages between sinuses
Epithelial cells arranged in concentric layers
A cluster of B cells with a pale germinal center
A sleeve of lymphocytes around a central artery
questions.why: A Hassall's corpuscle is a rounded whorl of flattened epithelial cells wrapped in concentric layers. It sits in the medulla of the thymus and has no match in other lymphatic organs. On a slide it looks like a small pink onion slice among the T cells.
notes: This describes a splenic cord (Billroth's cord) in the red pulp of the spleen. It would be the answer for the tissue that removes worn-out red cells.
Correct. A thymic corpuscle is a whorl of epithelial cells in concentric layers.
This is a lymphatic follicle (nodule) with a germinal center, as in the outer cortex of a lymph node. Pick it for a question about where B cells multiply in a node.
This is splenic white pulp, where lymphocytes cluster around central arteries. Choose it for a question about the immune tissue of the spleen.
questions.answerText: Epithelial cells arranged in concentric layers

questions.q: In which region of the thymus are Hassall's corpuscles found?
options: The cortex
The medulla
The connective tissue septa
The capsule
questions.why: Hassall's corpuscles, also called thymic corpuscles, are found in the medulla, the paler inner region of each thymic lobule. The medulla holds fewer, more mature T cells, so the corpuscles stand out clearly there. Finding them is a reliable way to locate the medulla on a thymus slide.
notes: The cortex is the outer region packed with immature T cells, and it has no thymic corpuscles. Pick the cortex for a question about where pre-T cells first multiply and mature.
Correct. Thymic corpuscles are a feature of the medulla.
The septa are inward extensions of the capsule that divide each lobe into lobules. They would be the answer for what separates one thymic lobule from the next.
The capsule is the connective tissue covering of the whole thymus. Choose it for a question about what surrounds the organ and sends extensions inward.
questions.answerText: The medulla

questions.q: Which structure is a primary lymphatic organ?
options: A lymph node
A palatine tonsil
The thymus
The spleen
questions.why: Primary lymphatic organs are where lymphocytes form and mature, and there are only two of them: red bone marrow and the thymus. The thymus is primary because T cells finish maturing there. The spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, and MALT are secondary organs where mature lymphocytes meet invaders.
notes: A lymph node is a secondary organ that filters lymph along the collecting vessels. It would be the answer for where lymph is cleaned before returning to the blood.
The palatine tonsils are secondary lymphatic tissue in the lateral walls of the oropharynx. Choose them for a question about the tonsils most often infected and removed.
Correct. The thymus is a primary lymphatic organ where T cells mature.
The spleen is the largest lymphatic organ, but it is secondary because mature lymphocytes there respond to pathogens in the blood. Pick the spleen if the question asked which organ filters the blood.
questions.answerText: The thymus

questions.q: Which organ produces both mature B cells and pre-T cells?
options: The spleen
Red bone marrow
The tonsils
The thymus
questions.why: All lymphocytes form from stem cells in red bone marrow. B cells stay in the marrow until they are mature, and T cell precursors (pre-T cells) leave the marrow and travel to the thymus. That makes red bone marrow the starting point for every lymphocyte and the maturation site for B cells.
notes: The spleen is a secondary organ that filters blood and houses mature lymphocytes. It would be the answer for where old red blood cells are removed.
Correct. Red bone marrow makes the stem-cell-derived lymphocytes, releasing mature B cells and pre-T cells.
The tonsils are secondary lymphatic tissue guarding the throat. Choose them for a question about lymphatic tissue that traps inhaled and swallowed pathogens.
The thymus receives pre-T cells but does not produce them, and it does not make B cells. Pick the thymus if the question asked where T cells finish maturing.
questions.answerText: Red bone marrow

questions.q: In which thymic region do pre-T cells multiply and begin to mature?
options: The capsule
The medulla
The cortex
A thymic corpuscle
questions.why: Pre-T cells arriving from the red bone marrow settle in the outer cortex of each thymic lobule. There they multiply and mature with help from thymic epithelial cells and dendritic cells. The cells that survive this process move inward to the medulla before leaving the thymus.
notes: The capsule is the connective tissue covering of the thymus, not a place where cells develop. Choose it for a question about what surrounds the organ and divides it into lobules.
The medulla is where T cells go after they have matured in the cortex. Pick the medulla if the question asked which region holds fewer, more mature T cells.
Correct. The cortex is where pre-T cells proliferate and begin maturing.
A thymic corpuscle is a whorl of epithelial cells in the medulla, not a region where T cells multiply. It would be the answer for the concentric structure used to identify the thymic medulla.
questions.answerText: The cortex

questions.q: Which feature lets you tell a thymus slide apart from a lymph node slide?
options: Germinal centers in the outer cortex
A capsule of dense connective tissue
Trabeculae extending inward from the capsule
Thymic corpuscles in the medulla
questions.why: Thymic (Hassall's) corpuscles, whorls of epithelial cells in concentric layers, are found only in the thymic medulla. Both the thymus and a lymph node have a connective tissue capsule with inward extensions, so those features do not separate them. Germinal centers point the other way, toward a lymph node, because the thymus has no follicles.
notes: Germinal centers inside follicles are typical of a lymph node's outer cortex, and the thymus has no follicles. Pick germinal centers if the question asked which feature identifies a lymph node.
Both the thymus and lymph nodes have a dense connective tissue capsule, so it cannot tell them apart. The capsule would be the answer for what covers the outside of either organ.
Both organs have inward extensions of the capsule, called trabeculae in a lymph node and septa in the thymus. Choose trabeculae for a question about what divides a lymph node into compartments.
Correct. Thymic corpuscles are unique to the thymic medulla.
questions.answerText: Thymic corpuscles in the medulla

questions.q: A T cell has finished developing in the thymic cortex. Where does it move next before it leaves the thymus?
options: A connective tissue septum
The capsule
The medulla
A thymic corpuscle
questions.why: T cells mature as they move from the outer cortex inward to the medulla of each thymic lobule. The medulla therefore holds the more mature T cells, which then leave the thymus and travel to secondary organs such as lymph nodes and the spleen. This inward path explains why the cortex holds immature cells and the medulla holds mature ones.
notes: Septa are connective tissue partitions between lobules, not a place where T cells collect. Choose a septum for a question about what divides a thymic lobe into lobules.
The capsule is the connective tissue covering on the outside of the thymus, the opposite direction from where maturing T cells travel. Pick it for a question about what encloses the whole organ.
Correct. Maturing T cells move inward from the cortex to the medulla.
A thymic corpuscle is a whorl of epithelial cells inside the medulla, not a region T cells move into. It would be the answer for the structure that identifies the medulla on a slide.
questions.answerText: The medulla

questions.q: Which thymic cells form a barrier around developing T cells and release thymic hormones?
options: Plasma cells
Epithelial cells
Dendritic cells
Macrophages
questions.why: Thymic epithelial cells make up the supporting framework of the thymus. They form a barrier around the developing T cells and release thymic hormones that help the T cells mature. In the medulla, some of these same epithelial cells are wrapped into the concentric thymic corpuscles.
notes: Plasma cells are antibody-making cells that come from activated B cells, and they are not part of the thymic cortex. They would be the answer for the antibody-secreting cells in a lymph node medulla.
Correct. Thymic epithelial cells surround developing T cells and release thymic hormones.

Dendritic cells in the thymic cortex assist pre-T cells as they mature, but they do not release thymic hormones. Pick dendritic cells if the question asked which cells help present antigens to developing T cells.
Macrophages engulf debris, including the many T cells that die by apoptosis in the thymus. Choose macrophages for a question about which cells clean up dead cells.
questions.answerText: Epithelial cells

questions.q: What divides the thymus into lobes and lobules?
options: Connective tissue septa from the capsule
Whorls of thymic corpuscles
Venous sinuses of the red pulp
Germinal centers of follicles
questions.why: A capsule of connective tissue surrounds the thymus, separating its two lobes. Extensions of this capsule reach inward and divide each lobe into lobules. Each lobule then has its own cortex and medulla.
notes: Correct. Connective tissue from the capsule extends inward to divide the thymus into lobes and lobules.
Thymic corpuscles are whorls of epithelial cells in the medulla, not partitions. Choose them for a question about a feature unique to the thymic medulla.
Venous sinuses are wide blood channels in the red pulp of the spleen. Pick them for a question about where blood collects after passing through the splenic cords.
Germinal centers are the pale centers of follicles where B cells multiply, and the thymus has none. They would be the answer for a feature of the outer cortex of a lymph node.
questions.answerText: Connective tissue septa from the capsule

questions.q: A lymphatic organ in the mediastinum, above the heart and behind the sternum, is large in a child but shrinks after puberty. Which organ is it?
options: The spleen
Red bone marrow
The pharyngeal tonsil
The thymus
questions.why: The thymus sits in the mediastinum, above the heart and behind the sternum. It is large in infants and children, when large numbers of T cells are being produced, and then shrinks after puberty. In older adults it is mostly replaced by fat.
notes: The spleen sits in the upper left abdomen behind the stomach, not in the mediastinum. Pick the spleen for a question about a lymphatic organ protected by the lower left ribs.
Red bone marrow is in the spongy bone of the axial skeleton and limb girdles, not a single organ in the mediastinum. Choose it for a question about where all lymphocytes form.

The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) is on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx. It also tends to shrink with age, but it is in the throat, so pick it for a question about tissue that blocks the back of the nose in children.
Correct. The thymus lies behind the sternum and shrinks after puberty.
questions.answerText: The thymus

questions.q: What has happened to most of the thymus in an older adult?
options: It has turned into red bone marrow
It has doubled in size
It has been largely replaced by fat
It has moved down into the abdomen
questions.why: The thymus is largest in infants and children, when the body is building its supply of T cells. After puberty it shrinks steadily, and in older adults most of its tissue has been replaced by fat. The T cells it produced earlier in life continue to live and divide in the secondary lymphatic organs.
notes: The thymus does not become marrow. Red bone marrow is a separate primary organ located in spongy bone, which is where all lymphocytes form throughout life.
The thymus gets smaller with age, not larger. Students sometimes assume organs grow with the body, but the thymus is at its relative largest in childhood.
Correct. After puberty the thymus shrinks and is mostly fat in older adults.
The thymus stays in the mediastinum, above the heart and behind the sternum, for life. Aging changes its size and makeup, not its location, so an abdominal location would fit the spleen instead.
questions.answerText: It has been largely replaced by fat

questions.q: A slide of the thymic medulla shows rounded whorls of flattened epithelial cells in concentric layers. What are these whorls?
options: Billroth's cords
Hassall's corpuscles
Germinal centers
Lymphatic follicles
questions.why: Concentric whorls of epithelial cells in the thymic medulla are Hassall's corpuscles, also called thymic corpuscles. They are found nowhere else in the lymphatic system, so seeing them confirms both that the tissue is thymus and that you are looking at the medulla. The surrounding cells are mature T cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells.
notes: Billroth's cords are the splenic cords of the red pulp, packed with red cells and macrophages. Choose them for a question about the tissue between the venous sinuses of the spleen.
Correct. Whorls of epithelial cells in the thymic medulla are Hassall's corpuscles.
Germinal centers are the pale centers of follicles where B cells multiply. They are made of lymphocytes, not epithelial cells, so pick them for a question about B cell proliferation in a node.

Lymphatic follicles are round clusters of lymphocytes, mostly B cells, found in lymph nodes, tonsils, the spleen, and Peyer patches. Pick follicles for a question about the dense B cell clusters in a node's outer cortex.
questions.answerText: Hassall's corpuscles

questions.q: A baby is born without a thymus. Which cells would fail to mature normally?
options: B cells
Erythrocytes
Platelets
T cells
questions.why: The thymus is the primary lymphatic organ where T cells mature. Pre-T cells are still made in the red bone marrow, but without a thymus they have nowhere to finish developing, so the child would have very few functional T cells. B cells, red cells, and platelets all form and mature in the red bone marrow, so they would not depend on the thymus.
notes: B cells form and mature in the red bone marrow, so they do not need the thymus. Pick B cells if the question described a child with a red bone marrow defect.
Erythrocytes are produced entirely in the red bone marrow from the myeloid line. They would be the answer for a question about a marrow failure causing anemia.
Platelets come from megakaryocytes in the red bone marrow. Choose platelets for a question about a marrow problem that raises the risk of bleeding.
Correct. T cells need the thymus to mature.
questions.answerText: T cells

questions.q: Which cell type is NOT normally found in the thymic cortex?
options: Dendritic cells
Immature T cells
Plasma cells
Epithelial cells
questions.why: The thymic cortex holds densely packed immature T cells along with dendritic cells, epithelial cells, and macrophages that support and clean up after them. Plasma cells are activated B cells that secrete antibodies, and they belong in places where B cells respond to antigens, such as the medulla of a lymph node. They are not part of the T cell nursery in the thymic cortex.
notes: Dendritic cells are present in the thymic cortex, where they assist pre-T cells as they mature. Choose them for a question about cells that help T cells learn to recognize antigens.
Immature T cells are the most numerous cells of the thymic cortex. Pick them if the question asked which cells crowd the outer region of a thymic lobule.
Correct. Plasma cells are not residents of the thymic cortex.
Epithelial cells form the framework of the thymic cortex and release thymic hormones. They would be the answer for the cells that make thymic hormones.
questions.answerText: Plasma cells

questions.q: Why is red bone marrow classified as a primary lymphatic organ?
options: Lymphocytes form there, and B cells mature there
Worn-out red blood cells are removed there
Lymphocytes there meet swallowed pathogens
Lymph passing through it is filtered of bacteria
questions.why: A primary lymphatic organ is a place where lymphocytes are made and mature. Every lymphocyte starts from stem cells in red bone marrow, and B cells also complete their maturation there. The other jobs listed belong to secondary organs, where mature lymphocytes do their work.
notes: Correct. Lymphocyte formation and B cell maturation make red marrow a primary organ.
Removing worn-out red cells is a job of the spleen's red pulp. This would be the answer for a question about what the spleen does to old erythrocytes.
Meeting swallowed pathogens is the job of the tonsils and MALT, which guard mucosal surfaces. Choose this for a question about lymphatic tissue in the throat or gut lining.
Filtering lymph is the job of lymph nodes, which are secondary organs along the collecting vessels. Pick this for a question about why lymph nodes swell during an infection.
questions.answerText: Lymphocytes form there, and B cells mature there

questions.q: Red bone marrow fills the spaces inside which kind of bone tissue?
options: Spongy bone
Compact bone
Dense regular connective tissue
Hyaline cartilage
questions.why: Spongy bone is a lattice of thin bony plates called trabeculae with open spaces between them. In the axial skeleton, the limb girdles, and the proximal ends of the humerus and femur, those spaces are filled with red bone marrow, where blood cells and lymphocytes are made. Compact bone is solid and has no room for marrow.
notes: Correct. Red bone marrow fills the spaces between the trabeculae of spongy bone.

Compact bone is the dense outer layer of bone built from tightly packed osteons, with only tiny canals for vessels. Pick compact bone for a question about the bone tissue that resists bending and forms the outer shell.
Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments, built of parallel collagen fibers with no marrow spaces. It would be the answer for the tissue that attaches muscle to bone.

Hyaline cartilage covers joint surfaces and forms the costal cartilages, and it has no blood vessels or marrow. Choose it for a question about the tissue at the ends of long bones in a synovial joint.
questions.answerText: Spongy bone

questions.q: Which lymphatic organ has two lobes, each divided into lobules with a cortex and a medulla?
options: The spleen
A lymph node
The thymus
A palatine tonsil
questions.why: The thymus is bilobed, meaning it has two lobes, and connective tissue from its capsule divides each lobe into lobules. Each lobule has an outer cortex of immature T cells and an inner medulla with mature T cells and thymic corpuscles. A lymph node also has a cortex and medulla, but it is a single small bean-shaped organ, not two lobes.
notes: The spleen is organized into red pulp and white pulp, not lobes with a cortex and medulla. Pick the spleen for a question about red pulp and white pulp.
A lymph node does have a cortex and a medulla, but it is a single bean-shaped structure with no lobes. Choose a lymph node for a question about an organ with afferent and efferent lymphatic vessels.
Correct. The thymus has two lobes divided into lobules, each with a cortex and a medulla.
A palatine tonsil is a mass of lymphatic tissue with deep pits called crypts, without lobes or a medulla. It would be the answer for lymphatic tissue in the lateral walls of the oropharynx.
questions.answerText: The thymus

questions.q: On a thymus slide, each lobule has a darker outer region. What is this region, and why does it stain darker?
options: The medulla, because it is crowded with mature T cells
The capsule, because it is made of dense collagen
The medulla, because it holds the thymic corpuscles
The cortex, because it is packed with immature T cells
questions.why: The outer region of each thymic lobule is the cortex. It is crowded with immature T cells, and their tightly packed nuclei take up a lot of stain, so the cortex looks darker. The medulla in the center has fewer T cells and looks paler, which is the opposite of what students often expect.
notes: The medulla is the inner region, and it actually holds fewer T cells than the cortex, so it stains lighter. It would be the answer for the paler central region with mature T cells.
The capsule is a thin covering around the whole thymus, not the outer region of each lobule. Choose the capsule for a question about what encloses the thymus and divides it into lobules.
The medulla is the inner, paler region, not the outer one, although it does hold the thymic corpuscles. Pick the medulla for a question about where Hassall's corpuscles are found.
Correct. The cortex is the darker outer region, packed with immature T cells.
questions.answerText: The cortex, because it is packed with immature T cells

questions.q: What is the paler inner region of a thymic lobule called?
options: The germinal center
The hilum
The cortex
The medulla
questions.why: The inner region of each thymic lobule is the medulla. It looks paler than the cortex because it holds fewer T cells, and those T cells are the more mature ones. The medulla also contains the thymic (Hassall's) corpuscles.
notes: A germinal center is the pale center of a lymphatic follicle where B cells multiply, and the thymus has no follicles. It would be the answer for the pale area inside a follicle of a lymph node.
A hilum is the indented spot where vessels enter or leave an organ, such as a lymph node or the spleen. Choose the hilum for a question about where efferent vessels leave a lymph node.
The cortex is the darker outer region packed with immature T cells. Pick the cortex for a question about where pre-T cells first multiply.
Correct. The medulla is the paler inner region of each thymic lobule.
questions.answerText: The medulla

questions.q: Which cell type is found in both the cortex and the medulla of the thymus?
options: Megakaryocytes
Plasma cells
Epithelial cells
Erythrocytes
questions.why: Thymic epithelial cells form the supporting framework of the whole thymus, so they are found in both the cortex and the medulla. In the medulla, some of them are wrapped into the concentric thymic corpuscles. The two regions differ mainly in their T cells: immature and crowded in the cortex, fewer and more mature in the medulla.
notes: Megakaryocytes are giant cells of the red bone marrow that break apart to form platelets. They would be the answer for a question about where platelets come from.
Plasma cells are antibody-making cells that come from activated B cells, and they are not residents of the thymus. Pick plasma cells for a question about the cells in the medulla of a lymph node.
Correct. Thymic epithelial cells are found in both the cortex and the medulla.
Erythrocytes are red blood cells that travel inside blood vessels, not resident cells of thymic tissue. Choose them for a question about what fills the cords and sinuses of the splenic red pulp.
questions.answerText: Epithelial cells

questions.q: Unlike a lymph node, the thymus has no afferent lymphatic vessels and no follicles. What does this tell you about the thymus?
options: It is not a lymphatic organ
It does not contain any lymphocytes
It does not filter lymph
It filters blood like the spleen
questions.why: Afferent vessels are the vessels that carry lymph into a lymph node so it can be filtered. Because the thymus has none, lymph never flows through it, and the thymus is not a filter. Its job is to mature T cells, which makes it a primary lymphatic organ rather than a filtering organ like a lymph node.
notes: The thymus is a lymphatic organ, in fact a primary one, because T cells mature there. Not filtering lymph does not remove it from the lymphatic system; red bone marrow does not filter lymph either.

The thymus is packed with lymphocytes, especially immature T cells in its cortex. This choice confuses having no follicles with having no lymphocytes; follicles are just one way lymphocytes can be clustered.
Correct. With no afferent vessels, the thymus does not filter lymph.
Filtering blood is the job of the spleen, which has red pulp and venous sinuses that the thymus lacks. Pick this for a question about how the spleen differs from a lymph node.
questions.answerText: It does not filter lymph

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes where T cells develop?
options: Form in the thymus, then mature in red bone marrow
Form in the tonsils, then mature in lymph nodes
Form and mature entirely in the spleen
Form in red bone marrow, then mature in the thymus
questions.why: All lymphocytes, T cells included, form from stem cells in the red bone marrow. T cell precursors, called pre-T cells, leave the marrow and travel to the thymus, where they mature. Mature T cells then leave the thymus for the secondary organs, such as lymph nodes and the spleen.
notes: This reverses the order. The marrow is the starting point for every lymphocyte, and the thymus is the finishing school for T cells.
The tonsils and lymph nodes are secondary organs where mature lymphocytes meet invaders, not where they form. Choose these for a question about where T cells respond to an infection.
The spleen is a secondary organ where mature lymphocytes respond to blood-borne pathogens. Pick the spleen for a question about filtering blood, not about T cell development.
Correct. T cells form in the red bone marrow and mature in the thymus.
questions.answerText: Form in red bone marrow, then mature in the thymus

questions.q: Where are the hemocytoblasts, the stem cells that give rise to every blood cell including lymphocytes?
options: In the spleen
In the thymus
In red bone marrow
In yellow bone marrow
questions.why: Hemocytoblasts are pluripotent stem cells, meaning each one can become many kinds of blood cell. They live in the red bone marrow, which is why red marrow is the site of hematopoiesis (blood cell formation) and a primary lymphatic organ. Every erythrocyte, leukocyte, and platelet traces back to these cells.
notes: The spleen makes red blood cells in the fetus, but in adults it filters blood and stores platelets rather than holding the stem cells. Choose the spleen for a question about removing worn-out red cells.
The thymus receives pre-T cells from the marrow but has no hemocytoblasts. Pick the thymus for a question about where T cells mature.
Correct. Hemocytoblasts are in the red bone marrow.
Yellow bone marrow is mostly fat and is not an active blood-forming tissue in adults. It would be the answer for what fills the medullary cavity of an adult long bone shaft.
questions.answerText: In red bone marrow

questions.q: A lymph node has more afferent vessels bringing lymph in than efferent vessels carrying it out. What is the effect of this arrangement?
options: Lymph speeds up and leaves the node faster
Lymph bypasses the node and enters the blood directly
Lymph slows down inside the node for filtering
Lymph flows backward out of the afferent vessels
questions.why: Afferent vessels carry lymph into a lymph node, and fewer efferent vessels carry it out at the hilum. Because more lymph comes in than can quickly leave, the flow slows down inside the node. That gives macrophages time to engulf bacteria and debris and gives lymphocytes time to meet invaders.
notes: Narrowing the exit does the opposite of speeding lymph up. Students who pick this are thinking of a nozzle, but here the many incoming vessels feed into fewer outgoing ones, so lymph backs up and slows.

Lymph must pass through nodes before it reaches the ducts and the subclavian veins. This choice ignores the fixed route of lymph: capillaries, collecting vessels, nodes, trunks, ducts, and then the veins.
Correct. More afferent than efferent vessels slows lymph so the node can filter it.
Valves in the lymphatic vessels keep lymph moving one way, toward the heart. Backflow is what valves prevent, so pick valves as the answer to a question about how lymph is kept from flowing backward.
questions.answerText: Lymph slows down inside the node for filtering

questions.q: Where are the large clusters of lymph nodes that a clinician can feel during an exam?
options: The brain, spinal cord, and eyes
The palms, soles, and scalp
The fingertips, toes, and lips
The neck, armpits, and groin
questions.why: Lymph nodes cluster in the cervical (neck), axillary (armpit), and inguinal (groin) regions, as well as deep in the thorax and abdomen. The superficial clusters in the neck, armpits, and groin are the ones a clinician can feel through the skin. When they are swollen and tender, it usually means the nodes are fighting an infection in the region they drain.
notes: The central nervous system has no lymphatic capillaries, so there are no node clusters in the brain or spinal cord. Pick these structures for a question about places where lymphatic capillaries are absent.
These are not sites of node clusters. Students sometimes pick them because they are easy to touch, but the palpable clusters sit where limbs and the head join the trunk.
These areas drain toward nodes farther up the limb or in the neck, but they do not hold node clusters themselves. Choosing them confuses the area a node drains with where the node actually sits.
Correct. The cervical, axillary, and inguinal clusters are the ones felt during an exam.
questions.answerText: The neck, armpits, and groin

questions.q: What tissue forms the capsule around a lymph node?
options: Stratified squamous epithelium
Dense connective tissue
Hyaline cartilage
Smooth muscle
questions.why: A lymph node is wrapped in a capsule of dense connective tissue, which is rich in collagen fibers that make it tough. Extensions of the capsule called trabeculae reach inward and divide the node into compartments. Afferent lymphatic vessels pierce the capsule to bring lymph in.
notes: Stratified squamous epithelium is a protective lining in areas of abrasion, such as the epidermis, mouth, and esophagus. Pick it for a question about the lining of the oral cavity, not a capsule around an organ.
Correct. The capsule of a lymph node is dense connective tissue.
Hyaline cartilage covers joint surfaces and supports the trachea, and it has no role in lymph nodes. It would be the answer for the C-shaped rings that hold the trachea open.

Smooth muscle is found in the walls of larger lymphatic vessels and helps push lymph along, but it does not form the capsule of a node. Choose smooth muscle for a question about how lymph moves through larger vessels.
questions.answerText: Dense connective tissue

questions.q: What are the trabeculae of a lymph node?
options: Vessels that carry lymph out at the hilum
Inward extensions of the capsule that form compartments
Clusters of B cells with pale germinal centers
Channels just beneath the capsule where lymph enters
questions.why: Trabeculae are strands of dense connective tissue that extend inward from the capsule of a lymph node. They divide the node into compartments and carry blood vessels into the interior. The same word is used in bone and the spleen for internal supporting strands, so the idea of an inner framework carries over.
notes: Vessels leaving at the hilum are the efferent lymphatic vessels. Pick efferent vessels for a question about how filtered lymph exits a node.
Correct. Trabeculae are inward extensions of the capsule that divide the node into compartments.
Clusters of B cells with pale germinal centers are lymphatic follicles in the outer cortex. Choose follicles for a question about where B cells multiply in a node.
The channel just beneath the capsule is the subcapsular sinus, where lymph first enters. It would be the answer for the first space lymph reaches after the afferent vessels.
questions.answerText: Inward extensions of the capsule that form compartments

questions.q: Which cells dominate the outer cortex of a lymph node?
options: Erythrocytes
T cells
Plasma cells
B cells
questions.why: The outer cortex of a lymph node holds the lymphatic follicles, which are dense, round clusters made mostly of B cells. When an antigen arrives, B cells in a follicle multiply in a pale germinal center. The deep cortex beneath it holds mostly T cells.
notes: Erythrocytes are red blood cells that stay in blood vessels and are not a resident cell of lymph node tissue. They would be the answer for the cells that fill the red pulp of the spleen.
T cells dominate the deep cortex of a lymph node, just inside the outer cortex. Pick T cells for a question about the deep cortex.
Plasma cells are concentrated in the medulla of a lymph node. Choose plasma cells for a question about the inner region of a node.
Correct. The follicles of the outer cortex are made mostly of B cells.
questions.answerText: B cells

questions.q: Which cells make up most of the deep cortex of a lymph node?
options: Plasma cells
T cells
Macrophages
B cells
questions.why: The deep cortex of a lymph node lies between the B cell follicles of the outer cortex and the medulla. It is made mostly of T cells, with dendritic cells that present antigens to them. This layered arrangement lets B cells and T cells each have their own zone while staying close enough to work together.
notes: Plasma cells are found mainly in the medulla. They would be the answer for the antibody-secreting cells of the inner node.
Correct. The deep cortex is mostly T cells.
Macrophages are concentrated along the medullary sinuses, where they engulf bacteria and debris. Choose them for a question about the cells lining the sinuses of the medulla.
B cells dominate the follicles of the outer cortex, not the deep cortex. Pick B cells for a question about the outer cortex.
questions.answerText: T cells

questions.q: The medulla of a lymph node contains medullary cords and medullary sinuses. Which cells line the medullary sinuses?
options: Thymic epithelial cells
Megakaryocytes
Macrophages
Erythrocytes
questions.why: The medullary sinuses are channels that lymph flows through on its way to the efferent vessels at the hilum. They are lined with macrophages, which engulf bacteria, debris, and even cancer cells as the lymph passes. The medullary cords between the sinuses hold B cells and plasma cells.
notes: Thymic epithelial cells are found only in the thymus, where they support developing T cells. Pick them for a question about the cells that release thymic hormones.
Megakaryocytes are giant cells in red bone marrow that break apart into platelets. They would be the answer for a question about platelet formation.
Correct. Macrophages line the medullary sinuses and clean the lymph as it passes.
Erythrocytes are red blood cells, which stay in the blood and are not part of a lymph node's sinuses. Choose them for a question about the splenic red pulp.
questions.answerText: Macrophages

questions.q: Where in a lymph node are the lymphatic nodules (follicles) found?
options: In the medulla
In the outer cortex
In the hilum
In the deep cortex
questions.why: Lymphatic nodules, also called follicles, are round clusters of mostly B cells located in the outer cortex of a lymph node. When an antigen reaches the node, B cells in a follicle multiply in a pale germinal center. The deeper layers of the node have different jobs: T cells in the deep cortex and macrophages along the medullary sinuses.
notes: The medulla is the inner region of cords and sinuses with B cells, plasma cells, and macrophages, not follicles. Pick the medulla for a question about where plasma cells collect.
Correct. Follicles sit in the outer cortex of a lymph node.
The hilum is the indented side where blood vessels enter and efferent vessels leave. It would be the answer for where filtered lymph exits the node.
The deep cortex holds mostly T cells and dendritic cells in a more diffuse arrangement. Choose it for a question about the T cell zone of a node.
questions.answerText: In the outer cortex

questions.q: What does a primary lymphatic nodule mainly contain?
options: T cells
Plasma cells
B cells
Macrophages
questions.why: A primary lymphatic nodule is a round cluster made mainly of B cells that have not yet met their antigen. When an antigen arrives, the nodule develops a pale germinal center of multiplying B cells and becomes a secondary nodule. The B cells there then become plasma cells and memory B cells.
notes: T cells are mainly found in the deep cortex, outside the nodules. Pick T cells for a question about the deep cortex of a node.
Plasma cells form later, after B cells are activated, and they collect in the medulla. They would be the answer for the antibody-secreting cells of a node.
Correct. A primary nodule is made mainly of B cells.
Macrophages are concentrated along the sinuses of the medulla. Choose them for a question about the cells that engulf bacteria in lymph.
questions.answerText: B cells

questions.q: What makes a lymphatic nodule a secondary nodule?
options: It is found only in the medulla of the thymus
It lacks lymphocytes and contains only macrophages
It sits in the deep cortex and contains mostly T cells
It formed after antigen exposure and has a germinal center
questions.why: A secondary nodule develops when B cells in a primary nodule meet an antigen. The B cells multiply in a pale central area called a germinal center and become plasma cells and memory B cells. A primary nodule, by contrast, is a cluster of B cells without a germinal center.
notes: The thymus has no nodules at all, and its medulla holds mature T cells and thymic corpuscles. This would fit a question about where Hassall's corpuscles are found.
Nodules are made of lymphocytes, mostly B cells. Macrophages line the medullary sinuses, so choose this for a question about the cells that clean lymph in the medulla.
The deep cortex is the T cell zone of a node, and nodules are B cell clusters in the outer cortex. Pick this for a question about the deep cortex.
Correct. A secondary nodule forms in response to an antigen and has a germinal center.
questions.answerText: It formed after antigen exposure and has a germinal center

questions.q: In which abdominopelvic region is the spleen located?
options: The left hypochondriac region
The epigastric region
The left lumbar region
The right hypochondriac region
questions.why: The spleen sits in the upper left abdomen, against the diaphragm and behind the stomach, which places it in the left hypochondriac region. Hypochondriac means below the cartilage of the ribs, and the lower left ribs protect the spleen. This is why a hard blow to the left upper abdomen can rupture it.
notes: Correct. The spleen is in the left hypochondriac region.
The epigastric region is the upper middle region, holding much of the stomach and part of the liver. Choose it for a question about pain just below the sternum.

The left lumbar region is below the left hypochondriac region, beside the umbilical region, and contains the descending colon. It would be the answer for a question about the region lateral to the umbilicus on the left.
The right hypochondriac region holds most of the liver and the gallbladder. Pick it for a question about where the liver mainly sits.
questions.answerText: The left hypochondriac region

questions.q: Which is the largest lymphatic organ in the body?
options: The spleen
The thymus
A palatine tonsil
A lymph node
questions.why: The spleen is the largest lymphatic organ in the body. It sits in the upper left abdomen behind the stomach and filters blood rather than lymph. Its white pulp carries out immune functions, and its red pulp removes worn-out red blood cells and platelets.
notes: Correct. The spleen is the largest lymphatic organ.
The thymus is large in children but shrinks after puberty, and even at its largest it is smaller than the spleen. Pick the thymus for a question about where T cells mature.
The palatine tonsils are the largest of the tonsils, but they are much smaller than the spleen. They would be the answer for the largest tonsil, which is usually the one removed in a tonsillectomy.
Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped organs, numbering in the hundreds. Choose a lymph node for a question about the organs that filter lymph.
questions.answerText: The spleen

questions.q: What forms the covering and internal framework of the spleen?
options: A layer of stratified squamous epithelium
A dense connective tissue capsule and trabeculae
Plates of hyaline cartilage and perichondrium
A sheet of skeletal muscle with tendons
questions.why: Like a lymph node, the spleen is wrapped in a capsule of dense connective tissue. Strands called trabeculae extend inward from the capsule and form part of the internal framework, carrying the trabecular arteries and veins. Inside this framework are the red pulp and the white pulp.
notes: Stratified squamous epithelium is a protective lining in places of abrasion such as the skin, mouth, and esophagus. Pick it for a question about the lining of the esophagus.
Correct. The spleen has a dense connective tissue capsule with trabeculae extending inward.
Hyaline cartilage supports structures such as the trachea and covers joint surfaces. It would be the answer for the tissue forming the C-shaped tracheal rings.
Skeletal muscle forms the muscles that move the skeleton, and it is not part of the spleen. Choose skeletal muscle for a question about the skeletal muscle pump that squeezes lymphatic vessels.
questions.answerText: A dense connective tissue capsule and trabeculae

questions.q: Which description fits the white pulp of the spleen?
options: Concentric whorls of epithelial cells in a medulla
Follicles with germinal centers beneath a subcapsular sinus
Small islands of lymphocytes clustered around central arteries
Venous sinuses and cords full of red cells and macrophages
questions.why: White pulp is lymphatic tissue made of lymphocytes, both B cells and T cells, clustered around the central arteries. It appears as small islands scattered through the much larger red pulp. White pulp handles the spleen's immune function, responding to pathogens carried in the blood.
notes: Concentric whorls of epithelial cells are thymic (Hassall's) corpuscles in the medulla of the thymus. Choose them for a question about identifying thymus tissue.
Follicles beneath a subcapsular sinus describe the outer cortex of a lymph node. This would be the answer for a question about lymph node structure.
Correct. White pulp is islands of lymphocytes around central arteries.
This describes red pulp, which makes up most of the spleen and filters old red cells from the blood. Pick it for a question about red pulp.
questions.answerText: Small islands of lymphocytes clustered around central arteries

questions.q: What is the red pulp of the spleen made of?
options: Dense connective tissue strands that extend from the capsule
Venous sinuses and splenic cords with red cells and macrophages
Lymphocytes clustered in islands around the central arteries
Medullary cords and sinuses that drain to efferent vessels
questions.why: Red pulp makes up most of the spleen. It is built of wide blood channels called venous sinuses and the splenic cords (Billroth's cords) between them, which are full of red blood cells, macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Here macrophages remove worn-out red cells and platelets as blood moves from the cords into the sinuses.
notes: Connective tissue strands from the capsule are trabeculae, which form part of the spleen's framework. They would be the answer for what carries the trabecular arteries and veins into the spleen.
Correct. Red pulp is venous sinuses and splenic cords packed with red cells and macrophages.
Lymphocytes around central arteries form the white pulp, the spleen's immune tissue. Pick this for a question about white pulp.
Medullary cords and sinuses form the medulla of a lymph node, where filtered lymph heads toward the efferent vessels. Choose this for a question about the inner region of a lymph node.
questions.answerText: Venous sinuses and splenic cords with red cells and macrophages

questions.q: What are Billroth's cords?
options: The splenic cords of the red pulp, between the venous sinuses
Whorls of epithelial cells inside the thymic medulla
Medullary cords inside a lymph node
Sleeves of lymphocytes around the central arteries
questions.why: Billroth's cords is another name for the splenic cords, the strips of tissue in the red pulp that lie between the venous sinuses. They are packed with red blood cells, macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. As blood squeezes from the cords into the sinuses, old and damaged red cells get caught and are eaten by macrophages.
notes: Correct. Billroth's cords are the splenic cords of the red pulp.
Whorls of epithelial cells in the thymic medulla are Hassall's (thymic) corpuscles. They would be the answer for the feature used to identify the thymic medulla.
Medullary cords are in the medulla of a lymph node and hold B cells and plasma cells. Choose them for a question about lymph node structure, since Billroth's cords belong to the spleen.
Lymphocyte sleeves around central arteries are the white pulp of the spleen. Pick this for a question about white pulp.
