questions.answerText: The splenic cords of the red pulp, between the venous sinuses

questions.q: Which list correctly gives functions of the splenic red pulp?
options: Removing worn-out blood cells, storing platelets, and fetal red cell formation
Maturing T cells, releasing thymic hormones, and forming corpuscles
Absorbing dietary fats, forming chyle, and draining to the cisterna chyli
Filtering lymph, forming follicles, and draining to efferent vessels
questions.why: The red pulp is where the spleen handles the blood itself. Macrophages in its cords remove worn-out red blood cells and platelets, the red pulp stores a supply of platelets, and in the fetus it makes red blood cells. The white pulp, in contrast, carries out the immune response to blood-borne pathogens.
notes: Correct. Red pulp removes worn-out cells, stores platelets, and makes red cells in the fetus.
These are functions of the thymus, where T cells mature with help from epithelial cells and thymic hormones. Pick this list for a question about the thymus.
These are the jobs of the lacteals of the small intestine, which absorb dietary fat as milky chyle. This list would answer a question about lacteals.
These are features of a lymph node, which filters lymph and holds follicles in its outer cortex. Choose this list for a question about lymph node function.
questions.answerText: Removing worn-out blood cells, storing platelets, and fetal red cell formation

questions.q: What is the dense connective tissue covering of a lymph node called?
options: The capsule
The hilum
The cortex
The trabecula
questions.why: The outer covering of a lymph node is its capsule, a layer of dense connective tissue. Afferent lymphatic vessels pass through the capsule to deliver lymph into the subcapsular sinus just beneath it. Trabeculae extend inward from the capsule to divide the node into compartments.
notes: Correct. The capsule is the dense connective tissue covering of a lymph node.
The hilum is the indented side of the node where blood vessels enter and efferent vessels leave. It would be the answer for where filtered lymph exits.
The cortex is the region just inside the capsule, holding B cell follicles and the T cell zone. Pick the cortex for a question about where follicles are found.
A trabecula is an inward extension of the capsule, not the covering itself. Choose trabeculae for a question about what divides the node into compartments.
questions.answerText: The capsule

questions.q: Which region of a lymph node contains mostly T cells and dendritic cells?
options: The deep cortex
The capsule
The medullary sinus
The outer cortex
questions.why: The deep cortex, sometimes called the inner cortex, lies between the B cell follicles of the outer cortex and the medulla. It holds mostly T cells, with dendritic cells that present antigens to them. The node is layered so that each type of lymphocyte has its own zone.
notes: Correct. The deep cortex is the T cell zone of a lymph node.
The capsule is the dense connective tissue covering, not a region full of lymphocytes. Choose the capsule for a question about what covers the outside of the node.
The medullary sinuses are channels lined with macrophages that lymph passes through before leaving. They would be the answer for where macrophages clean lymph near the exit.
The outer cortex holds the follicles, which are mostly B cells. Pick the outer cortex for a question about where B cells cluster.
questions.answerText: The deep cortex

questions.q: Where in a lymph node are plasma cells concentrated?
options: In the trabeculae
In the capsule
In the medulla
In the deep cortex
questions.why: After B cells are activated in the follicles of the outer cortex, many become plasma cells that collect in the medullary cords of the medulla. There they secrete antibodies into the lymph that leaves the node. The medulla also holds B cells and macrophages along its sinuses.
notes: Trabeculae are connective tissue strands that divide the node into compartments. They would be the answer for the inward extensions of the capsule.
The capsule is a connective tissue covering with no lymphocyte zones. Choose the capsule for a question about the outer covering of a node.
Correct. Plasma cells are concentrated in the medulla.
The deep cortex holds mostly T cells and dendritic cells. Pick it for a question about the T cell zone.
questions.answerText: In the medulla

questions.q: A lymphatic nodule that formed in response to an antigen and shows multiplying B cells is called what?
options: A primary nodule
A thymic corpuscle
A secondary nodule
A splenic cord
questions.why: Lymphatic nodules start as primary nodules, clusters of B cells that have not yet met their antigen. Once an antigen arrives, the B cells multiply in a pale germinal center, and the nodule is then called a secondary nodule. The B cells in a secondary nodule become plasma cells and memory B cells.
notes: A primary nodule is a cluster of mainly B cells before antigen exposure, without a germinal center. Pick it for a question about a resting B cell cluster.
A thymic corpuscle is a whorl of epithelial cells in the thymic medulla, not a cluster of B cells. Choose it for a question about identifying thymus tissue.
Correct. A secondary nodule forms after antigen exposure and has proliferating B cells.
A splenic cord (Billroth's cord) is a strip of red pulp between venous sinuses in the spleen. It would be the answer for where old red cells are caught and removed.
questions.answerText: A secondary nodule

questions.q: Which bones protect the spleen?
options: The lower left ribs
The left hip bone
The sternum
The lower right ribs
questions.why: The spleen sits in the upper left abdomen against the diaphragm, behind the stomach. The lower left ribs curve around it and protect it. When those ribs are fractured, or the left upper abdomen takes a hard blow, the spleen can tear and bleed heavily.
notes: Correct. The lower left ribs protect the spleen.
The left hip bone surrounds the lower abdominopelvic cavity, far below the spleen. It would be the answer for a question about the bone that houses the iliac crest, a site for marrow samples.
The sternum is in the midline of the anterior chest and lies in front of the thymus and heart. Choose it for a question about which bone sits in front of the thymus.
The lower right ribs protect the liver, which fills most of the right upper abdomen. Pick them for a question about the bones that shield the liver.
questions.answerText: The lower left ribs

questions.q: Which tissue of the spleen carries out its immune functions?
options: The capsule
White pulp
Red pulp
The venous sinuses
questions.why: White pulp is the spleen's lymphatic tissue, made of B cells and T cells clustered around the central arteries. As blood flows past, these lymphocytes respond to pathogens carried in the blood. Red pulp, which makes up most of the organ, handles the blood itself by removing old cells.
notes: The capsule is the dense connective tissue covering of the spleen and has no lymphocyte clusters. Choose the capsule for a question about what surrounds the organ.
Correct. White pulp carries out the spleen's immune function.
Red pulp filters blood and removes worn-out red cells and platelets, rather than mounting immune responses. Pick red pulp for a question about removing old erythrocytes.
Venous sinuses are wide blood channels within the red pulp. They would be the answer for where blood collects after leaving the splenic cords.
questions.answerText: White pulp

questions.q: Which tissue of the spleen contains the venous sinuses and Billroth's cords?
options: White pulp
The medulla
Red pulp
The cortex
questions.why: Red pulp is made of venous sinuses and the splenic cords (Billroth's cords) between them. Blood moves from the cords into the sinuses, and macrophages remove old and damaged red cells along the way. Red pulp makes up most of the spleen, with white pulp scattered through it as small islands.
notes: White pulp is lymphocytes clustered around central arteries, with no venous sinuses. Pick white pulp for a question about the spleen's immune tissue.
The medulla is a region of a lymph node or the thymus, not of the spleen. It would be the answer for where plasma cells collect in a lymph node.
Correct. Venous sinuses and Billroth's cords make up the red pulp.
The spleen is not divided into a cortex and medulla; those terms describe a lymph node, the thymus, or the kidney. Choose the cortex for a question about where follicles sit in a lymph node.
questions.answerText: Red pulp

questions.q: Which job belongs to the red pulp of the spleen rather than the white pulp?
options: Mounting immune responses to blood-borne pathogens
Absorbing dietary fats
Maturing pre-T cells
Removing worn-out red blood cells
questions.why: Red pulp is where the spleen deals with the blood itself. Macrophages in its splenic cords catch and destroy worn-out red blood cells and platelets, and the iron from old red cells is saved for reuse. White pulp, by contrast, is lymphatic tissue that mounts immune responses.
notes: Mounting immune responses is the job of the white pulp, where lymphocytes surround the central arteries. Pick this for a question about white pulp.
Dietary fats are absorbed by the lacteals of the small intestine. This would be the answer for a question about what lacteals do.
Pre-T cells mature in the thymus, not the spleen. Choose this for a question about the job of the thymic cortex.
Correct. Red pulp removes worn-out red blood cells.
questions.answerText: Removing worn-out red blood cells

questions.q: During a physical exam, a clinician feels the neck, armpits, and groin for swollen glands. What structures is she checking?
options: Lymph nodes
Tonsils
Sweat glands
Lymphatic trunks
questions.why: Swollen glands are enlarged lymph nodes. The large superficial clusters of nodes sit in the cervical (neck), axillary (armpit), and inguinal (groin) regions, close enough to the skin to be felt. Nodes swell when they are fighting an infection in the area they drain, or when cancer cells have spread into them.
notes: Correct. The clinician is feeling the cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes.
The tonsils are in the throat, not the armpits or groin. Pick the tonsils for a question about lymphatic tissue seen at the back of the mouth.
Sweat glands are in the dermis all over the body and are far too small to feel. Students pick them because of the word glands, but in this setting glands is an informal name for lymph nodes.

Lymphatic trunks are large vessels deep in the trunk, formed by merging collecting vessels, and they cannot be felt through the skin. Choose them for a question about the vessels that empty into the lymphatic ducts.
questions.answerText: Lymph nodes

questions.q: A small, bean-shaped structure sits along a lymphatic collecting vessel and filters the lymph. What is it?
options: A lymph node
A lacteal
The thymus
The spleen
questions.why: Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped organs spaced along the collecting vessels. Lymph enters through afferent vessels, slows down inside, and is cleaned by macrophages while lymphocytes check it for invaders. Filtered lymph then leaves through efferent vessels at the hilum.
notes: Correct. A lymph node is a small bean-shaped filter along the collecting vessels.
A lacteal is a lymphatic capillary in an intestinal villus that absorbs dietary fat. It would be the answer for where chyle begins.
The thymus is a bilobed organ in the mediastinum where T cells mature, and it does not filter lymph. Choose it for a question about T cell maturation.
The spleen is a single large organ in the upper left abdomen that filters blood, not lymph. Pick the spleen for a question about filtering blood.
questions.answerText: A lymph node

questions.q: Old red blood cells broken down in the spleen release products into the splenic vein, which joins the hepatic portal vein. Which organ receives these products next?
options: The kidneys
The pancreas
The lungs
The liver
questions.why: Blood leaving the spleen drains into the splenic vein, which joins the hepatic portal vein. The hepatic portal vein carries blood straight to the liver before it returns to the heart. As a result, the breakdown products of old red cells reach the liver first, where they can be processed.
notes: The kidneys receive blood from the renal arteries off the abdominal aorta, not from the hepatic portal vein. Choose the kidneys for a question about the renal blood supply.

The splenic vein runs along the back of the pancreas and receives small veins from it, but it does not deliver blood into the pancreas. Pick the pancreas for a question about which organ the splenic vein passes behind.
The lungs receive blood through the pulmonary trunk after it returns to the right side of the heart, well after the liver. They would be the answer for where blood is sent to pick up oxygen.
Correct. The splenic vein feeds the hepatic portal vein, which delivers blood to the liver.
questions.answerText: The liver

questions.q: A slide of a lymph node's outer cortex shows a round cluster of B cells with a pale center where cells are multiplying. What is the pale center called?
options: A thymic corpuscle
A medullary sinus
The subcapsular sinus
A germinal center
questions.why: The pale center of a lymphatic follicle is called the germinal center. It forms after an antigen arrives, when B cells in the follicle begin multiplying rapidly. The dividing cells there become plasma cells and memory B cells, and a follicle with a germinal center is a secondary nodule.
notes: A thymic corpuscle is a whorl of epithelial cells found only in the thymic medulla. Choose it for a question about identifying the thymus.
A medullary sinus is a channel in the medulla, deep in the node, lined with macrophages. Pick it for a question about where macrophages clean lymph before it leaves.
The subcapsular sinus is the space just under the capsule where lymph first enters the node. It would be the answer for the first space lymph reaches after the afferent vessels.
Correct. The pale center of a follicle is the germinal center.
questions.answerText: A germinal center

questions.q: A patient takes a hard blow to the left upper abdomen and develops heavy internal bleeding from a torn lymphatic organ. Which organ is it?
options: The spleen
An inguinal lymph node
A palatine tonsil
The thymus
questions.why: The spleen sits in the left upper abdomen behind the stomach, protected by the lower left ribs. Its soft tissue tears easily and it holds a large volume of blood, so a tear causes heavy internal bleeding, called a ruptured spleen. Patients with mononucleosis are told to avoid contact sports because their enlarged spleen ruptures more easily.
notes: Correct. A blow to the left upper abdomen can rupture the spleen.

Inguinal lymph nodes are in the groin, far from the left upper abdomen, and they do not hold enough blood to cause heavy bleeding. Choose them for a question about swollen nodes after a leg infection.
The palatine tonsils are in the lateral walls of the oropharynx. They would be the answer for a question about bleeding after a tonsillectomy.
The thymus is in the mediastinum behind the sternum, not the left upper abdomen. Pick the thymus for a question about chest trauma near the sternum.
questions.answerText: The spleen

questions.q: Which structures divide a lymph node into compartments?
options: Anchoring filaments
Billroth's cords
Trabeculae
Hassall's corpuscles
questions.why: Trabeculae are inward extensions of the dense connective tissue capsule of a lymph node. They reach into the node and divide it into compartments, also carrying blood vessels inward. The spleen has trabeculae too, built the same way from its capsule.
notes: Anchoring filaments tie lymphatic capillaries to the surrounding tissue so the capillaries stay open. They would be the answer for what holds a lymphatic capillary open.
Billroth's cords are the splenic cords in the red pulp of the spleen. Pick them for a question about where old red cells are caught in the spleen.
Correct. Trabeculae divide a lymph node into compartments.
Hassall's corpuscles are whorls of epithelial cells in the thymic medulla. Choose them for a question about a feature unique to the thymus.
questions.answerText: Trabeculae

questions.q: What is the inner region of a lymph node, made of cords and sinuses, called?
options: The deep cortex
The medulla
The subcapsular sinus
The hilum
questions.why: The medulla is the inner region of a lymph node. It is made of medullary cords, which hold B cells and plasma cells, and medullary sinuses lined with macrophages. Lymph passes through the medullary sinuses last before leaving through the efferent vessels at the hilum.
notes: The deep cortex lies between the outer cortex and the medulla and holds mostly T cells. Pick it for a question about the T cell zone.
Correct. The medulla is the inner region of cords and sinuses.
The subcapsular sinus is the space just under the capsule, at the outer edge of the node. It would be the answer for where lymph first enters.
The hilum is the indented side of the node where vessels enter and leave, not the internal region. Choose it for a question about where efferent vessels exit.
questions.answerText: The medulla

questions.q: At which part of a lymph node do the efferent vessels leave and the blood vessels enter?
options: The outer cortex
The subcapsular sinus
The capsule
The hilum
questions.why: The hilum is the indented side of a bean-shaped lymph node. Efferent lymphatic vessels carry filtered lymph out at the hilum, and blood vessels enter and leave there too. Afferent vessels, in contrast, enter at many points around the convex surface through the capsule.
notes: The outer cortex holds B cell follicles just inside the capsule. Choose it for a question about where follicles with germinal centers are found.
The subcapsular sinus is the first space lymph enters after the afferent vessels. It would be the answer for the start of lymph's path through the node.
The capsule is where the afferent vessels enter, all around the curved surface of the node. Pick the capsule for a question about where lymph comes into the node.
Correct. Efferent vessels leave and blood vessels enter at the hilum.
questions.answerText: The hilum

questions.q: Which structure belongs to the spleen rather than to a lymph node?
options: Billroth's cords
The deep cortex
The subcapsular sinus
Afferent lymphatic vessels
questions.why: Billroth's cords, the splenic cords, are strips of red pulp between the venous sinuses of the spleen. They hold red cells and macrophages that remove old blood cells. Lymph nodes have no red pulp, so they have no splenic cords; their own cords are the medullary cords of the medulla.
notes: Correct. Billroth's cords are part of the spleen's red pulp.
The deep cortex is the T cell zone of a lymph node. Pick it for a question about where T cells concentrate in a node.
The subcapsular sinus is the space under a lymph node's capsule where lymph first enters. Choose it for a question about the first stop for lymph in a node.
Afferent lymphatic vessels bring lymph into a lymph node. The spleen has none because it filters blood, so these would be the answer for a structure found only in a node.
questions.answerText: Billroth's cords

questions.q: Splenic white pulp is arranged around which vessels?
options: The trabecular veins
The afferent lymphatic vessels
The central arteries
The venous sinuses
questions.why: White pulp forms sleeves of lymphocytes around the central arteries, which branch from the trabecular arteries. As blood travels through these arteries, the surrounding lymphocytes can detect blood-borne pathogens. Blood then moves on into the cords and sinuses of the red pulp.
notes: Trabecular veins carry blood from the venous sinuses toward the splenic vein. Choose them for a question about blood leaving the spleen.
The spleen has no afferent lymphatic vessels because it filters blood, not lymph. These would be the answer for vessels carrying lymph into a lymph node.
Correct. White pulp surrounds the central arteries.
Venous sinuses are channels in the red pulp, downstream of the white pulp. Pick them for a question about where blood collects after the splenic cords.
questions.answerText: The central arteries

questions.q: Lymph enters a lymph node through the afferent vessels. Which space does it flow into first?
options: The subcapsular sinus
The medullary sinuses
The efferent vessels
The cortical sinuses
questions.why: Lymph moves through a node in a fixed order: afferent vessels, subcapsular sinus, cortical sinuses, medullary sinuses, and then efferent vessels at the hilum. The subcapsular sinus is the space just under the capsule, so it is the first space the lymph reaches. From there the lymph trickles inward past the lymphocytes and macrophages.
notes: Correct. The subcapsular sinus is the first space lymph enters.
The medullary sinuses are the last sinuses lymph passes through before leaving. Pick them for a question about the final sinuses before the efferent vessels.
Efferent vessels carry lymph out at the hilum, at the very end of the path. Choose them for a question about how filtered lymph leaves a node.
The cortical sinuses come second, after the subcapsular sinus. They would be the answer for the step between the subcapsular sinus and the medullary sinuses.
questions.answerText: The subcapsular sinus

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares what lymph nodes and the spleen filter?
options: Lymph nodes filter lymph, and the spleen filters blood
Both lymph nodes and the spleen filter only lymph
Both lymph nodes and the spleen filter only blood
Lymph nodes filter blood, and the spleen filters lymph
questions.why: Lymph nodes sit along the lymphatic collecting vessels, so they clean lymph before it returns to the bloodstream. The spleen has no afferent lymphatic vessels; instead it receives the splenic artery and filters blood, removing old red cells and responding to blood-borne pathogens. Both are secondary lymphatic organs, but they sit on different fluid routes.
notes: Correct. Nodes filter lymph, and the spleen filters blood.
The spleen receives blood through the splenic artery and has no afferent lymphatic vessels. This would be true only of lymph nodes.
Lymph nodes receive lymph through afferent vessels, so they do not filter only blood. This would be true only of the spleen.
This reverses the two organs. A lymph node receives afferent lymphatic vessels, while the spleen receives the splenic artery, so match each organ to the fluid that flows into it.
questions.answerText: Lymph nodes filter lymph, and the spleen filters blood

questions.q: Why does the red pulp of the spleen look red?
options: It stores oxygen-rich fat droplets in its cords
Its venous sinuses and cords are full of red blood cells
Its lymphocytes contain a red pigment of their own
Its capsule is made of red-staining elastic fibers
questions.why: Red pulp is built from venous sinuses and splenic cords that are packed with red blood cells, along with macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. All those red cells give the tissue its color. White pulp looks different because it is made mostly of lymphocytes around the central arteries.
notes: The spleen does not store fat or oxygen as droplets. This choice confuses the spleen with fatty tissue such as yellow marrow; oxygen in blood is carried by hemoglobin inside red cells.
Correct. The red color comes from the red blood cells filling the sinuses and cords.
Lymphocytes have no red pigment; the red pigment of blood is hemoglobin, found in erythrocytes. Lymphocytes are what make white pulp look different from red pulp.
The capsule of the spleen is dense connective tissue, and it covers the outside rather than giving the inner pulp its color. Choose the capsule for a question about what surrounds the spleen.
questions.answerText: Its venous sinuses and cords are full of red blood cells

questions.q: What does MALT stand for?
options: Medulla-associated lymph tubules
Mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue
Muscle-attached lymphatic tract
Membrane-anchored lymphocyte tissue
questions.why: MALT stands for mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue. It is lymphatic tissue scattered in the mucous membranes that line the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts. Because these tracts open to the outside, MALT is positioned to meet pathogens right where they try to enter.
notes: MALT is not tied to the medulla of any organ, and it is tissue rather than tubules. Students who pick this are mixing it up with the medulla of a lymph node or thymus.
Correct. MALT is mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue.
MALT has nothing to do with muscle or a tract of vessels. This choice comes from guessing at the letters rather than remembering that MALT lives in mucous membranes.
MALT is not anchored to a membrane by filaments. Anchoring filaments belong to lymphatic capillaries, which would be the answer for what holds those capillaries open.
questions.answerText: Mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue

questions.q: In the wall of the digestive tract, in which layer is MALT scattered?
options: The adventitia
The muscularis externa
The lamina propria of the mucosa
The serosa
questions.why: The mucosa is the innermost layer of the gut wall, made of an epithelium, a lamina propria of areolar connective tissue beneath it, and a thin muscularis mucosae. MALT is scattered in the lamina propria, just under the epithelium that contacts food and microbes. That position lets lymphocytes meet pathogens as soon as they cross the lining.
notes: The adventitia is a fibrous outer layer that replaces the serosa on the esophagus. It would be the answer for the outer layer of the esophagus.
The muscularis externa is the smooth muscle layer that moves food along, with the myenteric plexus between its layers. Pick it for a question about peristalsis.
Correct. MALT sits in the lamina propria of the mucosa.
The serosa is the outermost layer of most of the gut, a serous membrane also called the visceral peritoneum. Choose it for a question about the outer covering of the stomach or intestines.
questions.answerText: The lamina propria of the mucosa

questions.q: MALT lines the mucous membranes of which body systems?
options: The bones, cartilages, and synovial joints
The heart chambers, arteries, veins, and capillaries
The brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves
The digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts
questions.why: MALT guards mucous membranes, which line the body tracts that open to the outside: the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts. These are the entry points where pathogens are most likely to get in. Placing lymphatic tissue right in these linings lets the body respond at the point of entry.
notes: Bones and synovial joints have no mucous membranes; synovial joints are lined by a synovial membrane instead. These would be the answer for a question about where synovial fluid is made.
The heart and blood vessels are lined by endothelium, not a mucous membrane, so they have no MALT. Pick them for a question about the tunica intima.
The brain and spinal cord have no mucous membranes and no lymphatic capillaries. Choose them for a question about places where lymphatic capillaries are absent.
Correct. MALT lines the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts.
questions.answerText: The digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts

questions.q: Lymphatic tissue scattered through the mucous membranes, rather than gathered into an encapsulated organ, is called what?
options: MALT
Lymph nodes
White pulp
Thymic lobules
questions.why: MALT, mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue, is lymphatic tissue in the mucous membranes of the body's tracts. It has no surrounding capsule, which sets it apart from encapsulated organs like lymph nodes, the spleen, and the thymus. Peyer patches in the ileum, the appendix, and the tonsils are larger collections of this kind of tissue.
notes: Correct. MALT is unencapsulated lymphatic tissue in mucous membranes.
Lymph nodes are encapsulated organs along the collecting vessels. Pick them for a question about the organs that filter lymph.
White pulp is lymphatic tissue inside the encapsulated spleen, around the central arteries. Choose it for a question about the immune tissue of the spleen.
Thymic lobules are subdivisions of the encapsulated thymus. They would be the answer for the units that each contain a cortex and medulla in the thymus.
questions.answerText: MALT

questions.q: The tonsils form a ring of lymphatic tissue around the entrance to which passage?
options: The esophagus
The pharynx
The trachea
The larynx
questions.why: The tonsils form a ring around the entrance to the pharynx, the throat, where the nasal cavity and the oral cavity open into it. The pharyngeal tonsil sits on the back wall of the nasopharynx, the palatine tonsils in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, and the lingual tonsils at the base of the tongue. This ring guards against pathogens that are inhaled or swallowed.
notes: The esophagus begins below the pharynx and carries food to the stomach. It would be the answer for the tube that passes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm.
Correct. The tonsils ring the entrance to the pharynx.
The trachea is the airway below the larynx, held open by C-shaped cartilage rings. Choose it for a question about the airway that splits at the carina.
The larynx is the voice box below the pharynx, guarded by the epiglottis rather than the tonsils. Pick the larynx for a question about the vocal folds.
questions.answerText: The pharynx

questions.q: What is the pharyngeal tonsil also called?
options: The uvula
The lingual tonsil
The adenoid
The epiglottis
questions.why: The pharyngeal tonsil is also called the adenoid. It is a single mass of lymphatic tissue on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, the part of the throat behind the nasal cavity. When it swells, especially in children, it can block airflow through the nose.
notes: The uvula is the fleshy tab hanging from the back of the soft palate, not lymphatic tissue. Pick the uvula for a question about the soft palate.
The lingual tonsils are a separate set of tonsils at the base of the tongue. They would be the answer for the tonsils that guard swallowed material at the tongue's root.
Correct. The pharyngeal tonsil is the adenoid.
The epiglottis is a cartilage flap that covers the larynx during swallowing. Choose it for a question about what keeps food out of the airway.
questions.answerText: The adenoid

questions.q: Where is the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) located?
options: In the lateral walls of the oropharynx
At the base of the tongue
On the posterior wall of the nasopharynx
At the openings of the auditory tubes
questions.why: The pharyngeal tonsil, or adenoid, sits on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, the uppermost part of the pharynx behind the nasal cavity. Because it is in the path of air coming through the nose, it guards against inhaled pathogens. It is the highest of the tonsils in the ring around the throat.
notes: The lateral walls of the oropharynx, between the palatal arches, hold the palatine tonsils. Pick this for a question about the palatine tonsils.
The base of the tongue holds the lingual tonsils. Choose this location for a question about the lingual tonsils.
Correct. The adenoid sits on the back wall of the nasopharynx.
The openings of the auditory tubes hold the small paired tubal tonsils. This would be the answer for a question about the tubal tonsils.
questions.answerText: On the posterior wall of the nasopharynx

questions.q: Where are the palatine tonsils located?
options: At the openings of the auditory tubes
In the lateral walls of the oropharynx
On the posterior wall of the nasopharynx
At the base of the tongue
questions.why: The palatine tonsils are a pair of lymphatic masses in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, tucked between the palatal arches. They are the largest tonsils and the ones you can see when someone opens wide and says ah. They are also the tonsils most often infected and removed.
notes: The openings of the auditory tubes hold the tubal tonsils. This would be the answer for the tonsils near the tube connecting the middle ear to the throat.
Correct. The palatine tonsils sit in the lateral walls of the oropharynx.
The posterior wall of the nasopharynx holds the single pharyngeal tonsil, or adenoid. Pick this for a question about the adenoid.
The base of the tongue holds the lingual tonsils. Choose this location for a question about the lingual tonsils.
questions.answerText: In the lateral walls of the oropharynx

questions.q: Where are the lingual tonsils located?
options: In the lateral walls of the oropharynx
At the base of the tongue
At the openings of the auditory tubes
On the posterior wall of the nasopharynx
questions.why: The lingual tonsils sit at the base, or root, of the tongue. Lingual means relating to the tongue, which makes the name a direct clue to the location. They are the lowest tonsils in the ring and guard swallowed material on its way into the pharynx.
notes: The lateral walls of the oropharynx hold the palatine tonsils. Choose this for a question about the tonsils usually removed in a tonsillectomy.
Correct. The lingual tonsils are at the base of the tongue.
The openings of the auditory tubes hold the tubal tonsils. This would be the answer for a question about the tubal tonsils.
The posterior wall of the nasopharynx holds the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid). Pick this for a question about the adenoid.
questions.answerText: At the base of the tongue

questions.q: How many pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids) are there?
options: Three
Two
Four
One
questions.why: There is a single pharyngeal tonsil, the adenoid, on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx in the midline. The palatine tonsils, by contrast, are paired, one in each lateral wall of the oropharynx. Remembering that the midline tonsil is single and the side tonsils are paired keeps the counts straight.
notes: There are not three adenoids. This guess comes from mixing up the count of tonsil types (pharyngeal, palatine, and lingual) with the count of the pharyngeal tonsil itself.
Two is the number of palatine tonsils, one in each lateral wall of the oropharynx. Pick two for a question about how many palatine tonsils there are.
There are not four adenoids. Students who pick this are usually adding up paired tonsils from different groups rather than counting the single midline adenoid.
Correct. The pharyngeal tonsil is a single midline structure.
questions.answerText: One

questions.q: How many palatine tonsils are there?
options: One
Four
Three
Two
questions.why: The palatine tonsils are paired, with one in each lateral wall of the oropharynx between the palatal arches. They are the largest tonsils and the ones you can see in a throat exam. The single tonsil is the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) in the midline of the nasopharynx.
notes: One is the count for the pharyngeal tonsil, the single adenoid in the midline. Pick one for a question about how many adenoids there are.
There are not four palatine tonsils. Students pick this when they add two paired groups together, such as the palatine and tubal tonsils, instead of counting one pair.
There are not three palatine tonsils. This guess comes from confusing the count of tonsil types with the count of one type.
Correct. The palatine tonsils are a pair.
questions.answerText: Two

questions.q: Which tonsil lies on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx?
options: A tubal tonsil
The pharyngeal tonsil
A palatine tonsil
A lingual tonsil
questions.why: The pharyngeal tonsil, also called the adenoid, is a single mass of lymphatic tissue on the back wall of the nasopharynx. It sits in the path of air entering through the nose, so it guards against inhaled pathogens. Its name comes from the pharynx, the part of the throat it lines.
notes: The tubal tonsils are in the nasopharynx too, but at the openings of the auditory tubes on the side walls rather than on the posterior wall. Pick them for a question about tonsils near the auditory tubes.
Correct. The pharyngeal tonsil sits on the posterior nasopharyngeal wall.
The palatine tonsils are in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, below the nasopharynx. Pick a palatine tonsil for a question about the tonsils visible when the mouth is open.
The lingual tonsils are at the base of the tongue. Choose them for a question about the lowest tonsils in the ring.
questions.answerText: The pharyngeal tonsil

questions.q: Which tonsils sit in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, between the palatal arches?
options: The tubal tonsils
The pharyngeal tonsil
The palatine tonsils
The lingual tonsils
questions.why: The palatine tonsils are paired masses of lymphatic tissue in each lateral wall of the oropharynx, between the palatal arches. They are named for their position near the palate. Being the largest tonsils, they are the ones most often infected and removed.
notes: The tubal tonsils are at the openings of the auditory tubes in the nasopharynx. They would be the answer for tonsils next to the tube leading to the middle ear.
The pharyngeal tonsil is on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, above the soft palate. Choose it for a question about the adenoid.
Correct. The palatine tonsils sit in the lateral walls of the oropharynx.
The lingual tonsils are at the base of the tongue, not in the lateral walls of the oropharynx. Pick them for a question about lymphatic tissue on the root of the tongue.
questions.answerText: The palatine tonsils

questions.q: Which tonsils lie at the base of the tongue?
options: The pharyngeal tonsil
The tubal tonsils
The palatine tonsils
The lingual tonsils
questions.why: The lingual tonsils sit at the base of the tongue. Lingual means relating to the tongue, so the name gives away the location. They are the lowest part of the tonsil ring and guard food and drink as they are swallowed.
notes: The pharyngeal tonsil is on the back wall of the nasopharynx, the highest point of the ring. Choose it for a question about the adenoid.
The tubal tonsils are at the openings of the auditory tubes in the nasopharynx. They would be the answer for tonsils near the auditory tube openings.
The palatine tonsils are in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, above and lateral to the base of the tongue. Pick them for a question about the tonsils removed in a tonsillectomy.
Correct. The lingual tonsils are at the base of the tongue.
questions.answerText: The lingual tonsils

questions.q: What is the main job of the ring of tonsils around the throat?
options: To guard against inhaled and swallowed pathogens
To mature T cells for the whole body
To filter lymph returning from the head
To filter blood and remove old red cells
questions.why: The tonsils sit where the nasal and oral cavities open into the pharynx, the path taken by everything we breathe in or swallow. Their lymphatic tissue traps pathogens, partly in deep pits called crypts, so lymphocytes can recognize them and start an immune response. That makes the tonsils a secondary lymphatic tissue that guards an entry point.
notes: Correct. The tonsils guard against pathogens that are inhaled or swallowed.
Maturing T cells is the job of the thymus, a primary lymphatic organ. This would be the answer for a question about the thymus.
Filtering lymph is the job of lymph nodes, such as the cervical nodes in the neck. Pick this for a question about what the cervical lymph nodes do.
Filtering blood and removing old red cells is the job of the spleen. Choose this for a question about the splenic red pulp.
questions.answerText: To guard against inhaled and swallowed pathogens

questions.q: Which organ, attached to the cecum, has a wall packed with lymphatic follicles and counts as MALT?
options: The appendix
The sigmoid colon
The gallbladder
The pancreas
questions.why: The appendix is a narrow tube hanging off the cecum, the first part of the large intestine. Its wall is packed with lymphatic follicles, so it is counted as part of the MALT that guards the digestive tract. Along with the Peyer patches of the ileum, it monitors the contents of the gut.
notes: Correct. The appendix is packed with lymphatic follicles and counts as MALT.
The sigmoid colon is the S-shaped last part of the colon before the rectum, far from the cecum. It would be the answer for the segment of large intestine just above the rectum.
The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile under the liver, and it is not known for lymphatic follicles. Pick it for a question about where bile is stored.
The pancreas is an accessory digestive gland that makes digestive enzymes and contains the pancreatic islets. Choose it for a question about the gland whose duct joins the bile duct.
questions.answerText: The appendix

questions.q: A child snores and breathes through the mouth because enlarged lymphatic tissue blocks the back of the nasal passage. Which tonsil is most likely enlarged?
options: The pharyngeal tonsil
A tubal tonsil
A palatine tonsil
A lingual tonsil
questions.why: The pharyngeal tonsil, or adenoid, sits on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, right where air from the nose passes into the throat. When it swells, which is common in children, it blocks airflow through the nose and forces mouth breathing. The other tonsils sit lower or off to the side and do not block the nasal airway this way.
notes: Correct. An enlarged adenoid blocks the back of the nasal passage.

The tubal tonsils sit at the openings of the auditory tubes, and swelling there tends to affect the ear tubes rather than block the nasal airway. They would be the answer for tonsils near the auditory tube openings.

The palatine tonsils are in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, so swelling there narrows the throat behind the mouth rather than the nasal passage. Pick a palatine tonsil for a sore throat with visible swollen masses.
The lingual tonsils are at the base of the tongue, well below the nasal passage. Choose them for a question about lymphatic tissue on the root of the tongue.
questions.answerText: The pharyngeal tonsil

questions.q: A surgeon performs a tonsillectomy, removing the largest tonsils, the pair most often infected. Which tonsils are removed?
options: The tubal tonsils
The lingual tonsils
The palatine tonsils
The pharyngeal tonsil
questions.why: The palatine tonsils are the largest tonsils, paired in the lateral walls of the oropharynx. Because they are large and directly in the path of food and air, they are the ones most often infected, and they are what a tonsillectomy usually removes. Removing the pharyngeal tonsil is a separate procedure called an adenoidectomy.
notes: The tubal tonsils are small paired tonsils at the auditory tube openings. They would be the answer for tonsils located in the side walls of the nasopharynx.
The lingual tonsils are at the base of the tongue and are not the usual target of a tonsillectomy. Pick them for a question about lymphatic tissue on the tongue's root.
Correct. A tonsillectomy usually removes the paired palatine tonsils.
The pharyngeal tonsil is single, not a pair, and its removal is called an adenoidectomy. Choose it for a question about an enlarged adenoid blocking the nose.
questions.answerText: The palatine tonsils

questions.q: Lymphatic tissue scattered in the lining of the intestine guards against swallowed pathogens. What is this tissue?
options: The deep cortex of a lymph node
The thymic cortex
Splenic white pulp
MALT
questions.why: Lymphatic tissue in the mucous membrane of the intestine is MALT, mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue. It sits in the lamina propria just beneath the epithelium, where it meets microbes that arrive with food. Larger collections, such as the Peyer patches of the ileum and the appendix, are part of the same system.
notes: The deep cortex is the T cell zone inside an encapsulated lymph node, not the gut lining. It would be the answer for where T cells concentrate in a node.
The thymic cortex is inside the thymus in the mediastinum, where immature T cells develop. Pick it for a question about where pre-T cells multiply.
Splenic white pulp is lymphatic tissue inside the spleen, around the central arteries. Choose it for a question about immune responses to blood-borne pathogens.
Correct. Lymphatic tissue in the intestinal lining is MALT.
questions.answerText: MALT

questions.q: Which of these is NOT lined by MALT?
options: The urinary tract
The inside of the blood vessels
The respiratory tract
The gastrointestinal tract
questions.why: MALT lines the mucous membranes of tracts that open to the outside of the body: the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts. Blood vessels are a closed system lined by endothelium, a simple squamous epithelium, not a mucous membrane. Since pathogens do not enter the body through the inside of a blood vessel, there is no MALT there.
notes: The urinary tract is lined by a mucous membrane with MALT. It would be a correct choice for a question asking which tracts MALT does guard.
Correct. Blood vessels are lined by endothelium, not a mucous membrane, so they have no MALT.
The respiratory tract is lined by a mucous membrane with MALT, guarding against inhaled pathogens. Choose it for a question about lymphatic tissue that meets inhaled microbes.
The gastrointestinal tract has abundant MALT, including Peyer patches and the appendix. Pick it if the question asked where Peyer patches are found.
questions.answerText: The inside of the blood vessels

questions.q: The tonsil ring guards which two openings into the pharynx?
options: The pharynx into the esophagus and the esophagus into the stomach
The nasal cavity into the nasopharynx and the mouth into the oropharynx
The larynx into the trachea and the trachea into the bronchi
The stomach into the duodenum and the ileum into the cecum
questions.why: Air enters the pharynx from the nasal cavity at the nasopharynx, and food and air enter from the mouth at the oropharynx. The tonsils are placed at these two entrances: the pharyngeal tonsil at the nasopharynx, and the palatine and lingual tonsils around the oropharynx. Everything inhaled or swallowed passes them first.
notes: These junctions are guarded by the upper and lower esophageal sphincters, not by tonsils. Choose this pair for a question about the sphincters of the esophagus.
Correct. The tonsils guard where the nasal and oral cavities open into the pharynx.
These junctions lie below the pharynx in the lower respiratory tract, where there is no ring of tonsils. Pick this pair for a question about the path of air below the larynx.

These are junctions inside the digestive tract guarded by the pyloric sphincter and the ileocecal valve. Lymphatic tissue near the ileocecal junction is Peyer patches and the appendix, so pick this for a question about gut MALT.
questions.answerText: The nasal cavity into the nasopharynx and the mouth into the oropharynx

questions.q: How does the pharyngeal tonsil differ from the palatine tonsils?
options: It is paired, while the palatine tonsils are single
It is the largest tonsil and the one usually removed
It sits at the base of the tongue, below them
It is single, while the palatine tonsils are paired
questions.why: The pharyngeal tonsil, or adenoid, is one mass on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, right in the midline. The palatine tonsils come as a pair, one in each lateral wall of the oropharynx. A structure sitting in the midline is often single, while structures on the side walls usually come in pairs.
notes: This reverses the counts. The midline adenoid is single, and the palatine tonsils sit one on each side, so they are paired.
The palatine tonsils, not the pharyngeal tonsil, are the largest and the ones usually removed in a tonsillectomy. This choice would describe the palatine tonsils.

The base of the tongue is the location of the lingual tonsils, and the pharyngeal tonsil is actually the highest tonsil, up in the nasopharynx. Pick the base of the tongue for a question about the lingual tonsils.
Correct. The pharyngeal tonsil is single and the palatine tonsils are a pair.
questions.answerText: It is single, while the palatine tonsils are paired

questions.q: A slide of the ileum wall shows large clusters of lymphatic follicles in the mucosa, with no capsule around them. What are these clusters?
options: Thymic lobules
Splenic white pulp
Lymph nodes
Peyer patches
questions.why: Peyer patches are clusters of lymphatic follicles in the wall of the ileum, the last part of the small intestine. They are a type of MALT, so they have no capsule, and they monitor the intestinal contents for pathogens. Their location in the ileum and their lack of a capsule separate them from encapsulated organs like lymph nodes.
notes: Thymic lobules are subdivisions of the thymus in the mediastinum, each with a cortex and medulla. They would be the answer for the units of the thymus.
White pulp is inside the spleen, around the central arteries. Choose it for a question about the spleen's immune tissue.
Lymph nodes are encapsulated organs along lymphatic collecting vessels, not clusters inside the intestinal mucosa. Pick them for a question about encapsulated filters of lymph.
Correct. Clusters of follicles in the ileum wall are Peyer patches.
questions.answerText: Peyer patches

questions.q: Peyer patches are found in the wall of which part of the digestive tract?
options: The esophagus
The ileum
The rectum
The stomach
questions.why: Peyer patches are clusters of lymphatic follicles in the wall of the ileum, the final segment of the small intestine. They are part of MALT and watch the intestinal contents for pathogens before material passes into the large intestine. The appendix, attached to the nearby cecum, is another gut structure packed with follicles.
notes: The esophagus carries food from the pharynx to the stomach and is not the site of Peyer patches. Pick the esophagus for a question about the tube that passes through the diaphragm.
Correct. Peyer patches are in the ileum.
The rectum is the last part of the large intestine before the anal canal. It would be the answer for where feces are stored before defecation.
The stomach churns food and has rugae and gastric pits, but Peyer patches are not a feature of it. Choose the stomach for a question about rugae.
questions.answerText: The ileum

questions.q: During a throat exam, a clinician sees a mass of lymphatic tissue on each side at the back of the mouth, between the palatal arches. Which tonsils are these?
options: The lingual tonsils
The pharyngeal tonsil
The palatine tonsils
The tubal tonsils
questions.why: The paired masses between the palatal arches are the palatine tonsils. They sit in the lateral walls of the oropharynx and are the tonsils you can see when a patient opens wide. The pharyngeal and tubal tonsils are hidden up in the nasopharynx, and the lingual tonsils are lower, on the base of the tongue.
notes: The lingual tonsils are on the base of the tongue, lower than the palatal arches and harder to see without a mirror. Pick them for a question about the root of the tongue.
The pharyngeal tonsil is single and sits up in the nasopharynx, out of view in a normal throat exam. Choose it for a question about the adenoid.
Correct. The visible paired masses between the palatal arches are the palatine tonsils.
The tubal tonsils are in the nasopharynx at the auditory tube openings, also out of view. They would be the answer for the tonsils near the auditory tubes.
questions.answerText: The palatine tonsils

questions.q: MALT and the tonsils are both secondary lymphatic tissue. What do they have in common?
options: Both guard mucosal entry points into the body
Both filter blood like the spleen
Both are primary organs where lymphocytes mature
Both are encapsulated filters along lymph vessels
questions.why: The tonsils and MALT are both lymphatic tissue embedded in mucous membranes. They sit where pathogens are most likely to enter: the tonsils at the entrance to the throat, and MALT along the linings of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts. Mature lymphocytes there meet invaders at the point of entry.
notes: Correct. Both guard mucosal surfaces where pathogens enter.
Filtering blood is the job of the spleen, which receives the splenic artery. Choose this for a question about the spleen.
The primary organs are red bone marrow and the thymus, where lymphocytes form and mature. Pick this for a question about the thymus or red marrow.
Encapsulated filters along lymphatic vessels are lymph nodes. MALT has no capsule, so this would be the answer for a question describing lymph nodes.
questions.answerText: Both guard mucosal entry points into the body

questions.q: Which structure seen at the back of the mouth is NOT a tonsil?
options: The pharyngeal tonsil
The lingual tonsil
The palatine tonsil
The uvula
questions.why: The three tonsils on the lab list are the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) in the nasopharynx, the palatine tonsils in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, and the lingual tonsils at the base of the tongue. The uvula is the small fleshy projection hanging from the back of the soft palate. It is muscle and connective tissue covered by mucosa, not a mass of lymphatic tissue.
notes: The pharyngeal tonsil, or adenoid, is a tonsil on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx. Pick it for a question about the tonsil that blocks nasal breathing when enlarged.
The lingual tonsils are tonsils at the base of the tongue. They would be the answer for the lowest tonsils in the ring.
The palatine tonsils are tonsils in the lateral walls of the oropharynx. Choose them for a question about the tonsils usually removed in a tonsillectomy.
Correct. The uvula hangs from the soft palate and is not a tonsil.
questions.answerText: The uvula

questions.q: Which choice correctly pairs a tonsil with its location?
options: Lingual tonsil: openings of the auditory tubes
Lingual tonsil: base of the tongue
Pharyngeal tonsil: base of the tongue
Palatine tonsil: posterior wall of the nasopharynx
questions.why: The lingual tonsils are at the base of the tongue, which matches their name, since lingual means of the tongue. The pharyngeal tonsil is on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, the palatine tonsils are in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, and the tubal tonsils are at the auditory tube openings. Matching each name to its location is the core of the tonsil identification task in lab.
notes: The openings of the auditory tubes are the site of the tubal tonsils. This location would be right for a question about the tubal tonsils.
Correct. The lingual tonsils sit at the base of the tongue.
The pharyngeal tonsil is up in the nasopharynx, not on the tongue. The base of the tongue would be right for the lingual tonsils.
The posterior wall of the nasopharynx is the location of the pharyngeal tonsil, not the palatine tonsil. Pick this location for a question about the adenoid.
questions.answerText: Lingual tonsil: base of the tongue

questions.q: Tonsils have deep pits in their surface that trap bacteria so lymphocytes can learn to recognize them. What are these pits called?
options: Crypts
Sinuses
Alveoli
Rugae
questions.why: Tonsillar crypts are deep pits that dip inward from the surface of a tonsil. Bacteria and debris get trapped in them, which brings the microbes into close contact with the lymphocytes inside the tonsil. This lets the immune system learn to recognize pathogens entering through the mouth and nose.
notes: Correct. The pits in the tonsils are crypts.

Sinuses are open spaces or channels, such as the sinuses of a lymph node that lymph flows through, or the paranasal sinuses in the skull. Pick sinuses for a question about the path of lymph through a node.
Alveoli are the tiny air sacs of the lungs where gas exchange happens. They would be the answer for the site of the respiratory membrane.
Rugae are folds in the lining of an organ that let it stretch, such as the folds of the empty stomach. Choose rugae for a question about the stomach lining.
questions.answerText: Crypts

questions.q: Infected, inflamed tonsils, common in childhood, are called what?
options: Lymphadenitis
Tonsillitis
Lymphedema
Splenomegaly
questions.why: Tonsillitis is infection and inflammation of the tonsils, most often the palatine tonsils. The suffix -itis means inflammation, so the name says exactly what is happening. Repeated bouts of tonsillitis are a common reason for a tonsillectomy.
notes: Lymphadenitis is inflammation of lymph nodes, which become swollen and tender while fighting an infection. Pick it for a question about tender nodes in the neck.
Correct. Inflamed, infected tonsils are tonsillitis.
Lymphedema is long-term swelling caused by blocked or missing lymphatic vessels, sometimes after nodes are removed. It would be the answer for a swollen arm after breast cancer surgery.
Splenomegaly is an enlarged spleen, seen in mononucleosis and leukemia. Choose it for a question about why patients with mono avoid contact sports.
questions.answerText: Tonsillitis

questions.q: Which lymphatic tissue lines the mucous membranes of the reproductive tract?
options: Red bone marrow
The thymic medulla
MALT
White pulp
questions.why: The reproductive tract opens to the outside of the body, so its mucous membrane is guarded by MALT, mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue. The same kind of tissue lines the digestive, respiratory, and urinary tracts. In each of these tracts, MALT lets lymphocytes meet pathogens at the point of entry.
notes: Red bone marrow is a primary lymphatic organ inside spongy bone. It would be the answer for where all lymphocytes form.
The thymic medulla is the inner region of the thymus in the mediastinum. Choose it for a question about where Hassall's corpuscles are found.
Correct. MALT lines the reproductive tract mucosa.
White pulp is lymphatic tissue inside the spleen, around the central arteries. Pick it for a question about the spleen's immune tissue.
questions.answerText: MALT

questions.q: Starting in the nasopharynx and moving down toward the base of the tongue, in which order do you meet the pharyngeal, palatine, and lingual tonsils?
options: Palatine, then pharyngeal, then lingual
Lingual, then palatine, then pharyngeal
Pharyngeal, then palatine, then lingual
Pharyngeal, then lingual, then palatine
questions.why: The pharyngeal tonsil is highest, on the back wall of the nasopharynx behind the nasal cavity. Below it, the palatine tonsils sit in the lateral walls of the oropharynx between the palatal arches. The lingual tonsils are lowest, on the base of the tongue where food enters the oropharynx.
notes: The palatine tonsils are in the oropharynx, below the nasopharynx, so they cannot come before the pharyngeal tonsil. This mistake comes from forgetting that the adenoid sits above the soft palate.
This is the correct order read backward, from the tongue up to the nasopharynx. Pick it only if the question asked you to start at the base of the tongue and move up.
Correct. The order going down is pharyngeal, palatine, and then lingual.
This swaps the palatine and lingual tonsils. The lingual tonsils are on the base of the tongue, which is the lowest point of the ring.
questions.answerText: Pharyngeal, then palatine, then lingual

questions.q: Which tonsils are paired and sit at the openings of the auditory tubes?
options: The pharyngeal tonsil
The palatine tonsils
The lingual tonsils
The tubal tonsils
questions.why: The tubal tonsils are small paired masses of lymphatic tissue at the openings of the auditory tubes in the side walls of the nasopharynx. The auditory tubes connect the middle ear to the throat, so these tonsils guard that passage. They sit close to the pharyngeal tonsil, which is on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx.
notes: The pharyngeal tonsil is in the nasopharynx near the auditory tubes, but it is single and sits on the posterior wall. It would be the answer for a question about the adenoid.
The palatine tonsils are paired too, but they sit in the lateral walls of the oropharynx. Pick them for a question about the tonsils removed in a tonsillectomy.
The lingual tonsils are on the base of the tongue, far below the auditory tubes. Choose them for a question about the lowest tonsils in the ring.
Correct. The tubal tonsils are paired and sit at the auditory tube openings.
questions.answerText: The tubal tonsils

questions.q: What is the general shape of a lymph node?
options: Flat and disc-shaped
Small and bean-shaped
Long and tubular
Branching and tree-like
questions.why: A lymph node is a small, bean-shaped organ wrapped in a connective tissue capsule. The indented side of the bean is the hilum, where blood vessels enter and the efferent lymphatic vessels leave. Afferent vessels enter around the rounded outer surface, so lymph passes all the way through the node before leaving.
notes: A flat disc shape describes an erythrocyte, the biconcave red blood cell. It would fit a question about red cell shape, not a lymphatic organ.
Correct. Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped organs with a hilum on the indented side.
A long, tubular shape describes a lymphatic vessel such as a collecting vessel or the thoracic duct. Pick it if the question asked about the vessels that carry lymph between nodes.
A branching, tree-like pattern describes the network of lymphatic capillaries and collecting vessels, or the bronchial tree of the lungs. A single node is a compact organ, not a branching system.
questions.answerText: Small and bean-shaped

questions.q: Which region of a lymph node lies just inside the capsule and is packed with lymphocytes in rounded clusters called follicles?
options: The cortex
The medulla
The capsule
The hilum
questions.why: The cortex is the outer region of a lymph node, just beneath the capsule. Its outer part holds follicles, rounded clusters of lymphocytes with pale germinal centers where B cells multiply, and its deeper part holds mostly T cells. Lymph filters through the cortex before moving into the medulla.
notes: Correct. The cortex is the outer region of the node, filled with lymphocyte follicles.

The medulla is the inner region of the node, made of medullary cords and sinuses lined with macrophages. Pick it if the question asked about the deep region where lymph collects before leaving the node.
The capsule is the dense connective tissue covering around the node, with trabeculae extending inward. It wraps the node but holds no follicles of lymphocytes.
The hilum is the indented side of the node where blood vessels enter and efferent vessels leave. Pick it if the question asked where filtered lymph exits the node.
questions.answerText: The cortex

questions.q: Where do lymph nodes cluster most heavily in the body?
options: Inside the vertebral canal around the spinal cord
In the palms and the soles of the feet
In the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions
Within the wall of the heart
questions.why: Lymph nodes gather in large groups in the neck (cervical), the armpit (axillary), and the groin (inguinal), with more deep groups in the thorax and abdomen. These regions sit where lymph from the head, the limbs, and the trunk collects on its way back to the blood. This is why a clinician feels the neck, armpits, and groin when checking for swollen nodes.
notes: The central nervous system does not have lymphatic capillaries, so nodes do not cluster around the spinal cord. Pick the vertebral canal for a question about where the spinal cord and its meninges sit.
The palms and soles have lymphatic capillaries draining them, but the nodes that filter that lymph sit farther up the limbs, mainly in the axillary and inguinal regions.
Correct. The cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions hold the largest superficial clusters of lymph nodes.
The heart wall is cardiac muscle with coronary vessels. Lymph from the heart drains to nodes in the mediastinum, not to clusters inside the heart wall.
questions.answerText: In the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions

questions.q: Which two organs are the primary lymphatic organs?
options: The spleen and the tonsils
The spleen and the lymph nodes
The lymph nodes and MALT
Red bone marrow and the thymus
questions.why: Primary lymphatic organs are where lymphocytes form and mature. All lymphocytes are made in red bone marrow, and B cells finish maturing there, while T cell precursors travel to the thymus to mature. The remaining lymphatic organs are secondary, meaning they are the places where mature lymphocytes meet invaders.
notes: The spleen and tonsils are secondary organs. The spleen filters blood and the tonsils guard the entrance to the throat, but neither is where lymphocytes mature.
The spleen and lymph nodes are both secondary organs. This pair would be right if the question asked which organs filter blood and lymph, respectively.
Lymph nodes and MALT are secondary lymphatic tissue where mature lymphocytes meet pathogens. Pick this pair for a question about where lymph is filtered and mucous membranes are guarded.
Correct. Red bone marrow and the thymus are where lymphocytes form and mature.
questions.answerText: Red bone marrow and the thymus

questions.q: Where do T cells mature?
options: In the tonsils
In the spleen
In the thymus
In the lymph nodes
questions.why: T cells start as stem cells in red bone marrow, but their precursors travel to the thymus to finish maturing. The thymus sits in the mediastinum, above the heart and behind the sternum. The T in T cell stands for thymus.
notes: The tonsils are secondary lymphatic tissue around the entrance to the throat. They hold mature lymphocytes that meet inhaled and swallowed pathogens, so pick them for that guarding role.
The spleen is a secondary organ in the upper left abdomen that filters blood. Mature T cells gather in its white pulp, but they did not mature there.
Correct. T cells mature in the thymus, which gives them their name.
Lymph nodes are secondary organs along the collecting vessels. Mature T cells settle in the deep cortex of a node, but they finished maturing in the thymus first.
questions.answerText: In the thymus

questions.q: Where is the spleen located?
options: In the upper left abdomen, behind the stomach
In a ring around the entrance to the throat
Behind the sternum in the mediastinum
Along the collecting vessels of the groin
questions.why: The spleen is the largest lymphatic organ and sits in the upper left abdomen against the diaphragm, behind the stomach. The lower left ribs protect it, which is why a hard blow to that area can rupture it. The splenic artery and vein pass through its hilum.
notes: Correct. The spleen lies in the upper left abdomen, behind the stomach and under the lower left ribs.
A ring around the entrance to the throat describes the tonsils. Pick it for a question about the lymphatic tissue that guards inhaled and swallowed material.
Behind the sternum in the mediastinum is the location of the thymus. Pick this location if the question asked where T cells mature.
Lymph nodes cluster along collecting vessels in the groin as the inguinal nodes. Pick this location for a question about the nodes that filter lymph from the lower limb.
questions.answerText: In the upper left abdomen, behind the stomach

questions.q: Which tissue of the spleen filters the blood and removes worn-out red blood cells?
options: The capsule
The hilum
Red pulp
White pulp
questions.why: Red pulp makes up most of the spleen and is built of venous sinuses and splenic cords full of red cells and macrophages. As blood squeezes through it, macrophages remove old and damaged red cells and platelets and save their iron for reuse. That is where the red pulp gets its color and its filtering job.
notes: The capsule is the connective tissue covering around the spleen. It shapes and protects the organ but does not filter blood.
The hilum is where the splenic artery and vein enter and leave the spleen. Pick it for a question about where vessels pass into the organ.
Correct. Red pulp is the spleen's filtering tissue, where macrophages remove worn-out red cells.
White pulp is made of lymphocytes clustered around central arteries and handles the spleen's immune function. Pick white pulp if the question asked which part of the spleen mounts immune responses.
questions.answerText: Red pulp

questions.q: What is another name for the pharyngeal tonsil?
options: The adenoid
The lingual tonsil
The palatine tonsil
The tubal tonsil
questions.why: The pharyngeal tonsil is a single tonsil on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, and it is also called the adenoid. When it swells, especially in children, it can block airflow through the nose. It is one of the tonsils that form a protective ring around the entrance to the throat.
notes: Correct. The pharyngeal tonsil is also called the adenoid.
The lingual tonsils sit at the base of the tongue and guard swallowed material. Pick them if the question asked which tonsils lie on the back of the tongue.
The palatine tonsils are the paired tonsils in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, the ones usually infected and removed. Pick them for a question about tonsillitis or a tonsillectomy.
The tubal tonsils are paired patches at the openings of the auditory tubes in the nasopharynx. They are neighbors of the pharyngeal tonsil but are not called the adenoid.
questions.answerText: The adenoid

questions.q: Which vessels carry lymph into a lymph node?
options: The afferent lymphatic vessels
The efferent lymphatic vessels
The lymphatic trunks
The renal collecting ducts
questions.why: Afferent vessels carry lymph into a node through several points on its capsule, and afferent means carrying toward. Lymph then passes through the subcapsular, cortical, and medullary sinuses before leaving through fewer efferent vessels at the hilum. Because more vessels enter than leave, lymph slows down inside the node, giving macrophages time to clean it.
notes: Correct. Afferent vessels bring lymph into the node through the capsule.
Efferent vessels carry filtered lymph out of the node at the hilum. Pick them if the question asked which vessels leave the node.
Lymphatic trunks are large vessels formed farther along the pathway, after lymph has passed through the nodes. They drain whole body regions into the ducts.
Collecting ducts belong to the kidney, where they carry urine toward the renal papilla. The name looks like lymphatic collecting vessels, but it is part of the urinary system.
questions.answerText: The afferent lymphatic vessels

questions.q: Which lymphatic organ filters the blood rather than the lymph?
options: The thymus
A palatine tonsil
A lymph node
The spleen
questions.why: The spleen is the only lymphatic organ that filters blood. Blood enters through the splenic artery, and in the red pulp macrophages remove worn-out red cells while lymphocytes in the white pulp watch for blood-borne pathogens. Lymph nodes do the matching job for lymph.
notes: The thymus is a primary organ where T cells mature, and it does not filter either blood or lymph. Pick it for a question about T cell maturation.
The palatine tonsils sit in the lateral walls of the oropharynx and guard against swallowed and inhaled pathogens. They trap bacteria in their crypts but do not filter the blood.
Lymph nodes filter lymph, not blood. Pick a lymph node if the question asked which organ cleans lymph before it returns to the bloodstream.
Correct. The spleen is the lymphatic organ that filters blood.
questions.answerText: The spleen

questions.q: Which secondary lymphatic tissue guards the mucous membranes of the digestive and respiratory tracts?
options: Red bone marrow
The spleen
MALT
The thymus
questions.why: MALT stands for mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue. It is lymphatic tissue placed in the linings of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts, where pathogens are most likely to enter. Examples include the tonsils, the Peyer patches of the ileum, and the follicles in the wall of the appendix.
notes: Red bone marrow is a primary organ where all lymphocytes form and B cells mature. Pick it for a question about where lymphocytes are made.
The spleen is a secondary organ, but it filters blood in the upper left abdomen instead of guarding mucosal linings. Pick it for a question about blood filtering.
Correct. MALT guards the mucous membranes of the body's tracts.
The thymus is a primary organ in the mediastinum where T cells mature. It sits behind the sternum, not in a mucous membrane.
questions.answerText: MALT

questions.q: Where do B cells mature?
options: In the thymus
In the spleen
In red bone marrow
In the tonsils
questions.why: All lymphocytes form from stem cells in red bone marrow. B cells stay in the marrow to finish maturing, while T cell precursors leave for the thymus. Once mature, B cells move to secondary organs, and when they meet an invader some become plasma cells that make antibodies.
notes: The thymus is where T cells mature, not B cells. Pick the thymus if the question asked about T cell maturation.
The spleen is a secondary organ where mature B cells gather in the white pulp. They arrive there already mature from the marrow.
Correct. B cells form and mature in red bone marrow.
The tonsils hold follicles where mature B cells multiply when they meet a pathogen. They are secondary tissue, not a place of maturation.
questions.answerText: In red bone marrow

questions.q: During a physical exam, a clinician feels tender, enlarged lumps in a patient's neck and armpit. Which structures are enlarged?
options: The lymph nodes
The lymphatic capillaries
The thoracic duct
The lacteals
questions.why: Swollen glands are enlarged lymph nodes. The cervical and axillary regions hold large clusters of nodes, and when the lymphocytes inside meet an infection they multiply, making the nodes swell and often become tender. That is why clinicians feel the neck, armpits, and groin during an exam.
notes: Correct. Tender, enlarged lumps in the neck and armpit are swollen lymph nodes.
Lymphatic capillaries are microscopic dead-end tubes in the tissues. They are far too small to feel, and they do not swell into lumps during an infection.
The thoracic duct runs deep in the thorax and abdomen and cannot be felt in the neck and armpit. Pick it for a question about the vessel that drains most of the body.
Lacteals are lymphatic capillaries inside the villi of the small intestine. Pick them for a question about fat absorption, not swelling in the neck or armpit.
questions.answerText: The lymph nodes

questions.q: A hard blow to the lower left ribs tears a soft lymphatic organ that holds a large volume of blood, causing heavy internal bleeding. Which organ is most at risk?
options: The thymus
A palatine tonsil
An inguinal lymph node
The spleen
questions.why: The spleen sits in the upper left abdomen under the lower left ribs, and it is the lymphatic organ that filters blood. Because it is soft and holds a large volume of blood, a tear causes heavy internal bleeding. Its location explains why rib injuries on the left side raise concern for a ruptured spleen.
notes: The thymus lies in the mediastinum behind the sternum, not under the lower left ribs. It also does not filter blood.
The palatine tonsils sit in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, far from the ribs. Pick them for a question about tonsillitis.
Inguinal lymph nodes lie in the groin and filter lymph, not blood. Pick them if the question asked which nodes drain the lower limb.
Correct. The spleen lies under the lower left ribs and holds a large volume of blood, so a tear bleeds heavily.
questions.answerText: The spleen

questions.q: A patient is diagnosed with a cancer of the lymphocytes in lymphatic tissue, classified as Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin type. Which disorder is this?
options: Lymphoma
Lymphedema
Splenomegaly
Edema
questions.why: Lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphocytes that arises in lymphatic tissue such as the lymph nodes. It is divided into Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin types. The suffix -oma means tumor, which separates it from the swelling disorders with similar names.
notes: Correct. Lymphoma is cancer of lymphocytes in lymphatic tissue.
Lymphedema is long-term swelling from blocked or missing lymphatic vessels. Its name shares the lymph- root, but it is a drainage problem, not a cancer.
Splenomegaly is an enlarged spleen. It can happen in some blood cancers such as leukemia, but the term names the enlargement, not a cancer of lymphatic tissue.
Edema is swelling in the interstitial spaces when fluid leaks out faster than the lymphatics can drain it. It is fluid buildup, not cancer.
questions.answerText: Lymphoma

questions.q: To learn whether a cancer has begun to spread, a surgeon checks the first lymph node that a region drains into. What is this node called?
options: The sentinel node
The afferent node
The efferent node
The germinal node
questions.why: Lymph passes through nodes in a set order, so cancer cells traveling in lymph reach the first node along the route before any others. That first node is called the sentinel node, meaning the guard. If it is free of cancer, the surgeon has good evidence the cancer has not spread through the lymph.
notes: Correct. The sentinel node is the first node a region drains into.
Afferent is the name of the vessels that carry lymph into a node, not a type of node. Students choose this because afferent means toward, but no node is called the afferent node.
Efferent is the name of the vessels that carry lymph out of a node at the hilum. Pick efferent vessels for a question about where filtered lymph leaves a node.
Germinal centers are the pale centers of lymphatic follicles where B cells multiply. The term describes a region inside a node, not the first node in a drainage route.
questions.answerText: The sentinel node

questions.q: Lymph nodes sit along the collecting vessels and are packed with immune cells. Why is this placement effective for fighting infection?
options: The nodes store extra lymph and release it when blood volume drops
The nodes send cleaned lymph back out into the tissue spaces to reuse it
The nodes add fresh fluid to the lymph so it flows faster toward the heart
Lymph must pass through them, so pathogens are caught before reaching the blood
questions.why: Every collecting vessel passes through one or more nodes on its way to the trunks, so all lymph is screened before it rejoins the blood. Inside a node, lymph slows down because more afferent vessels enter than efferent vessels leave. Macrophages engulf bacteria and debris, and lymphocytes meet invaders and start an immune response.
notes: Nodes filter lymph rather than storing it. The spleen stores platelets and monocytes, which may be the source of this mix-up.
Lymph never returns to the tissue spaces. After filtering, it leaves the node through efferent vessels and continues toward the trunks and ducts.
Nodes do not add fluid. Lymph actually slows down inside a node so the immune cells have time to clean it.
Correct. Placing nodes along the route means pathogens in lymph are filtered out before reaching the blood.
questions.answerText: Lymph must pass through them, so pathogens are caught before reaching the blood

questions.q: A bacterial infection is spreading in the bloodstream. Why is the spleen, rather than the lymph nodes, positioned to catch these pathogens directly?
options: The spleen sits along the thoracic duct and filters its contents
Lymph nodes contain no lymphocytes to fight infection
Blood flows through the spleen, while lymph nodes filter only lymph
