The spleen receives afferent lymphatic vessels that carry blood into it
questions.why: The splenic artery brings blood into the spleen, where it passes the lymphocytes of the white pulp and the macrophages of the red pulp before leaving by the splenic vein. That lets the spleen screen blood for pathogens while it also removes worn-out red cells. Lymph nodes sit on lymphatic vessels and only see lymph, so they catch pathogens that enter from the tissues.
notes: The thoracic duct runs through the thorax and empties into the veins at the base of the neck. The spleen lies in the upper left abdomen and is not on the duct's path.
Lymph nodes are packed with lymphocytes in their cortex. They fight infection well, but only in lymph, not in the bloodstream.
Correct. The spleen filters blood, so it can catch pathogens circulating in the bloodstream.
Afferent lymphatic vessels belong to lymph nodes and carry lymph, not blood. The spleen receives blood through the splenic artery at its hilum.
questions.answerText: Blood flows through the spleen, while lymph nodes filter only lymph

questions.q: The thymus is large in children but shrinks after puberty and is mostly fat in older adults. Which explanation fits its job?
options: It is where B cells mature, and that happens mostly in childhood
It stores fat for growth, which is used up after puberty
It is where T cells mature, and most of that maturing happens early in life
It filters lymph, and children produce more lymph than adults
questions.why: The thymus is a primary lymphatic organ in the mediastinum where T cell precursors from the marrow mature. A large supply of mature T cells is built up in infancy and childhood, so the gland is biggest and busiest then. After puberty the thymus shrinks and is gradually replaced by fat, while the mature T cells it produced live on in the secondary organs.
notes: B cells mature in red bone marrow, not the thymus. Pick red bone marrow if the question asked where B cells finish maturing.
This reverses the story. The thymus becomes fatty as it shrinks in adults, but fat storage was never its job.
Correct. The thymus matures T cells, and most of that work happens early in life.
The thymus does not filter lymph. It has no afferent vessels and no follicles, which separates it from a lymph node.
questions.answerText: It is where T cells mature, and most of that maturing happens early in life

questions.q: The tonsils form a ring around the entrance to the throat, where food and air pass. Why does this location suit their job?
options: They drain lymph from the head straight into the thoracic duct
They filter the blood before it travels on to reach the brain
They are where T cells mature before entering the bloodstream
They meet inhaled and swallowed pathogens early, at the entry point
questions.why: Tonsils are secondary lymphatic tissue that sit where food and air enter the body. Their deep pits, called crypts, trap bacteria so the lymphocytes inside can learn to recognize them and mount a defense. Placing them at this shared entry point lets them meet pathogens before those pathogens reach deeper tissues.
notes: Lymph from the head drains through cervical nodes into the jugular trunks and then a duct. Tonsils are lymphatic tissue, not drainage vessels.
Filtering blood is the job of the spleen in the upper left abdomen. The tonsils sit in mucous membranes and sample what passes through the throat.
T cells mature in the thymus in the mediastinum. Pick the thymus for a question about T cell maturation.
Correct. Tonsils guard the entry point for inhaled and swallowed pathogens.
questions.answerText: They meet inhaled and swallowed pathogens early, at the entry point

questions.q: Peyer patches are clusters of lymphatic follicles that watch the intestinal contents. Where are they found?
options: In the wall of the ileum
In the wall of the esophagus
In the wall of the rectum
In the wall of the stomach
questions.why: Peyer patches are part of MALT, the lymphatic tissue that guards mucous membranes. They sit in the wall of the ileum, the last part of the small intestine, where they sample the intestinal contents for pathogens. The appendix, just beyond the ileum, also has a wall packed with lymphatic follicles.
notes: Correct. Peyer patches are in the wall of the ileum.
The esophagus is a muscular tube carrying food to the stomach, lined with stratified squamous epithelium. Pick it for a question about the tube behind the trachea.
The rectum is the last part of the large intestine, storing feces before elimination. Pick it for a question about the end of the large intestine.
The stomach wall has gastric pits and glands that secrete acid and enzymes. It does not hold the named clusters called Peyer patches.
questions.answerText: In the wall of the ileum

questions.q: Which lymphatic organ lies in the mediastinum, above the heart and behind the sternum?
options: The thymus
A palatine tonsil
The cisterna chyli
The spleen
questions.why: The thymus sits in the mediastinum, above the heart and just behind the sternum. It is a primary lymphatic organ where T cells mature. It is large in children and shrinks after puberty, so in older adults it is mostly fat.
notes: Correct. The thymus lies behind the sternum, above the heart.
The palatine tonsils sit in the lateral walls of the oropharynx. Pick them for a question about the tonsils usually removed in a tonsillectomy.
The cisterna chyli is a lymphatic sac in the abdomen where the thoracic duct begins. It is a vessel, not an organ, and it lies below the diaphragm.
The spleen lies in the upper left abdomen, behind the stomach and under the lower left ribs. Pick it for a question about the organ that filters blood.
questions.answerText: The thymus

questions.q: A teenager with mononucleosis is told to avoid contact sports for several weeks. Which enlarged lymphatic organ could rupture from a hard hit?
options: A palatine tonsil
An axillary lymph node
The thymus
The spleen
questions.why: Mononucleosis, caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, enlarges the spleen, a condition called splenomegaly. An enlarged spleen extends beyond the protection of the lower left ribs and is easier to tear. Because the spleen holds a large volume of blood, a rupture causes heavy internal bleeding.
notes: The palatine tonsils can be inflamed in throat infections, but they sit in the throat and do not bleed heavily into the abdomen. Pick them for a question about tonsillitis.
Axillary lymph nodes can swell during infection, but a swollen node does not rupture with heavy internal bleeding. Pick them for a question about swollen glands in the armpit.
The thymus lies behind the sternum and is not the organ enlarged and endangered in mononucleosis. Pick it for a question about T cell maturation.
Correct. The spleen enlarges in mononucleosis and can rupture.
questions.answerText: The spleen

questions.q: Which feature of the appendix wall links it to the body's immune defenses?
options: Its wall is lined with bile-producing cells
Its wall contains clusters of hormone-producing islets
Its wall is packed with lymphatic follicles
Its wall is made mostly of skeletal muscle
questions.why: The appendix is a narrow tube off the cecum whose wall is packed with lymphatic follicles, clusters of lymphocytes. This makes it part of the mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue (MALT), along with the tonsils and Peyer patches, which guards the openings and lining of the digestive tract. The lymphocytes in these follicles respond to bacteria in the intestine.
notes: Bile-producing cells are hepatocytes, found in the liver. Pick this feature for the liver, not the appendix.
Hormone-producing islets are the pancreatic islets, the endocrine part of the pancreas. This feature would be the answer for the pancreas.
Correct. Lymphatic follicles in the wall make the appendix part of MALT.

The wall of the digestive tract below the esophagus is smooth muscle, not skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscle appears at the two ends of the tract, such as the external anal sphincter, so pick it for voluntary control at those ends.
questions.answerText: Its wall is packed with lymphatic follicles

questions.q: Which two lymphatic organs are primary organs, where lymphocytes form and mature?
options: Red bone marrow and the spleen
The thymus and the lymph nodes
The spleen and the tonsils
Red bone marrow and the thymus
questions.why: Primary lymphatic organs are where lymphocytes are produced and become mature. All lymphocytes form in red bone marrow, where B cells also mature, while T cell precursors travel to the thymus to mature there. The other lymphatic organs are secondary, meaning they are where mature lymphocytes meet invaders.
notes: Red bone marrow is primary, but the spleen is secondary, a filter of the blood where mature lymphocytes respond to blood-borne pathogens. Pick the spleen if the question asked which organ filters blood.
The thymus is primary, but lymph nodes are secondary organs that filter lymph. They would be the answer if the question asked where lymph is cleaned before it returns to the blood.
Both are secondary organs. The spleen filters blood and the tonsils guard the entrance to the throat; pick the tonsils if the question asked which tissue traps inhaled and swallowed pathogens.
Correct. Red bone marrow and the thymus are the primary lymphatic organs.
questions.answerText: Red bone marrow and the thymus

questions.q: What does the spleen filter, and where is it located?
options: It filters lymph, in the mediastinum behind the sternum
It filters blood, in the upper right abdomen beneath the liver
It filters lymph, in the upper left abdomen behind the stomach
It filters blood, in the upper left abdomen behind the stomach
questions.why: The spleen is the largest lymphatic organ, and unlike a lymph node it filters blood rather than lymph. It sits in the upper left abdomen against the diaphragm, behind the stomach, protected by the lower left ribs. Its red pulp removes worn-out red blood cells and platelets, and its white pulp mounts immune responses to blood-borne pathogens.
notes: The mediastinum behind the sternum is the location of the thymus, which does not filter lymph or blood. Choose that location if the question asked where T cells mature.
The spleen filters blood, but it lies on the left side. The upper right abdomen beneath the liver is where the gallbladder sits, so pick that location if the question asked about the gallbladder.
The location is right, but the spleen has no afferent lymphatic vessels bringing lymph in to be filtered. Filtering lymph is the job of the lymph nodes.
Correct. The spleen filters blood in the upper left abdomen.
questions.answerText: It filters blood, in the upper left abdomen behind the stomach

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares a lymph node and the spleen by what each one filters?
options: Both filter lymph, but the spleen handles a larger volume
A lymph node filters lymph, and the spleen filters blood
Both filter blood, but lymph nodes are spread throughout the body
A lymph node filters blood, and the spleen filters lymph
questions.why: Lymph nodes sit along the collecting vessels, and lymph enters them through afferent vessels so macrophages and lymphocytes can clean it before it reaches the blood. The spleen has no afferent lymphatic vessels; blood arrives through the splenic artery instead, and the spleen filters that blood. Both are secondary lymphatic organs, but they guard two different fluids.
notes: The spleen is the largest lymphatic organ, but it does not receive lymph to filter. Students pick this because the spleen is a lymphatic organ and assume it must handle lymph.
Correct. Nodes clean lymph and the spleen cleans blood.
Lymph nodes do not filter blood; they lie along lymphatic vessels and clean lymph. Only the spleen filters blood, so this choice gives the nodes the spleen's job.
This swaps the two fluids. Lymph nodes receive lymph through afferent lymphatic vessels, while the spleen receives blood from the splenic artery.
questions.answerText: A lymph node filters lymph, and the spleen filters blood

questions.q: A football player takes a hard blow to the lower left ribs and develops signs of heavy internal bleeding. Which lymphatic organ is most likely injured?
options: The spleen
The thymus
The appendix
The Peyer patches
questions.why: The spleen sits in the upper left abdomen against the diaphragm, just under the lower left ribs, so a blow there can tear it. It is a soft, blood-filled organ whose red pulp is packed with venous sinuses, and a large volume of blood passes through it from the splenic artery. A tear therefore bleeds heavily, which is why a ruptured spleen is a surgical emergency.
notes: Correct. The spleen lies under the lower left ribs and bleeds heavily when torn.
The thymus lies in the mediastinum behind the sternum, above the heart, not under the lower left ribs. Pick it if the question asked where T cells mature.
The appendix hangs from the cecum in the lower right abdomen, far from the lower left ribs. It would be the answer for a lymphatic organ that can rupture and cause peritonitis.
Peyer patches are clusters of lymphatic follicles in the wall of the ileum, the end of the small intestine. Choose them if the question asked which MALT watches the intestinal contents.
questions.answerText: The spleen

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the regions of a lymph node and where lymph enters and leaves?
options: A capsule surrounds a cortex and a medulla; lymph enters through efferent vessels and leaves through afferent vessels at the hilum
A capsule surrounds a cortex and a medulla; lymph enters at the hilum and leaves through vessels across the capsule
A capsule surrounds red pulp and white pulp; blood enters and leaves through vessels at the hilum
A capsule surrounds a cortex and a medulla; lymph enters through afferent vessels and leaves through efferent vessels at the hilum
questions.why: A lymph node is wrapped in a dense connective tissue capsule, with an outer cortex of follicles (mostly B cells), a deeper cortex of T cells, and an inner medulla lined with macrophages. Several afferent vessels pierce the capsule to bring lymph in, and fewer efferent vessels carry it out at the hilum, the indented side of the node. Because more vessels enter than leave, lymph slows down inside the node, giving time for filtering.
notes: This swaps afferent and efferent. Afferent means carrying toward (lymph comes in), and efferent means carrying away (lymph goes out).
The sites are reversed. Many afferent vessels enter all around the capsule, and the hilum is where the efferent vessels leave and blood vessels enter.
Red pulp and white pulp are the regions of the spleen, which filters blood. Pick this description if the question asked about the structure of the spleen.
Correct. Afferent vessels bring lymph in through the capsule, and efferent vessels carry it out at the hilum.
questions.answerText: A capsule surrounds a cortex and a medulla; lymph enters through afferent vessels and leaves through efferent vessels at the hilum

questions.q: Which primary lymphatic organ is the site where all lymphocytes, including future T cells, first form?
options: The spleen
Red bone marrow
The lymph nodes
The thymus
questions.why: All lymphocytes form from stem cells in red bone marrow. B cells and NK cells stay in the marrow to mature, while T cell precursors leave and travel to the thymus to finish maturing. That is why both red bone marrow and the thymus count as primary lymphatic organs, but only the marrow is where every lymphocyte begins.
notes: The spleen is a secondary organ where mature lymphocytes respond to blood-borne pathogens. It would be the answer if the question asked which organ filters blood.
Correct. Every lymphocyte forms in red bone marrow, even the ones that mature elsewhere.
Lymph nodes are secondary organs where mature lymphocytes meet invaders carried in the lymph. Choose them if the question asked where lymph is filtered.
The thymus is a primary organ, but it is where T cells mature after arriving from the marrow, not where they first form. Pick the thymus if the question asked where T cells mature.
questions.answerText: Red bone marrow

questions.q: What does the term splenomegaly mean?
options: Enlarged lymph nodes.
An enlarged spleen.
Inflamed palatine tonsils.
Swelling from blocked lymph vessels.
questions.why: Splenomegaly names its structure in the word itself: the spleen, made larger. It can happen with an infection such as mononucleosis or with a blood disorder such as leukemia. An enlarged spleen ruptures more easily, which matters because the spleen sits just under the lower left ribs and holds a large volume of blood.
notes: Enlarged lymph nodes are lymphadenopathy, the swollen glands a clinician feels in the neck, armpit, and groin.
Correct. Splenomegaly is enlargement of the spleen, for example in mononucleosis or leukemia.
Inflamed tonsils, usually the palatine tonsils, are tonsillitis, which is common in childhood.
Long-term swelling from blocked, damaged, or missing lymphatic vessels is lymphedema.
questions.answerText: An enlarged spleen.

questions.q: What is lymphadenopathy?
options: Excess fluid in the interstitial space.
Enlargement of the lymph nodes.
Infection and swelling of the tonsils.
Enlargement of the spleen.
questions.why: Lymphadenopathy means the lymph nodes are enlarged. Nodes swell as they trap and fight pathogens, and they can also enlarge when cancer cells lodge in them. These are the swollen glands a clinician feels for in the neck, armpit, and groin.
notes: Excess interstitial fluid is edema, which happens when fluid leaks out faster than the lymphatics can carry it away.
Correct. Lymphadenopathy means enlarged lymph nodes, often while they fight a nearby infection.
Infected, swollen tonsils are tonsillitis. Lymphadenopathy is about the lymph nodes.
An enlarged spleen is splenomegaly. Lymphadenopathy affects the lymph nodes, not the spleen.
questions.answerText: Enlargement of the lymph nodes.

questions.q: Edema and lymphedema both cause tissue swelling. Which statement correctly compares the structure each one affects?
options: Edema comes from blocked or damaged lymphatic vessels; lymphedema is fluid built up in the lymph nodes.
Both affect the lymph nodes, which enlarge; lymphedema is simply the longer-lasting form of the same thing.
Edema is fluid built up in the interstitial space; lymphedema comes from blocked or damaged lymphatic vessels.
Edema affects the spleen as it enlarges; lymphedema affects the tonsils as they swell with infection.
questions.why: Both disorders show up as swelling, but they start in different places. Edema is excess fluid in the interstitial space, which builds up when fluid leaks out of the blood capillaries faster than the lymphatics can drain it. Lymphedema is a specific kind of edema caused by blocked, damaged, or missing lymphatic vessels, which is why it can follow surgery that removes lymph nodes.
notes: This mixes up the two. Edema is excess interstitial fluid, not a vessel problem, and lymphedema is caused by blocked, damaged, or missing lymphatic vessels, not fluid in the nodes.
Enlarged lymph nodes are lymphadenopathy. Edema affects the interstitial space and lymphedema affects the lymphatic vessels.
Correct. Edema is about the interstitial space, while lymphedema is caused by failed lymphatic vessels.
An enlarged spleen is splenomegaly and swollen tonsils are tonsillitis. Neither one is edema or lymphedema.
questions.answerText: Edema is fluid built up in the interstitial space; lymphedema comes from blocked or damaged lymphatic vessels.

questions.q: What makes the innate defenses nonspecific?
options: They grow faster and stronger with each repeat exposure to the same microbe
They are aimed at one antigen selected from a very large receptor library
They respond the same way to any invader, with no prior exposure needed
They act only against an invader the body has already met once before
questions.why: Innate defenses use a fixed set of recognition patterns shared by many microbes, so the response to a first encounter and a fiftieth encounter looks the same and starts within minutes. Requiring a prior encounter and growing stronger with repetition describe adaptive memory, which innate defenses do not have. Choosing one antigen from a large receptor library describes lymphocyte clonal selection, the defining feature of the specific arm.
questions.answerText: They respond the same way to any invader, with no prior exposure needed

questions.q: What does the lysozyme in tears and saliva do to bacteria?
options: It coats the bacterial surface so that phagocytes can grip it more easily
It builds a pore in the bacterial membrane out of complement proteins
It keeps the bacterium from attaching to the epithelial surface underneath
It breaks down the peptidoglycan that makes up the bacterial cell wall
questions.why: Lysozyme is an enzyme that cleaves the sugar backbone of peptidoglycan, so the wall fails and the bacterium bursts under its own osmotic pressure. Coating a surface for easier grip is opsonization, done by complement C3b and by antibody, not by lysozyme. Pore formation is the job of the membrane attack complex. Blocking attachment describes the physical role of mucus rather than an enzyme.
questions.answerText: It breaks down the peptidoglycan that makes up the bacterial cell wall

questions.q: Which leukocyte is most abundant in blood and arrives first in large numbers at an infected tissue?
options: The monocyte
The eosinophil
The neutrophil
The basophil
questions.why: Neutrophils are roughly 60 to 70 percent of circulating white cells and are the first wave of phagocytes to leave the capillaries at an infection site. Monocytes arrive later and mature into macrophages that clean up debris. Eosinophils rise mainly with parasites and allergy, and basophils are rare cells that release histamine rather than doing bulk phagocytosis.
questions.answerText: The neutrophil

questions.q: What does a natural killer cell recognize on the cells it destroys?
options: Free bacteria circulating in the blood and in the lymph
One specific antigen it was programmed in advance to match
Antibody coated proteins dissolved in the plasma
Body cells that have lost their normal self surface markers
questions.why: An NK cell surveys body cells for the self markers a healthy cell displays, and it kills the ones that have lost them, which is common in virus infected and tumor cells. Free bacteria are handled by phagocytes and complement, not by NK killing. Matching one preselected antigen describes a T or B lymphocyte, and NK cells act without that kind of specificity. Dissolved plasma proteins are not targets for a killing cell.
questions.answerText: Body cells that have lost their normal self surface markers

questions.q: What does interferon released by a virus infected cell do?
options: It warns neighboring cells to make proteins that block replication
It binds the virus directly and keeps it from entering any host cell
It digests the protein coat of the virus once it is inside a cell
It draws neutrophils out of the blood and into the infected tissue
questions.why: Interferon is a warning signal, not a weapon. The infected cell is usually lost, but its interferon puts nearby cells into an antiviral state so the next round of virus meets resistance. Binding a virus directly to block entry is neutralization, which antibody does. Digesting a viral coat is not an interferon function, and drawing neutrophils into tissue is chemotaxis driven by chemokines and complement fragments.
questions.answerText: It warns neighboring cells to make proteins that block replication

questions.q: What does the membrane attack complex of complement do to a target cell?
options: It forms a pore in the membrane so water and ions rush in and the cell lyses
It coats the target surface so that phagocytes bind and engulf it faster
It sets up a chemical gradient that draws phagocytes toward the infection
It forms a clot that seals the infected area off from the surrounding tissue
questions.why: The late complement proteins assemble into a ring that punches a hole in the membrane, and osmosis does the rest as water follows solute into the cell. Coating for easier engulfment and setting up a gradient are also real complement jobs, done by C3b (opsonization) and by smaller fragments (chemotaxis), which is exactly why they make good distractors here. Clotting walls off infection but is a function of fibrin, not complement.
questions.answerText: It forms a pore in the membrane so water and ions rush in and the cell lyses

questions.q: How does the mucociliary escalator of the airway protect the lungs?
options: Cilia engulf and digest the particles that land on the airway surface
Cilia sweep particles trapped in mucus up toward the pharynx to be swallowed
Mucus triggers antibody release into the airway within a minute of exposure
Mucus kills inhaled bacteria with the strong acid that goblet cells secrete
questions.why: Mucus is the sticky trap and the cilia are the conveyor, moving the loaded mucus upward so the particles end up swallowed instead of settling in the alveoli. Airway mucus is not acidic; the strong acid barrier is in the stomach. Cilia are motile extensions and do not phagocytize. Antibody in secretions helps at mucosal surfaces, but it is an adaptive response that takes days, not a minute.
questions.answerText: Cilia sweep particles trapped in mucus up toward the pharynx to be swallowed

questions.q: Which chemical barrier destroys most swallowed bacteria before they reach the small intestine?
options: Bile salts released into the duodenum
Gastric acid, which sits at a pH near 2
Mucus lining the wall of the esophagus
Surfactant secreted by the airway lining
questions.why: Stomach contents sit near pH 2, acidic enough to denature the proteins of most swallowed organisms before they ever reach the absorptive surface of the gut. Bile salts emulsify fat and enter downstream of the stomach. Esophageal mucus lubricates and shields the wall but does not kill. Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and has nothing to do with the swallowed route.
questions.answerText: Gastric acid, which sits at a pH near 2

questions.q: A child cannot make functional neutrophils. Which problem should you expect?
options: Failure to produce antibody after a routine childhood vaccination
Inability to raise body temperature at all during an infection
Loss of the skin barrier with widespread water loss through it
Repeated bacterial infections with little pus at the infected site
questions.why: Neutrophils do the bulk of early bacterial phagocytosis, and pus is largely spent neutrophils, so losing them means both frequent bacterial infection and an infected site that looks quiet rather than purulent. Antibody production is a B cell job and would be unaffected. Fever is set by the hypothalamus in response to pyrogens from macrophages and does not require neutrophils. The skin barrier is structural and independent of leukocyte counts.
questions.answerText: Repeated bacterial infections with little pus at the infected site

questions.q: A large burn destroys the epidermis over a wide area. Which innate defense is lost first?
options: The physical barrier that keeps microbes out of the tissue
The cellular defense provided by natural killer cells
The complement proteins circulating in the plasma
The chemical barrier provided by gastric acid
questions.why: Intact skin is the first line, a mechanical seal that microbes cannot cross, and a burn that removes the epidermis opens a wide door before any other defense is touched. Gastric acid guards the swallowed route and is unrelated to skin. NK cells and complement are still present and functional after a burn, which is why burn patients still mount responses once organisms get in; the problem is that organisms now get in easily.
questions.answerText: The physical barrier that keeps microbes out of the tissue

questions.q: Complement fragments and bacterial products build up in an infected tissue. What do they do to neutrophils in nearby capillaries?
options: They draw the neutrophils out toward the source of the signal
They make the neutrophils release antibody into the surrounding plasma
They keep the neutrophils from sticking to the wall of the vessel
They make the neutrophils divide rapidly while still inside the vessel
questions.why: This is chemotaxis: phagocytes follow the rising concentration of these molecules, and the same signals make them stick to the endothelium first so they can squeeze out. Neutrophils are end stage cells and do not divide in the bloodstream. Antibody secretion belongs to plasma cells. Preventing adhesion would block the response, the opposite of what these signals do.
questions.answerText: They draw the neutrophils out toward the source of the signal

questions.q: A bacterium becomes coated with the complement fragment C3b. What happens to the rate at which macrophages engulf it?
options: It stays the same, because phagocytes ignore anything coating a target
It increases, but only once antibody against the bacterium is also present
It increases, because the coating gives the phagocyte a surface it can grip
It decreases, because the coating hides the bacterial surface from view
questions.why: Macrophages carry receptors for C3b, so a coated bacterium is far easier to bind and pull in than a bare one. That process is opsonization, and it works whether or not antibody is around, which is why complement is useful on a first exposure. A coating that hid the surface would be a bacterial defense, like a capsule, not a host one.
questions.answerText: It increases, because the coating gives the phagocyte a surface it can grip

questions.q: A patient is given interferon during a viral illness. Which cells does it act on to slow the infection?
options: The B cells, which it drives to secrete antibody more quickly
The uninfected cells nearby, which it readies against the virus
The already infected cells, which it destroys outright
The virus particles in plasma, which it binds and neutralizes
questions.why: Interferon protects the cells that have not yet been infected by inducing enzymes that shut down viral protein synthesis if the virus arrives. It does not kill the cell that released it, and it does not bind virus particles, which is antibody work. Driving antibody secretion is a cytokine effect of helper T cells, not the antiviral action interferon is named for.
questions.answerText: The uninfected cells nearby, which it readies against the virus

questions.q: A person is infected with the same bacterium a second time. How does the innate response compare with the first time?
options: It is absent, because the adaptive system now handles this organism alone
It is faster and larger, because innate cells remember the first exposure
It is the same speed and the same size, because innate defenses store no memory
It is slower, because the first exposure used up the available innate cells
questions.why: Innate recognition is genetically fixed, so a repeat exposure gets an identical response beginning within minutes. Faster and larger on repeat exposure describes the adaptive secondary response, which is happening at the same time but is a different system. Innate cells are continually replaced from bone marrow, so they are not used up, and innate defenses do not switch off once adaptive immunity exists.
questions.answerText: It is the same speed and the same size, because innate defenses store no memory

questions.q: A splinter drives bacteria into the dermis. Which cell meets them first, before any new cells arrive from the blood?
options: The helper T cell waiting in the nearest lymph node
The macrophage already resident in the tissue
The neutrophil arriving from the bloodstream
The plasma cell secreting antibody into the wound
questions.why: Tissues are patrolled by resident macrophages that are on site at time zero, which is why they are the cells that detect the invasion and release the signals that call everyone else. Neutrophils are fast but still have to marginate and cross the vessel wall, which takes an hour or more. Plasma cells and helper T cells belong to the adaptive response and act days later.
questions.answerText: The macrophage already resident in the tissue

questions.q: A patient's neutrophils reach an infected tissue in normal numbers and engulf bacteria normally, but the bacteria survive inside them. Which step failed and what follows?
options: Adherence failed, so the phagocytes cannot bind the bacteria at all
Killing inside the phagosome failed, so the engulfed bacteria survive
Diapedesis failed, so the phagocytes cannot leave the capillary at all
Chemotaxis failed, so bacteria spread while phagocytes stay in the blood
questions.why: Phagocytosis has ordered steps: chemotaxis, adherence, engulfment, then digestion in the phagolysosome. The case states that the cells arrived and engulfed normally, so the first three steps worked and only the killing step is left. Chemotaxis and diapedesis failures would show up as phagocytes that never reach the tissue, and an adherence failure would prevent engulfment, which the case explicitly says occurred.
questions.answerText: Killing inside the phagosome failed, so the engulfed bacteria survive

questions.q: A virus stops its host cell from displaying the self markers that cytotoxic T cells read. Predict the effect on natural killer cell activity against that cell.
options: NK killing increases, because missing self markers is what NK cells act on
NK killing decreases, because NK cells need those markers to find a target
NK killing is unchanged, because NK cells respond only to antibody coating
NK killing stops, because NK cells act only when a helper T cell approves
questions.why: The two systems are complementary: a cytotoxic T cell needs the display, and an NK cell kills when the display is missing, so a virus that hides the markers escapes one system and walks into the other. NK cells do not need the markers to identify a target, they need their absence. They also do not require antibody or helper T permission, which is what lets them act on the first day of an infection.
questions.answerText: NK killing increases, because missing self markers is what NK cells act on

questions.q: A patient makes normal antibody and has normal phagocytes but lacks the late complement proteins. Which defense is lost while the rest stays intact?
options: Antibody production is lost, since complement is what activates B cells
Opsonization is lost, so phagocytes can no longer bind bacteria at all
Direct lysis is lost, though opsonization and chemotaxis are intact
Chemotaxis is lost, so phagocytes no longer migrate toward an infection
questions.why: The complement cascade splits into early components, which produce C3b for opsonization and small fragments for chemotaxis, and late components, which build the membrane attack complex. Losing only the late proteins removes lysis and leaves the early functions working. Opsonization and chemotaxis would be lost with an early block instead. Complement supports antibody responses but does not create them, so B cells still work.
questions.answerText: Direct lysis is lost, though opsonization and chemotaxis are intact

questions.q: After a week of broad spectrum antibiotics a patient develops diarrhea from a resistant organism that has overgrown the colon. Which innate defense was weakened, and why does overgrowth follow?
options: Natural killer surveillance of the intestinal lining was suppressed by the drug
Gastric acid was neutralized, so swallowed organisms now survive the stomach
Complement lysis failed, since complement requires intact gut flora to work
Competition from the resident flora was lost, leaving space and nutrients open
questions.why: The normal flora is a nonspecific defense: it occupies attachment sites and consumes nutrients, so a newcomer has nowhere to establish. An antibiotic that clears the flora removes that competition, and a resistant organism expands into the empty niche. Antibiotics do not change gastric pH, complement works independently of gut bacteria, and NK cells are not the defense being removed here.
questions.answerText: Competition from the resident flora was lost, leaving space and nutrients open

questions.q: What are the four classic cardinal signs of acute inflammation?
options: Bruising, heat, dryness, and weakness
Redness, heat, swelling, and pain
Pallor, coolness, swelling, and numbness
Redness, coolness, shrinkage, and itching
questions.why: Each sign traces to a vascular change: redness and heat from arteriolar dilation, swelling from increased capillary permeability, and pain from mediators plus pressure on nerve endings. Pallor and coolness would mean reduced blood flow, the opposite of what inflammation does. Shrinkage and dryness are not features of an inflamed tissue, which gains fluid rather than losing it.
questions.answerText: Redness, heat, swelling, and pain

questions.q: Which cell releases the histamine that starts the vascular changes of inflammation?
options: The mast cell
The plasma cell
The helper T cell
The natural killer cell
questions.why: Mast cells sit in connective tissue right where injury occurs and degranulate within seconds, dumping preformed histamine into the interstitium. Plasma cells secrete antibody days later, helper T cells release cytokines that direct adaptive responses, and NK cells kill abnormal body cells. None of the three carries the histamine granules that start the vascular response.
questions.answerText: The mast cell

questions.q: What does histamine do to the arterioles supplying an injured area?
options: It stiffens their walls without changing their diameter
It dilates them only after the tissue has finished healing
It constricts them, reducing local blood flow
It dilates them, increasing local blood flow
questions.why: Arteriolar dilation is the first vascular event, and it is what delivers the extra blood that makes the area red and warm. Constriction would reduce delivery of plasma proteins and phagocytes, the opposite of what the response needs. Vessel walls do not stiffen during inflammation, and the dilation happens within minutes of injury, not after repair.
questions.answerText: It dilates them, increasing local blood flow

questions.q: Which change in the capillaries produces the swelling of inflammation?
options: Increased velocity of blood through the capillary bed
Decreased hydrostatic pressure inside the capillary itself
Increased permeability, which lets fluid and protein leave the blood
Decreased permeability, which traps fluid inside the capillary lumen
questions.why: Mediators such as histamine make endothelial cells pull apart, and fluid with plasma protein moves into the interstitium, which is the edema you can see and feel. Decreased permeability would keep fluid in the vessel and produce no swelling. Faster flow does not by itself push fluid out, and a fall in capillary hydrostatic pressure would favor reabsorption, again the wrong direction.
questions.answerText: Increased permeability, which lets fluid and protein leave the blood

questions.q: What is diapedesis?
options: Leukocytes squeezing between endothelial cells to leave the vessel
Leukocytes sticking to the vessel wall just before they exit it
Leukocytes migrating along a chemical gradient within the tissue
Leukocytes engulfing and digesting a bacterium they have bound
questions.why: Diapedesis is the crossing step, when a leukocyte deforms and slips through the gap between endothelial cells into the tissue. Sticking to the wall beforehand is margination, following the gradient once outside is chemotaxis, and engulfing the organism is phagocytosis. These are four consecutive steps, and separating them in order is exactly what this competency asks for.
questions.answerText: Leukocytes squeezing between endothelial cells to leave the vessel

questions.q: What do pyrogens do at the hypothalamus?
options: They keep the hypothalamus from sensing the temperature of the blood
They increase heat loss by dilating the blood vessels of the skin
They raise the temperature set point the hypothalamus defends
They lower the set point so that the body begins to cool itself
questions.why: A pyrogen resets the thermostat upward, and the body then uses its ordinary heat gaining reflexes to reach the new target. Lowering the set point and increasing skin heat loss are what an antipyretic causes once the pyrogen is blocked. The hypothalamus continues to sense blood temperature perfectly well during fever, which is why it can defend the higher value so precisely.
questions.answerText: They raise the temperature set point the hypothalamus defends

questions.q: Which cell arrives at an inflamed site after the neutrophils and clears debris and dead cells?
options: The natural killer cell, which lyses cells with abnormal markers
The monocyte, which becomes a macrophage once in the tissue
The neutrophil, which arrives in the first hours after injury
The plasma cell, which secretes antibody into the tissue fluid
questions.why: Monocytes follow the neutrophil wave by roughly a day, transform into macrophages, and do the long duty of ingesting debris, dead neutrophils, and remaining organisms while releasing signals for repair. The neutrophil is the early responder named in the stem itself. Plasma cells and NK cells have real jobs in defense but neither is the debris clearing cell of an inflamed wound.
questions.answerText: The monocyte, which becomes a macrophage once in the tissue

questions.q: What is pus made of?
options: Clotted blood and fibrin strands only
Antibody rich plasma containing no cells
Lymph draining out of the injured region
Dead neutrophils, tissue debris, and fluid
questions.why: Neutrophils die where they work, and the accumulation of spent cells with liquefied debris is what you see as pus, which is why a patient who cannot make neutrophils forms very little of it. A clot is fibrin and trapped red cells and looks quite different. Cell free plasma and lymph are clear fluids, not the thick creamy material that defines an abscess.
questions.answerText: Dead neutrophils, tissue debris, and fluid

questions.q: Why does an inflamed area look red and feel warm?
options: Arteriolar dilation increases blood flow, bringing more warm blood to it
Fluid leaking into the tissue space raises the local temperature directly
Neutrophils generate heat as a byproduct of digesting the bacteria
Blood flow slows down, so blood lingers long enough to warm the tissue
questions.why: Redness and heat are one mechanism seen two ways: more blood in the area means more hemoglobin visible through the skin and more core temperature blood delivered to a surface that is normally cooler. Edema fluid arrives at the same temperature as the blood it came from and adds no heat of its own. Phagocytosis does not generate measurable local warming, and slowed flow would make an area look dusky and feel cool.
questions.answerText: Arteriolar dilation increases blood flow, bringing more warm blood to it

questions.q: Aspirin reduces inflammatory pain by blocking prostaglandin synthesis. What does that tell you about prostaglandins at an injury?
options: They pull fluid out of the tissue and return it to the capillary blood
They sensitize pain endings so that ordinary stimuli begin to hurt
They constrict local vessels and reduce blood flow to the injured tissue
They kill bacteria directly in the fluid surrounding the injured cells
questions.why: If removing prostaglandins removes pain, prostaglandins must be part of what generates it, and their role is to lower the threshold of nociceptors so that light pressure on a sore finger is felt as pain. Prostaglandins in inflammation promote dilation rather than constriction. They have no antibacterial activity, and they favor fluid leaving the capillary rather than returning to it.
questions.answerText: They sensitize pain endings so that ordinary stimuli begin to hurt

questions.q: A splinter enters the dermis. Which sequence of events follows?
options: Vasodilation, chemical release, leukocyte exit, increased permeability
Leukocyte exit, chemical release, vasodilation, increased permeability
Increased permeability, leukocyte exit, vasodilation, chemical release
Chemical release, vasodilation, increased permeability, leukocyte exit
questions.why: Damaged cells and resident mast cells release mediators first, and everything downstream is a response to those signals: vessels dilate, then they leak, then leukocytes stick and cross the wall. Any order that puts a vascular change before the chemical signal reverses cause and effect. Leukocyte exit has to come last of the four, because the cells need the adhesion signals and the widened gaps in order to leave.
questions.answerText: Chemical release, vasodilation, increased permeability, leukocyte exit

questions.q: Why does inflammatory edema fluid contain far more protein than the fluid normally filtered from a capillary?
options: Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls sharply during an inflammatory response
Lymphatic vessels actively pump protein from the blood into the tissue
Neutrophils manufacture and secrete protein into the interstitial fluid
The widened gaps between endothelial cells let plasma protein pass through
questions.why: A normal capillary holds protein back, so ordinary filtrate is nearly protein free; inflammation changes the wall itself, and once the gaps are wide enough albumin follows the water out. Hydrostatic pressure actually rises in inflammation because of upstream dilation. Lymphatics drain protein away from tissue rather than delivering it, and the protein in an exudate comes from plasma, not from neutrophil synthesis.
questions.answerText: The widened gaps between endothelial cells let plasma protein pass through

questions.q: A patient's hypothalamic set point has just risen to 39 C while body temperature is still 37 C. What does the patient feel and do?
options: Feels hot and dilates skin vessels, because heat production has risen
Feels cold and shivers, because the body is now below its set point
Feels hot and sweats, because the set point has risen above normal
Feels normal, because 37 C is a perfectly normal body temperature
questions.why: The hypothalamus compares actual temperature with the set point, and a 2 degree gap in that direction is read as being too cold no matter what the absolute number is. Shivering and skin vasoconstriction follow, which is why the chills of a rising fever feel so convincing. Sweating and skin vasodilation are heat loss responses and occur when actual temperature is above the set point, which happens later when the fever breaks.
questions.answerText: Feels cold and shivers, because the body is now below its set point

questions.q: Aspirin brings a fever down. What has it done to the hypothalamic set point?
options: It blocked the skin receptors from sensing temperature at any level
It cooled the blood directly as the blood passed through the skin
It lowered the set point, so heat loss responses such as sweating turn on
It raised the set point further, so the patient begins shivering again
questions.why: Antipyretics work upstream, by blocking the prostaglandin that raised the set point, so the thermostat returns toward 37 C and the body, now above target, sweats and dilates skin vessels until temperature falls. Raising the set point is what the pyrogen did. The drug does not act on skin receptors and does not cool blood directly; the cooling is the body's own response to a corrected set point.
questions.answerText: It lowered the set point, so heat loss responses such as sweating turn on

questions.q: How does a moderate fever aid defense?
options: It speeds immune cell activity and slows the growth of many pathogens
It denatures every bacterial protein once temperature passes 39 C
It removes the need for phagocytes to enter the infected tissue
It stops histamine release and so brings the swelling to an end
questions.why: A few degrees raises the rate of nearly every enzymatic and cellular process, including phagocyte movement and lymphocyte proliferation, while many pathogens replicate best at 37 C and do less well above it. Bacterial proteins are not denatured at 39 C; temperatures that would do that would kill the patient first. Fever supports phagocytes rather than replacing them, and it does not end the swelling.
questions.answerText: It speeds immune cell activity and slows the growth of many pathogens

questions.q: A person takes an antihistamine immediately after an insect sting. Predict the effect on local blood flow and on swelling.
options: Blood flow rises but swelling is reduced, since the two changes are unrelated
Blood flow falls while swelling increases, since fluid can no longer drain away
Blood flow and swelling are both unchanged, since histamine only causes itching
Blood flow falls and swelling is reduced, since both follow histamine action
questions.why: Histamine does two things at once, dilating arterioles and opening gaps between endothelial cells, so blocking its receptors reduces both the extra flow and the leak that follows it. The two effects cannot separate, since they come from the same mediator acting on the same vascular bed. Antihistamines do not impair lymphatic drainage, and histamine drives far more than itching, which is why the drug works on the swelling too.
questions.answerText: Blood flow falls and swelling is reduced, since both follow histamine action

questions.q: A patient on a drug that strongly suppresses inflammation cuts a finger. Predict what happens to the redness and to bacterial clearance.
options: No change in either, since inflammation does not affect phagocyte delivery
Less redness and slower clearance, since phagocyte delivery also falls
Less redness and faster clearance, since fewer cells crowd the site of injury
More redness and slower clearance, since the vessels remain dilated throughout
questions.why: The cardinal signs are not side effects of defense, they are the delivery system: dilation and leakage bring the phagocytes and plasma proteins to the wound. Suppress the vascular response and you lose both the visible signs and the delivery, so infection clears more slowly. That trade is the reason anti inflammatory therapy raises infection risk, and it is why the option pairing less redness with faster clearance is the one students most often want to choose.
questions.answerText: Less redness and slower clearance, since phagocyte delivery also falls

questions.q: An inflamed ankle is swollen although the patient has normal plasma albumin, normal venous pressure, and normal lymphatic drainage. Working back from the swelling, what explains it?
options: Increased capillary permeability caused by inflammatory mediators
Reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure from a low albumin level
Raised venous pressure backing fluid up in the capillary bed
Blocked lymphatic drainage from the whole of the affected limb
questions.why: Edema has four classic causes, and this case rules out three of them by stating that albumin, venous pressure, and lymph drainage are all normal, which leaves a change in the capillary wall itself. Inflammatory mediators do exactly that, opening gaps so both fluid and protein escape. Each of the other three would produce swelling under different conditions, which is why they are worth knowing, but none of them fits the findings here.
questions.answerText: Increased capillary permeability caused by inflammatory mediators

questions.q: A febrile child suddenly begins sweating heavily and her skin flushes. What changed at the hypothalamus, and what happens to core temperature next?
options: The hypothalamus stopped regulating, so temperature will now drift freely
The set point is unchanged, so the sweating will not alter temperature
The set point fell, so heat loss responses bring core temperature down
The set point rose, so heat production will push temperature higher still
questions.why: When the pyrogen clears, the thermostat drops back toward 37 C while the body is still at 39 C, so the patient is suddenly above target and turns on sweating and skin vasodilation. Those responses are the fever breaking, and temperature falls over the next hour. A rising set point produces the opposite picture, shivering and pale cool skin, and a hypothalamus that had stopped regulating would not produce a coordinated heat loss response at all.
questions.answerText: The set point fell, so heat loss responses bring core temperature down

questions.q: Which cell is responsible for humoral immunity?
options: The cytotoxic T lymphocyte
The tissue macrophage
The natural killer cell
The B lymphocyte
questions.why: Humoral immunity is named for the body fluids, and its agent is the B cell, whose descendants pour antibody into blood and lymph. The cytotoxic T cell carries out cell mediated immunity instead, killing infected cells directly. Macrophages and NK cells contribute to defense but belong to the innate side and do not produce antibody.
questions.answerText: The B lymphocyte

questions.q: An activated B cell divides. What do most of its daughter cells become, and what do they secrete?
options: Plasma cells, which secrete antibody
Cytotoxic cells, which secrete perforin
Memory T cells, which secrete cytokines
Macrophages, which secrete digestive enzymes
questions.why: The effector form of a B cell is the plasma cell, packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum and dedicated to antibody export; a smaller share of the daughters become memory B cells instead. Perforin comes from cytotoxic T cells and NK cells. A B cell cannot become a T cell or a macrophage, since those arise from separate lineages.
questions.answerText: Plasma cells, which secrete antibody

questions.q: Which targets does humoral immunity handle best?
options: Cells of a transplanted organ from another person
Bacteria and toxins free in the blood and in the lymph
Viruses that are already replicating inside a body cell
Tumor cells growing in the middle of a solid tissue
questions.why: Antibody is a soluble protein that circulates in body fluids, so it can only reach a target that is also out in those fluids: extracellular bacteria, free virus particles between cells, and dissolved toxins. Anything hidden inside a cell, including a replicating virus, a tumor cell, or a graft cell, has to be handled by cell mediated immunity, because antibody cannot cross the plasma membrane to reach it.
questions.answerText: Bacteria and toxins free in the blood and in the lymph

questions.q: Which cell directly kills a virus infected body cell?
options: The cytotoxic T cell
The plasma cell
The helper T cell
The B cell
questions.why: The cytotoxic T cell is the killer of the adaptive system: it inspects a cell's surface display and destroys the cell if the display includes foreign fragments. Plasma cells and B cells work through secreted antibody and never touch a target cell. Helper T cells direct the response with cytokines but do not deliver the lethal hit themselves.
questions.answerText: The cytotoxic T cell

questions.q: How does a cytotoxic T cell kill its target?
options: It secretes antibody that coats the target cell and dissolves it
It cuts off the target cell's supply of oxygen and glucose
It releases perforin and granzymes that trigger apoptosis in the target
It engulfs the target cell whole and digests it in a lysosome
questions.why: Perforin opens a channel in the target membrane and granzymes enter through it to trigger the cell's own suicide program, which kills the cell and its viral contents together with little spill into the tissue. Engulfing a whole cell is what a macrophage does. T cells never secrete antibody, and no immune cell kills by starving a target of oxygen or glucose.
questions.answerText: It releases perforin and granzymes that trigger apoptosis in the target

questions.q: What is the main job of the helper T cell?
options: It engulfs bacteria in tissue and digests them in a phagosome
It releases cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells
It lyses infected body cells directly using perforin and granzymes
It secretes the bulk of the antibody produced during a response
questions.why: The helper T cell is the hub of the adaptive response: it reads displayed antigen and then licenses both arms with chemical signals, which is why losing it damages antibody and killing responses at the same time. Direct lysis is the cytotoxic T cell's role, antibody secretion belongs to plasma cells, and phagocytosis is done by macrophages and neutrophils.
questions.answerText: It releases cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells

questions.q: Which cell engulfs an antigen and displays a fragment of it to a helper T cell?
options: The plasma cell
The cytotoxic T cell
The red blood cell
The dendritic cell
questions.why: Dendritic cells and macrophages are the professional antigen presenting cells: they take material in from the tissue, break it down, and hold a fragment on the surface where a helper T cell can read it. A plasma cell is a secretory end cell and presents nothing. Cytotoxic T cells read displays rather than create them, and red cells have no nucleus and no presenting machinery.
questions.answerText: The dendritic cell

questions.q: What does clonal selection mean?
options: Every lymphocyte in the body responds to every antigen that enters the body
The thymus builds a brand new receptor design after each separate infection
An antigen binds the lymphocyte whose receptor already fits and expands it
A lymphocyte reshapes its receptor until it fits the antigen it has just met
questions.why: The receptor repertoire is generated before any antigen is seen, so an infection does not teach the immune system anything new; it selects the rare cell that already matched and expands it into a clone. That is why the response takes days on a first exposure, since the starting population is tiny. Receptors do not reshape themselves to fit, and a response involving every lymphocyte would have no specificity at all.
questions.answerText: An antigen binds the lymphocyte whose receptor already fits and expands it

questions.q: A bacterial toxin circulating in the plasma is bound and inactivated before it can reach its target tissue. Which arm of adaptive immunity did that?
options: Humoral immunity, using antibody against an extracellular target
Cell mediated immunity, using cytotoxic T cells against the toxin
Cell mediated immunity, using helper T cells to digest the toxin
Innate immunity, using natural killer cells to lyse the toxin
questions.why: A dissolved toxin is extracellular, so the tool that reaches it is a soluble one, and antibody binding that blocks the toxin from attaching to its target is neutralization. Cytotoxic T cells kill cells and cannot act on a free molecule. Helper T cells signal and do not digest anything, and NK cells lyse abnormal body cells, not molecules.
questions.answerText: Humoral immunity, using antibody against an extracellular target

questions.q: A body cell infected with a virus is destroyed while neighboring healthy cells are left alone. Which arm did this, and how did it choose the target?
options: Humoral immunity, with antibody dissolving the membrane of the infected cell
Cell mediated immunity, killing any cell found near the site of the infection
Cell mediated immunity, reading foreign fragments displayed on the cell surface
Humoral immunity, with antibody entering the cell and killing the virus inside
questions.why: A cell that is making viral protein puts pieces of it on its surface, and a cytotoxic T cell whose receptor matches that fragment kills only the cells carrying it, which is what spares the neighbors. Antibody cannot cross into a cell, and antibody does not dissolve membranes on its own. Killing everything nearby would describe indiscriminate damage rather than the targeted mechanism this arm uses.
questions.answerText: Cell mediated immunity, reading foreign fragments displayed on the cell surface

questions.q: A transplanted kidney is attacked and destroyed by the recipient's immune system. Which arm carries the main burden of that rejection?
options: Humoral immunity, because antibody is the only defense against foreign tissue
Innate immunity, because rejection begins within seconds of the transplant
Neither arm, because transplanted tissue is not recognized as foreign at all
Cell mediated immunity, because the targets are whole cells from another person
questions.why: Graft cells display surface markers the recipient's T cells read as foreign, so the destruction follows the same route as killing an infected cell: T cell recognition then direct attack. Antibody can contribute to rejection but is not the main mechanism and cannot handle intact cells the way T cells do. Rejection develops over days to weeks, not seconds, and foreign tissue is very much recognized, which is the whole problem.
questions.answerText: Cell mediated immunity, because the targets are whole cells from another person

questions.q: A virus destroys a patient's helper T cells. Predict the effect on antibody production.
options: It stops within a day, because helper T cells make all the antibody
It falls, because B cells depend on helper T signals for a full response
It rises, because B cells are released from helper T cell inhibition
It is unchanged, because B cells work entirely on their own
questions.why: Most antigens require B cells to receive cytokine help from an activated helper T cell before they proliferate and switch to high output antibody secretion, so losing helpers weakens the humoral arm even though the B cells themselves are intact. Helper T cells stimulate rather than inhibit, so removing them cannot raise output. They also secrete no antibody themselves, and the decline develops over months rather than in a day.
questions.answerText: It falls, because B cells depend on helper T signals for a full response

questions.q: Why does antibody alone fail to clear a virus that is already inside a host cell?
options: Antibody cannot enter a cell, so the infected cell itself has to be killed
Antibody is broken down by stomach acid before it can reach the cell
Antibody binds only sugars, and viral particles are built only of protein
Antibody works only after the infected cell has already died on its own
questions.why: Antibody is a large plasma protein and stays outside cells, so it is excellent at catching virus in transit between cells and useless against a virus replicating within one. Clearing that infection needs a cytotoxic T cell to destroy the factory. Stomach acid is irrelevant to antibody in the tissues, antibody binds protein epitopes readily, and waiting for the cell to die would let the virus finish replicating first.
questions.answerText: Antibody cannot enter a cell, so the infected cell itself has to be killed

questions.q: A body cell is displaying a fragment of a protein it made itself from viral instructions. Which cell reads that display?
options: The helper T cell, which inspects only material engulfed from outside
The B cell, which binds only antigen that is free in the tissue fluid
The plasma cell, which reads displays before it secretes its antibody
The cytotoxic T cell, which inspects what a cell is making inside itself
questions.why: Displays of a cell's own internal products are read by cytotoxic T cells, which is how any nucleated cell reports what it is manufacturing and how an infected one gives itself away. Helper T cells read the other display route, the one that carries material an antigen presenting cell took in from outside, so mixing these two up is the classic error here. B cells bind free antigen directly, and plasma cells simply secrete.
questions.answerText: The cytotoxic T cell, which inspects what a cell is making inside itself

questions.q: A bacterium survives inside macrophages rather than in the tissue fluid. Which arm is needed to control it?
options: Humoral immunity, because the target is a bacterium rather than a virus
Neither arm, because a macrophage is part of the innate defenses
Cell mediated immunity, because the target now sits inside a cell
Humoral immunity, because antibody can follow the bacterium into the cell
questions.why: The arm you need is set by where the target is, not by what kind of organism it is, so a bacterium hiding inside a cell is a cell mediated problem just as a virus would be. Antibody cannot follow it in. Classifying by organism type is the trap in this card, and thinking that innate cells are off limits to adaptive help misses the fact that T cells activate macrophages to kill what they hold.
questions.answerText: Cell mediated immunity, because the target now sits inside a cell

questions.q: An infant is born without a thymus but makes B cells normally. Predict what happens to cell mediated immunity and to antibody responses that require helper T cells.
options: Cell mediated immunity fails but every antibody response remains fully normal
Cell mediated immunity is normal while antibody responses fail completely
Both arms stay normal, because B cells can take over the work of T cells
Cell mediated immunity fails and helper dependent antibody responses are weak
questions.why: T cells mature in the thymus, so no thymus means no functional T cells of either kind. That wipes out cell mediated immunity outright and also cripples the humoral responses that need helper T cytokines, even though the B cells themselves are present and healthy. Expecting antibody to be untouched is the common mistake, because it treats the two arms as independent when helper T cells sit upstream of both.
questions.answerText: Cell mediated immunity fails and helper dependent antibody responses are weak

questions.q: Trace the humoral response to a bacterium that enters through a cut. Which order of events is correct?
options: Helper T activation, antibody secretion, antigen presentation, B cell expansion
Antigen presentation, helper T activation, B cell expansion, antibody secretion
B cell expansion, antigen presentation, antibody secretion, helper T activation
Antibody secretion, antigen presentation, helper T activation, B cell expansion
questions.why: An antigen presenting cell has to take up and display the antigen before any T cell can respond, the activated helper then licenses the matching B cell, the B cell clone expands, and only the plasma cells at the end of that chain secrete antibody. Every incorrect sequence here puts antibody or expansion before the recognition step that authorizes it, which is why a primary response takes several days rather than minutes.
questions.answerText: Antigen presentation, helper T activation, B cell expansion, antibody secretion

questions.q: A patient clears extracellular bacteria normally but cannot control viruses inside cells and does not reject a skin graft. Which part of adaptive immunity is defective?
options: The complement system, since complement lyses infected body cells
The phagocytes, since phagocytes are what reject a transplanted graft
The T cell arm, since both failures involve killing whole cells
The B cell arm, since antibody is what clears virus inside cells
questions.why: Working backward from the findings: clearing extracellular bacteria proves antibody and phagocytes are working, and the two failures both require recognizing and destroying intact cells, which is exactly what cytotoxic T cells do. A B cell defect would show up as the opposite pattern, with extracellular infections predominating. Complement lyses bacteria rather than performing targeted killing of body cells, and phagocytes do not drive graft rejection.
questions.answerText: The T cell arm, since both failures involve killing whole cells

questions.q: A vaccine produces good antibody but no cytotoxic T response against a virus that can spread directly from one cell to the next. Predict how well it protects.
options: It blocks virus moving through the fluid but not virus passing cell to cell
It blocks both routes, since antibody reaches a virus wherever the virus goes
It blocks neither route, since antibody plays no part in antiviral defense
It blocks cell to cell spread but not free virus traveling in the blood
questions.why: Antibody patrols the extracellular space, so it intercepts free particles and can prevent the initial infection, but a virus that moves through direct contact between cells never enters that space and is never exposed. Clearing those infected cells requires the cytotoxic T response this vaccine failed to raise. The last option reverses the logic exactly, giving antibody access to the one route it cannot reach.
questions.answerText: It blocks virus moving through the fluid but not virus passing cell to cell

questions.q: How many polypeptide chains build one antibody monomer, and of which kinds?
options: Four chains, two heavy and two light
Two chains, one heavy and one light
Six chains, four heavy and two light
Four chains, all four the same size
questions.why: Two long heavy chains pair with each other and each picks up a short light chain, giving the Y shaped monomer with four chains in total. Two chains would give only half a Y and only one binding site. Six chains and four identical chains do not match the symmetric two arm structure that lets a single antibody grip two identical epitopes at once.
questions.answerText: Four chains, two heavy and two light

questions.q: Which part of the antibody actually binds the antigen?
options: The hinge that sits between the two arms
The sugar groups attached to the stem
The variable regions at the tips of the arms
The constant region that makes up the stem
questions.why: The amino acid sequence at the arm tips differs from one antibody clone to the next, and that variability is what creates a pocket shaped for one epitope. The constant region of the stem is identical within a class and is read by phagocytes and complement rather than by antigen. The hinge sets how widely the arms can spread, and the attached sugars do not form the binding pocket.
questions.answerText: The variable regions at the tips of the arms

questions.q: How many antigen binding sites does a single antibody monomer have?
options: One
Two
Four
Ten
questions.why: Each arm of the Y carries one binding site, so a monomer such as IgG has two, and both sites bind the same epitope. Ten is the count for an IgM pentamer, which is five monomers joined together, so it is a real number for a real antibody but not for a monomer. One site would make bridging two targets impossible, which is why a monovalent fragment cannot agglutinate.
questions.answerText: Two

questions.q: What does the constant region of the heavy chain determine?
options: How many antigen binding sites the monomer will carry
Whether the antibody folds correctly after it is made
The antibody class and the effector mechanisms it can trigger
Which particular antigen the antibody will be able to bind
questions.why: The stem is the handle: its sequence defines the class as IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, or IgD, and it decides whether complement can be fixed, whether a phagocyte receptor can bind it, and where the antibody is distributed. Antigen specificity comes from the variable tips instead. The number of binding sites depends on how many monomers join, not on the class alone, and folding is not what the constant region encodes.
questions.answerText: The antibody class and the effector mechanisms it can trigger

questions.q: What is an epitope?
options: The small region of an antigen that an antibody actually binds
The binding pocket formed at the tip of the antibody arm
Any whole foreign protein that the body recognizes as nonself
The carbohydrate group that establishes the antibody class
questions.why: An antigen is usually a large molecule with several distinct surface patches, and each patch that a specific antibody can bind is an epitope, which is why one protein can raise several different antibodies. The pocket on the antibody side is the binding site, not the epitope, and swapping those two terms is the most common slip here. The whole molecule is the antigen rather than the epitope.
questions.answerText: The small region of an antigen that an antibody actually binds

questions.q: Which antibody class appears first in a primary response and circulates as a pentamer?
options: IgE
IgM
IgG
IgA
questions.why: IgM is the first class a newly activated B cell secretes, and joining five monomers gives it ten binding sites, which makes it very effective at clumping antigen and at fixing complement even before affinity has improved. IgG appears later and dominates the secondary response. IgA is the secretory class of mucous surfaces and IgE is the class bound to mast cells.
questions.answerText: IgM

questions.q: Which antibody class is most abundant in plasma and is the only one that crosses the placenta?
options: IgM
IgA
IgD
IgG
questions.why: IgG makes up roughly three quarters of plasma antibody, and its stem is recognized by a transport receptor in the placenta, so a fetus receives the mother's IgG before birth. IgM is too large a molecule to cross and stays in the bloodstream. IgA crosses into milk and other secretions rather than the placenta, and IgD sits on B cell surfaces with little role in plasma.
questions.answerText: IgG

questions.q: Which antibody mechanism describes antibody binding a toxin so that the toxin cannot attach to a host cell?
options: Agglutination
Opsonization
Complement fixation
Neutralization
questions.why: Neutralization is pure blockade: the antibody covers the part of the toxin or virus that would have docked onto a cell, so the target is harmless even though nothing has been destroyed. Agglutination clumps particles together, opsonization tags a target for a phagocyte, and complement fixation recruits the cascade to lyse it. All four are antibody functions, so the distinction is what each one does to the target.
questions.answerText: Neutralization

questions.q: Anti-A serum is mixed with a drop of a patient's blood on a slide and the red cells clump. Which mechanism produced the clumping, and what does the result tell you?
options: Neutralization, so those red cells carry the A antigen
Agglutination, so those red cells lack the A antigen
Precipitation, so soluble A antigen is present in the plasma
Agglutination, so those red cells carry the A antigen
questions.why: Each antibody bridges two cells that both carry the epitope it binds, and thousands of such bridges form the visible clumps, so clumping with anti-A serum means the A antigen is on those cells. Neutralization blocks a toxin and produces nothing visible. Precipitation is the same bridging process acting on dissolved antigen rather than on cells, so it would not clump red cells.
questions.answerText: Agglutination, so those red cells carry the A antigen

questions.q: Why can a single antibody molecule link two separate bacterial cells together?
options: Because complement joins two antibody molecules end to end
Because it has two identical binding sites, one on each arm
Because its stem region binds a second bacterium directly
Because it changes shape to grip a new epitope after the first
questions.why: Both arms of a monomer carry the same specificity, so if two cells display the same epitope one antibody can hold one on each arm, and many antibodies doing this at once build a lattice. The stem binds phagocyte receptors and complement, not antigen. An antibody does not change its specificity after binding, and complement joining molecules together is not how a lattice forms.
questions.answerText: Because it has two identical binding sites, one on each arm

questions.q: Antibody coats a bacterium. What does a neutrophil bind in order to engulf it more efficiently?
options: The bare bacterial surface between antibodies
The hinge segments where the arms bend
The stem regions of the bound antibodies
The variable tips that are holding the antigen
questions.why: Once the arms are occupied by antigen, the stems all point outward, and the phagocyte has receptors for exactly that region, so the coated bacterium is easy to grasp. That is opsonization by antibody, and it is why coating a slippery encapsulated organism makes such a difference. The variable tips are already engaged with the antigen, and the bare surface is what the phagocyte struggled with in the first place.
questions.answerText: The stem regions of the bound antibodies

questions.q: Antibody binds a bacterial surface and complement is then activated at that spot. What happens to the bacterium?
options: Complement assembles a pore in its membrane, and it lyses
Complement digests the bacterial DNA and stops replication
Complement pulls the antibody off and recycles it for reuse
Complement blocks the bacterium from binding to host cells
questions.why: Antibody bound to a surface exposes a site on its stem that starts the classical complement pathway, and the cascade ends in a membrane attack complex that opens the cell to water and ions. Complement acts on the membrane, not on DNA. It does not remove the antibody, and blocking attachment to host cells is neutralization, which the antibody accomplishes on its own without complement.
questions.answerText: Complement assembles a pore in its membrane, and it lyses

questions.q: A mother's milk protects the lining of her infant's gut. Which antibody class does that, and where does it act?
options: IgM, acting on the lymph draining away from the intestine
IgA, acting on the mucosal surface facing the gut lumen
IgG, acting inside the infant's bloodstream after absorption
IgE, acting on mast cells within the wall of the intestine
questions.why: IgA is the class exported into secretions, including milk, saliva, and gut and airway mucus, and it works on the surface by blocking pathogens from ever attaching to the epithelium. IgG is the class transferred across the placenta into fetal blood, which is a different route for a different fluid. IgE arms mast cells for allergic responses, and IgM stays largely within the bloodstream.
questions.answerText: IgA, acting on the mucosal surface facing the gut lumen

questions.q: A patient's mast cells release histamine seconds after an antigen appears. Which antibody class was already bound to those mast cells?
options: IgM
IgA
IgE
IgG
questions.why: IgE is the one class whose stem binds mast cells and basophils, so it sits waiting on the cell surface long before the antigen arrives; when antigen links two of these antibodies together the cell degranulates immediately. IgG and IgM are free in plasma and produce slower responses involving complement and phagocytes. IgA is in secretions and does not arm mast cells.
questions.answerText: IgE

questions.q: An enzyme cuts antibodies at the hinge, separating the two arms from the stem. Predict which antibody functions are kept and which are lost.
options: Antigen binding is kept, while complement fixation and phagocyte binding are lost
Antigen binding is lost, while complement fixation and phagocyte binding remain
Both antigen binding and every effector function are lost after the cut
Both antigen binding and every effector function survive the cut intact
questions.why: Function follows structure here: the binding pockets live in the arms and survive the cut, while the recognition surfaces that complement and phagocyte receptors read live in the stem and are separated away. The freed arms can still neutralize a toxin but can no longer recruit anything to destroy it.
