Losing binding while keeping effector function would require the opposite anatomy, with antigen recognized by the stem.
questions.answerText: Antigen binding is kept, while complement fixation and phagocyte binding are lost

questions.q: A laboratory prepares antibody fragments that each carry only one binding site. Predict their effect on neutralizing a toxin and on agglutinating bacteria.
options: They still agglutinate bacteria but can no longer neutralize the toxin
They perform both functions as well as the intact antibody does
They perform neither function, since one site cannot bind an epitope
They still neutralize the toxin but can no longer agglutinate bacteria
questions.why: Neutralization needs only occupancy: covering the active part of a toxin with one binding site is enough. Agglutination needs bridging, and bridging needs at least two sites on the same molecule so that two particles can be held together. A single site binds an epitope perfectly well, so the fragment is not useless, it has just lost every function that depended on holding two things at once.
questions.answerText: They still neutralize the toxin but can no longer agglutinate bacteria

questions.q: IgM has ten binding sites and IgG has two. Predict which clumps bacteria more efficiently per molecule, and why.
options: IgM, because its binding sites each hold antigen far more tightly
IgG, because clumping depends on the stem region rather than the arms
IgM, because each molecule can bridge many more cells at one time
IgG, because its smaller size lets it reach between cells more easily
questions.why: Clumping is a bridging problem, so the number of sites per molecule is what matters most, and a pentamer with ten sites builds a lattice with far fewer molecules than a monomer with two. IgM achieves this despite individual sites that bind less tightly than mature IgG sites, which is exactly why the site count and not the affinity is the deciding factor. The stem plays no part in holding antigen.
questions.answerText: IgM, because each molecule can bridge many more cells at one time

questions.q: A patient's antibodies bind their antigen normally but never activate complement. Working back from that result, which region is abnormal?
options: The hinge, which controls only how widely the two arms can spread
The constant region of the heavy chain, which complement has to bind
The variable region at the arm tips, which forms the binding pocket
The light chain, which by itself creates the antigen binding pocket
questions.why: Normal antigen binding proves the variable tips are intact, so the fault has to be downstream of binding, in the stem region that the first complement protein docks onto. A variable region defect would have shown up as failed binding instead. The light chain contributes to the pocket but does not form it alone, and a hinge defect would change flexibility and bridging rather than abolish complement activation outright.
questions.answerText: The constant region of the heavy chain, which complement has to bind

questions.q: About how long after a first exposure does antibody become measurable in the plasma?
options: About 6 months
Within a few minutes
About 3 to 6 days
About 6 to 8 weeks
questions.why: The lag of the primary response is the time needed to find the one matching lymphocyte, activate it, expand the clone, and differentiate plasma cells, which takes several days and peaks around day 10 to 14. Minutes would describe an innate response or a preformed passive antibody. Weeks and months are far too long, which matters because it means a first infection is often over before antibody peaks.
questions.answerText: About 3 to 6 days

questions.q: How quickly does a secondary response produce antibody after a repeat exposure?
options: After about two weeks of steady exposure
Only after a full month has passed
Within hours to two or three days
After the same 3 to 6 day lag as the first time
questions.why: Memory cells are already numerous and already specific, so the slow search and expansion phase of the primary response is skipped and antibody rises almost immediately. Repeating the original lag would mean no memory had formed at all. Longer delays describe no immune system a person could survive with, and the whole point of vaccination is buying this speed in advance.
questions.answerText: Within hours to two or three days

questions.q: Which antibody class dominates the secondary response?
options: IgM
IgE
IgD
IgG
questions.why: Memory B cells have already switched their heavy chain constant region, so on a repeat exposure they secrete mostly IgG, which is longer lived in plasma and reaches the tissues more readily than IgM. IgM dominates the primary response and marks a recent first exposure, which is why the two classes are useful for dating an infection. IgE and IgD are minor in quantity and serve other roles.
questions.answerText: IgG

questions.q: What is a memory B cell?
options: A long lived descendant of an activated clone waiting for the same antigen
A plasma cell that keeps secreting antibody for the rest of a lifetime
A cell that stores antibody inside itself instead of releasing it
A cell that keeps a written record of every antigen the body has met
questions.why: When a clone expands, some daughters differentiate into antibody factories and others stay as small resting cells that persist for years, so the clone size for that one antigen is permanently larger. Plasma cells are short lived by comparison, which is why circulating antibody titer falls after an infection while protection persists. Memory cells do not stockpile antibody, they stand ready to make it.
questions.answerText: A long lived descendant of an activated clone waiting for the same antigen

questions.q: What defines active immunity?
options: The person's own immune system responds and forms lasting memory
Ready made antibody is transferred in from another person or animal
Innate barriers block the pathogen before any lymphocyte is involved
A drug suppresses the pathogen while the immune system stays idle
questions.why: Active means the person did the work: antigen entered, lymphocytes were selected and expanded, and memory cells remain afterward. Transferred antibody is passive immunity, protective right away but leaving nothing behind. Innate barriers are not immunity in this sense at all, and a drug that clears an organism does not create any immunological memory.
questions.answerText: The person's own immune system responds and forms lasting memory

questions.q: What defines passive immunity?
options: Phagocytes are stimulated to clear the pathogen without any antibody
Ready made antibody is transferred in, giving prompt short lived protection
The person makes antibody after a weakened form of the pathogen is given
Memory cells are transferred so the recipient responds faster next time
questions.why: In passive immunity the recipient contributes nothing but a bloodstream: the antibody works from the moment it arrives and then degrades over weeks, leaving no memory cells and no lasting protection. Making antibody after a weakened pathogen is artificial active immunity, the definition of vaccination. Clinical passive transfer moves antibody rather than cells, and phagocyte stimulation is not what the term describes.
questions.answerText: Ready made antibody is transferred in, giving prompt short lived protection

questions.q: A newborn is protected for several months by antibody received across the placenta. Which type of immunity is that?
options: Natural active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
Artificial active immunity
Natural passive immunity
questions.why: It is passive because the antibody came from the mother rather than from the infant's own response, and natural because it happened without any medical intervention. Natural active would mean the infant caught an infection and responded. Artificial passive covers the same transfer done deliberately, as with an injection of immune globulin, and artificial active is vaccination.
questions.answerText: Natural passive immunity

questions.q: A person receives a vaccine containing an inactivated virus. Which type of immunity does this produce?
options: Natural passive immunity
Artificial active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
Natural active immunity
questions.why: Active because the recipient's own lymphocytes recognize the antigen and build memory, and artificial because the exposure was deliberately arranged rather than an infection. Artificial passive would mean receiving antibody rather than antigen. Natural active immunity comes from actually catching the disease, which produces the same kind of memory at a much higher cost.
questions.answerText: Artificial active immunity

questions.q: A patient bitten by a venomous snake is given antivenom containing antibodies against the venom. Predict when protection begins and whether memory forms.
options: Protection is immediate and no memory forms afterward
Protection begins in about a week and lasting memory forms
Protection is immediate and lasting memory forms afterward
Protection begins in about a week and no memory forms
questions.why: Transferred antibody is already made, so it starts neutralizing venom as soon as it circulates, which is the entire reason passive transfer is used in an emergency. Nothing in the patient's own lymphocyte population has been selected or expanded, so once the transferred protein degrades over the following weeks, protection ends. A second bite later would find the patient no better prepared than the first.
questions.answerText: Protection is immediate and no memory forms afterward

questions.q: A child recovers from chickenpox and is protected for decades afterward. Which type of immunity did the illness produce?
options: Natural passive immunity
Artificial active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
Natural active immunity
questions.why: The child's own lymphocytes met the virus, expanded, and left memory cells behind, so the immunity is active, and because the exposure came from ordinary infection rather than a clinic, it is natural. Passive labels would require antibody arriving from someone else, which would not last decades. Artificial active would mean the same memory produced by a vaccine instead of by the disease.
questions.answerText: Natural active immunity

questions.q: Why does a booster dose of a vaccine raise antibody higher than the first dose did?
options: The second dose is given by a route that the body absorbs more quickly
The first dose left a much larger population of memory cells for that antigen
The second dose always contains a larger quantity of the antigen
The first dose left circulating antibody that adds to the second response
questions.why: Response size scales with how many matching lymphocytes are available at the moment of exposure, and the first dose converted a handful of cells into a large standing memory clone. Booster doses are not larger in antigen content, and the leftover antibody from the first dose is usually low and does not explain a ten fold or greater rise. Route of administration does not change the size of the clone that responds.
questions.answerText: The first dose left a much larger population of memory cells for that antigen

questions.q: Maternal antibody in an infant falls to very low levels by about six months of age. What does this predict about the infant's susceptibility?
options: Susceptibility rises, because borrowed protection fades and left no memory
Susceptibility falls, because the infant has now formed its own memory cells
Susceptibility stays unchanged, because memory cells came across with the antibody
Susceptibility rises briefly and then falls again without any further exposure
questions.why: Placental transfer moves antibody protein, not cells, so when that protein degrades the infant has nothing left over from it, and this window is exactly why the childhood vaccination schedule begins when it does. Forming memory would require the infant's own response to an antigen. Protection cannot return on its own without exposure to the antigen or another vaccine.
questions.answerText: Susceptibility rises, because borrowed protection fades and left no memory

questions.q: A patient receives immune globulin against hepatitis A after an exposure. If they are exposed again two years later, what will their response be?
options: No response at all, because the earlier globulin suppressed their immunity
An immediate response, because some of the transferred antibody still remains
A primary response, because the transferred antibody left no memory behind
A secondary response, because the transferred antibody trained their B cells
questions.why: Passive antibody protects while it is present and teaches nothing, so two years later the patient meets that virus as if for the first time, with the full several day lag. Transferred antibody does not instruct B cells. It also does not permanently suppress immunity, and injected immunoglobulin is gone within a few months, far short of two years.
questions.answerText: A primary response, because the transferred antibody left no memory behind

questions.q: A first vaccine dose raises antibody titer to 100 units and a booster raises it to 1600 units. What does that sixteen fold difference reflect?
options: A change in the antigen itself between the first and second injections
A far larger population of antigen specific cells responding this time
A stronger innate response to the second injection at the same site
A slower breakdown of antibody protein after the second dose is given
questions.why: The magnitude of an antibody response tracks the number of responding cells, and clonal expansion during the first dose left thousands of memory cells where there had been very few. Innate responses do not produce antigen specific antibody. Antibody breakdown rates do not change with dose number, and the antigen in a booster is deliberately the same as in the first dose.
questions.answerText: A far larger population of antigen specific cells responding this time

questions.q: Why does a vaccine given today not protect a traveler who leaves tomorrow?
options: Vaccines only work if they are given after exposure rather than before
The antigen in a vaccine has to be swallowed to reach the immune system
Antibody made from a vaccine is destroyed during the first day after injection
Active immunity needs days to weeks for clonal expansion and antibody output
questions.why: A vaccine supplies antigen, not protection, and the recipient still has to run the primary response, which takes about two weeks to reach useful titer. If protection is needed immediately, the only option is passive transfer of preformed antibody. Vaccines are given before exposure precisely because of this lag, and injected antigen reaches lymph nodes without needing to be swallowed.
questions.answerText: Active immunity needs days to weeks for clonal expansion and antibody output

questions.q: After a high risk animal bite a patient is given both immune globulin against rabies and the rabies vaccine. Explain what each contributes to protection over time.
options: The globulin protects immediately while the vaccine builds protection over weeks
The vaccine protects immediately while the globulin builds protection over weeks
Both protect immediately, so giving the two together is simply a precaution
Both take weeks to work, so protection cannot begin until the second week
questions.why: The two are given together because they cover different parts of the same timeline: preformed antibody neutralizes virus from the moment it is injected but fades, while the vaccine antigen starts a primary response that takes about two weeks and then persists as memory. Reversing them misreads which one is antibody and which is antigen. If both worked immediately, or neither did, there would be no reason to give two products at once.
questions.answerText: The globulin protects immediately while the vaccine builds protection over weeks

questions.q: Antibody appears on day 5 after a first exposure, peaks on day 12, is mostly IgM, and falls by day 30. A second exposure on day 60 gives antibody by day 2, ten times higher, mostly IgG. What accounts for the differences?
options: A larger dose of antigen on the second exposure than on the first exposure
Memory cells from the first exposure, numerous and already class switched
Antibody left over from the first exposure that was reactivated by the antigen
A stronger innate response on the second exposure that produced the IgG
questions.why: Three features change together, and one mechanism explains all three: memory cells are present in large numbers so the lag shortens and the peak rises, and they have already switched their heavy chain so the output is IgG rather than IgM. Leftover antibody had already fallen by day 30 and antibody molecules cannot be reactivated. Innate responses never make antibody, and nothing in the description says the dose changed.
questions.answerText: Memory cells from the first exposure, numerous and already class switched

questions.q: A patient who cannot make B cells receives an infusion of pooled immune globulin every four weeks. Predict their protection between infusions and whether they will ever need to stop.
options: Unprotected between doses, because transferred antibody acts only on the day given
Protected permanently after several doses, because the antibody stimulates B cells
Protected while the antibody lasts, no memory forms, and infusions go on
Protected while the antibody lasts, and memory builds so the infusions can stop
questions.why: Passive antibody is a supply, not a lesson: it works from the moment it is given, degrades over a few weeks, and leaves no cells behind, so the schedule is set by the half life of the protein rather than by any developing response. A patient with no B cells cannot make memory, so the treatment cannot become self sustaining. The antibody does last between doses, which is exactly why a four week interval works.
questions.answerText: Protected while the antibody lasts, no memory forms, and infusions go on

questions.q: A person exposed to the same virus twice became ill the first time but not the second, although their antibody titer was near zero just before the second exposure. Explain the protection.
options: Standing antibody must have been present but was too low for the test to detect
Innate defenses were permanently strengthened by the first infection
The virus had weakened between the first and the second exposure
Memory cells responded within a day or two, before the virus could establish itself
questions.why: Protection does not require antibody circulating at all times; it requires the ability to produce antibody faster than the pathogen can gain ground, and a memory clone does that within a couple of days. This is why a low titer years after vaccination does not necessarily mean protection has been lost. Innate defenses do not strengthen with experience, and nothing here suggests the virus itself changed.
questions.answerText: Memory cells responded within a day or two, before the virus could establish itself

questions.q: What is the immune system doing wrong in an allergy?
options: It is mounting a strong response against a harmless foreign substance
It is attacking the body's own tissues as though they were foreign
It is failing to respond because a needed component is missing
It is responding normally but far too slowly to be of any use
questions.why: In allergy the machinery works, the specificity works, and the target is genuinely foreign; the error is that the antigen posed no threat, so the damage comes from the response rather than from the pollen or the peanut. Attacking self tissue is autoimmunity and failing for lack of a component is immunodeficiency. Sorting these three by what has gone wrong is the whole of this competency.
questions.answerText: It is mounting a strong response against a harmless foreign substance

questions.q: What is the immune system doing wrong in an autoimmune disease?
options: It is overreacting to a harmless substance from outside the body
It cannot produce enough lymphocytes to fight ordinary infections
It responds only to antigens it has already encountered once before
It has lost tolerance and is attacking the body's own tissues
questions.why: Self tolerance is normally established by removing or silencing lymphocytes whose receptors match self molecules, and autoimmunity is the failure of that screening, so a normal immune attack is aimed at the wrong tissue. Overreacting to an outside antigen is allergy, in which the target really is foreign. A shortage of lymphocytes describes immunodeficiency, and responding to previously seen antigens is normal memory.
questions.answerText: It has lost tolerance and is attacking the body's own tissues

questions.q: What is the immune system doing wrong in an immunodeficiency?
options: A response is aimed at a self antigen instead of a foreign one
A response is far larger than the threat from the antigen warrants
A response is aimed at the correct antigen but in the wrong tissue
A component is missing or not working, so responses are too weak
questions.why: Immunodeficiency is a failure of capacity: a missing cell type, antibody class, or complement protein leaves a gap, and the patient presents with infections that a normal immune system would clear. Misdirected responses against self are autoimmunity and oversized responses to harmless antigens are allergy, so the three categories differ by whether the problem is too little, misaimed, or too much.
questions.answerText: A component is missing or not working, so responses are too weak

questions.q: Which combination triggers the immediate symptoms of an allergic reaction?
options: IgM bound to red cells, which release histamine when complement binds
IgA bound to plasma cells, which release cytokines when antigen binds
IgE bound to mast cells, which release histamine when antigen binds
IgG bound to neutrophils, which release lysozyme when antigen binds
questions.why: Sensitization puts IgE on mast cell surfaces during the first exposure, and on a later exposure the antigen bridges two of those antibodies and the cell degranulates within seconds, releasing histamine and producing the familiar symptoms. Neutrophils and red cells do not carry the granules or the receptors involved. Plasma cells secrete antibody and do not display it on their surface for this purpose.
questions.answerText: IgE bound to mast cells, which release histamine when antigen binds

questions.q: What happens to blood vessels and airways during anaphylaxis?
options: Vessels dilate and airway smooth muscle relaxes at the same time
Vessels constrict and leak while airway smooth muscle constricts
Vessels dilate and leak while airway smooth muscle constricts
Vessels constrict while airway smooth muscle relaxes and opens
questions.why: Anaphylaxis is a local allergic response occurring body wide, so the histamine effects you would see in one swollen finger happen everywhere at once: widespread vasodilation and leak drop blood pressure while bronchoconstriction closes the airway. Vasoconstriction and bronchodilation are the opposite pattern and are what treatment aims to restore. The danger comes from both systems failing at once.
questions.answerText: Vessels dilate and leak while airway smooth muscle constricts

questions.q: Which cell does HIV infect and destroy?
options: The red blood cell
The helper T cell
The plasma cell
The neutrophil
questions.why: HIV enters cells carrying the CD4 surface protein, and the helper T cell is the main one, which is why a virus that infects a single cell type dismantles so much of the immune system. Plasma cells and neutrophils are not the virus target, though both function poorly once helper T support is gone. Red cells have no nucleus and cannot support viral replication.
questions.answerText: The helper T cell

questions.q: A patient sneezes and develops watery eyes every spring when tree pollen is in the air. Classify this and name the error.
options: Immunodeficiency, since the response fails to clear the pollen entirely
A normal response, since pollen is foreign and should be attacked hard
Allergy, since a strong response is aimed at a harmless foreign antigen
Autoimmunity, since the response is aimed at the patient's own tissue
questions.why: Pollen is foreign but harmless, and the symptoms come entirely from the patient's own histamine release rather than from anything the pollen does, which is the definition of an allergic response. The target is not self, so this is not autoimmunity. It is not immunodeficiency either, since the response is vigorous rather than weak, and calling it normal ignores the fact that most people inhale pollen with no symptoms at all.
questions.answerText: Allergy, since a strong response is aimed at a harmless foreign antigen

questions.q: A patient's blood contains antibodies that bind and damage their own thyroid cells. Classify this and name the error.
options: Autoimmunity, since self tolerance for a thyroid antigen has failed
Allergy, since the antibody was raised against an outside substance
Immunodeficiency, since the thyroid can no longer defend itself
A normal response, since damaged cells are always targeted this way
questions.why: The antibody is specific, well made, and working exactly as designed; the failure is in tolerance, because a B cell clone that should have been eliminated for recognizing a self antigen was allowed to mature. Allergy would require the antigen to come from outside the body. The immune system here is too active rather than deficient, and healthy self tissue is not normally attacked by antibody.
questions.answerText: Autoimmunity, since self tolerance for a thyroid antigen has failed

questions.q: A young child has repeated bacterial infections and blood tests show almost no antibody of any class. Classify this and name the error.
options: Autoimmunity, since antibody is being destroyed by the patient's own cells
Allergy, since the repeated infections have sensitized the child's mast cells
A normal finding, since young children do not produce antibody at all
Immunodeficiency, since a needed component of the response is absent
questions.why: Recurrent infection plus a missing component is the signature of immunodeficiency, and the absent antibody points to the B cell arm specifically, which fits the bacterial pattern of infection. Nothing here describes an attack on self tissue or a response to a harmless antigen. Children do produce their own antibody, beginning in the first months of life as maternal antibody fades, so this is not a normal age related finding.
questions.answerText: Immunodeficiency, since a needed component of the response is absent

questions.q: Predict what happens to arterial blood pressure during anaphylaxis, and why.
options: It falls, because dilation and fluid leak cut both resistance and volume
It rises, because the immune response raises cardiac output sharply
It stays steady, because histamine acts on airways rather than vessels
It falls, because histamine directly stops the heart from contracting
questions.why: Two histamine effects push pressure the same direction at once: dilating arterioles everywhere lowers total peripheral resistance, and increased capillary permeability moves plasma into the tissues so venous return falls too. Since pressure depends on both, the drop can be severe. Histamine acts strongly on vessels as well as airways, and the fall is a vascular problem rather than a failure of cardiac contraction.
questions.answerText: It falls, because dilation and fluid leak cut both resistance and volume

questions.q: Epinephrine reverses the dangerous changes of anaphylaxis. Which two actions does it provide?
options: Vasodilation to improve perfusion and bronchoconstriction to trap more oxygen
Vasoconstriction to raise blood pressure and bronchodilation to open the airway
Vasodilation to improve tissue perfusion and bronchodilation to open the airway
Vasoconstriction to raise blood pressure and bronchoconstriction to slow airflow
questions.why: Epinephrine acts on alpha receptors in vascular smooth muscle to constrict vessels and on beta receptors in airway smooth muscle to relax them, which is precisely the opposite of what histamine did to each tissue. Adding more vasodilation would deepen the fall in pressure. Bronchoconstriction would worsen the airway obstruction, and trapping air is not a benefit in any respiratory situation.
questions.answerText: Vasoconstriction to raise blood pressure and bronchodilation to open the airway

questions.q: Three patients: the first makes antibody against their own joint tissue, the second collapses minutes after eating peanut, the third has fungal infections that never fully clear. Classify them in order.
options: Autoimmunity, immunodeficiency, allergy
Autoimmunity, allergy, immunodeficiency
Allergy, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency
Immunodeficiency, allergy, autoimmunity
questions.why: Sort by what is wrong rather than by how sick the patient looks. Antibody against self tissue is a tolerance failure, a violent response within minutes of a harmless food is an IgE driven allergy, and infections that a normal immune system would clear point to a missing or failing component. Persistent fungal infection in particular suggests a T cell problem, since cell mediated immunity handles those organisms.
questions.answerText: Autoimmunity, allergy, immunodeficiency

questions.q: As HIV destroys helper T cells over years, predict what happens to cell mediated immunity and to antibody responses, and what the patient develops as a result.
options: Only cell mediated immunity weakens, so antibody responses stay fully normal
Only antibody responses weaken, so cell mediated immunity stays fully normal
Both arms strengthen at first, so the patient resists infection unusually well
Both arms weaken and infections appear that a healthy system would clear
questions.why: The helper T cell sits upstream of both arms, licensing cytotoxic T cells and providing the cytokines most B cells need, so destroying it produces a combined deficiency even though only one cell type is infected. That is why the illnesses that follow include organisms handled by antibody and organisms handled by cell mediated immunity. Expecting only one arm to fail underestimates how central the helper T cell is.
questions.answerText: Both arms weaken and infections appear that a healthy system would clear

questions.q: A patient has normal antibody levels, normal T cell counts, and no unusual infections, but has painful inflamed joints and antibodies in the blood that bind their own cartilage. Working from these findings, classify the disorder.
options: Allergy, since the joint inflammation follows exposure to an outside antigen
Two disorders at once, since inflammation and antibody cannot share one cause
Autoimmunity, since the response is intact and specific but directed at self
Immunodeficiency, since inflamed joints show the defenses cannot cope
questions.why: Normal counts and no unusual infections rule out immunodeficiency, and nothing foreign is described, which rules out allergy, leaving self directed antibody as the finding that explains the joint damage. The inflammation is the expected consequence of that antibody binding tissue and recruiting the inflammatory response, so one mechanism accounts for both findings rather than two separate disorders.
questions.answerText: Autoimmunity, since the response is intact and specific but directed at self
